rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when channel inventory is clean, unit volumes are growing in double digits, and metal prices are stable or falling; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a false dawn.

call.headline: Early up-cycle after two washed-out summers. Prefer appliance brand owners with clean channels and the lifestyle brands with pricing power; hold contract makers for the PLI volume story but do not pay for margins they will never have.
points: The GST cut on ACs, large TVs and dishwashers and a cleared channel have reset demand, so volumes should compound off a low base.
Copper and the rupee are still against the brand owners, so margin recovery lags volume recovery by a quarter or two.
Compressor and component localisation under the next PLI leg is a multi-year capex theme, not a quarterly one.
would_change: A third washed-out summer that refills the channel
A copper spike or a sharply weaker rupee that outruns price hikes
A reversal of the GST cut or a PLI target miss at a large contract maker

explainer.tell_a_friend: Consumer durables companies make or brand the things a household buys every few years on EMI: the air-conditioner, the fridge, the fan, the TV, the wedding gold. There are three kinds. Brand owners design and market the box and buy much of it from someone else; they live on summer heat, dealer shelf space and the copper price. Contract makers assemble phones and ACs for brands at a thin, fixed margin and win only on volume, which the PLI scheme has handed them since 2021. Lifestyle brands like a jeweller or a premium innerwear maker set their own price and keep the most. The cycle runs on two clocks: the summer and the festive quarter decide each year, while commodities, interest rates and policy set the longer swing. The 2022 and 2024 summers were booms, 2023 and 2025 were washouts, and then a GST cut before Diwali 2025 reset demand. Today the channel is clean and volumes are recovering, but copper is still high. Watch channel inventory after each season, gross margin, and the copper price.

glossary.def: Household goods that last years: appliances, electronics, furniture, jewellery and watches. Called white goods when they are large kitchen or laundry appliances.
A split or window air-conditioner for one room. The category that makes or breaks an Indian durables summer.
Assembling a product for a brand that sells it under its own name. EMS builds the brand's design; ODM designs it too.
Production-linked incentive: a government cash payment of roughly 4-6% on incremental sales of goods made in India, for phones, IT hardware, AC and LED components.
Global brands adding a second manufacturing base outside China, often India.
Sales minus raw materials and components, divided by sales. The commodity squeeze shows here first.
Finished goods sitting with distributors and dealers, already sold by the company but not yet to a household.
Pushing stock onto dealers at quarter-end to book sales. Shows up as rising receivable days.
Sales per rupee of plant and equipment. A contract maker turning assets 6 times a year can live on a 3% margin.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.
Money tied up in inventory and unpaid dealer bills, minus unpaid supplier bills. Swings with the season.
New plant spending divided by the yearly wear charge. Above 1 means building, near 1 means coasting.
The Bureau of Energy Efficiency's 1-to-5 star label on appliances. The scale is tightened every couple of years, so last year's 5-star becomes this year's 3-star.
An AC whose compressor runs at variable speed and uses less power. Now most of the market.
A rule that a product, including an imported one, must meet an Indian standard before it can be sold. Blocks cheap imports.
The global treaty phasing down HFC refrigerant gases. India's freeze starts in 2028, forcing new gases and compressors.
The rule that a brand must collect and recycle a set share of the e-waste from what it sold.
BIS certification of gold purity with a unique six-digit ID per piece, mandatory since 2021-23. Favours organised jewellers.
Jewellers borrow gold from banks instead of buying it, paying a lease rate; the cost sits in the interest line.
The weight of gold sold. When the price rallies, sales in rupees rise while grammage falls.
The goods and services tax rate band. ACs and large TVs moved from the 28% slab to 18% in 2025.
Big electronics chains like Croma, Reliance Digital and Vijay Sales, which negotiate hard on margins.
An instalment plan where the brand or financier absorbs the interest. Most big-ticket purchases in India use one.

c1.story:
Walk into any Indian home and you can read its last decade of big decisions off the walls. The split AC bought the summer the kids started complaining. The double-door fridge that replaced the single-door one. The ceiling fans that came with the flat. The television upgraded for a World Cup. And, in a locker somewhere, the wedding gold. These are consumer durables: things a family buys once every few years, often on an EMI, and talks about at dinner for a week.

The industry that sells them looks like one sector on a screener. It is really three businesses that happen to share a showroom.

The first is the appliance brand owner. Think Voltas, Blue Star, LG, Whirlpool. Its real assets are a name, a dealer network and a service van that turns up when the compressor dies in May. Increasingly, it does not even build the whole box; a contract maker does. The second is that contract maker: Dixon, Amber, PG Electroplast. It assembles phones, televisions, ACs and washing machines for brands that put their own logo on the front. It earns a thin, fixed slice per unit and makes its money by making a staggering number of units. The third is the lifestyle brand: Titan's Tanishq, Page's Jockey innerwear, Welspun's towels, Doms pencils. Here the customer pays for the name on the box, and the company sets the price.

Why does this matter so much? Because the same headline lands differently behind each door. A copper spike hurts the brand owner, whose AC is full of copper tubing, but barely touches the contract maker, which passes metal costs straight through to the brand. A lost smartphone account is a disaster for the contract maker and irrelevant to Titan. A gold rally inflates Tanishq's sales while doing nothing for a fan maker.

A single-digit margin is normal for a brand owner, the whole model for a contract maker, and a red flag for a lifestyle brand.

So before you look at a single ratio, ask which door the company walks through. Several straddle: LG builds much of what it sells, Crompton and V-Guard mix fans, pumps and kitchen appliances. That is fine. It just means the market will reprice each piece of the business at a different moment.
c1.read:
The three tiles are the three doors. Read each from top to bottom, and read the bar before anything else.

  • The name and the line under it describe how the company makes money: designing and marketing an appliance it often buys from someone else, assembling for brands at a fixed margin under the PLI scheme, or owning both the brand and the shop.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Notice that the brand-owner tile holds the familiar cooling names, while the contract tile holds names most households have never heard of, even though their products sit in those same households.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company gets to keep. Lifestyle brands sit at high, because a jeweller or an innerwear brand sets its own price. Appliance brand owners sit at medium: they keep a modest slice after the dealer's cut and the copper bill. Contract makers sit at low, by design.
  • The bet line is what you are actually wagering on when you buy that kind of stock: summer and copper for brand owners, volume and asset turns for contract makers, aspiration and pricing power for lifestyle brands.

Then read the analogy and the so-what underneath. The so-what is the practical rule: judge each door's margin against its own norm, never against the other doors. A contract maker with a thin margin and fast-turning plants can earn a better return on capital than a brand owner with a fatter margin.

c2.story:
Pick up a new split AC and ask where it was really made. The answer is a chain with five links, and India owns the middle of it far more than the ends.

The first link is raw materials and components. Copper tubing, aluminium fins, steel sheet, plastic resin, and then the expensive bits: the compressor, which is the heart of an AC or fridge; the display panel, which is most of a television's cost; the printed circuit boards and chips that run everything. Much of the metal can be bought at home from Hindalco and the steel mills. The compressor, the panel and the chip mostly arrive by ship from China and East Asia.

The second link is assembly. This is where India has changed most since 2020. When the government banned imports of ACs filled with refrigerant and launched production-linked incentives for phones and components, assembly lines sprang up around Noida for electronics and around Sri City and Chennai for ACs and phones. Dixon, Amber and PG Electroplast grew from small vendors into some of the market's most watched stocks on the back of this one station.

The third link is brand and design: the name, the star rating, the warranty, the ad with a cricketer in it. The fourth is distribution, where Croma, Reliance Digital, Vijay Sales, Amazon, Flipkart and thousands of local dealers take their cut. The fifth is the household, very often with Bajaj Finance or a bank quietly sitting beside it at the billing counter, turning a big purchase into a zero-cost EMI.

India now assembles the box. It does not yet make the heart of the machine.

That gap is the single most important fact about this kitchen. Because the compressor and the panel are imported, a weaker rupee or a Chinese export curb lands on Indian margins within a quarter, whichever logo is on the front. It is also why the government's next push, the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme approved in 2025, targets exactly those imported parts.
c2.read:
The diagram has two layers: the five stations across the top, and the band row underneath that tells you who holds each one.

The five boxes run from raw materials on the left to the household on the right. Under each name you get what happens there and who stands there. Read the who lines in sequence and you can watch the cast change: Chinese compressor and panel makers on the left, Indian contract makers in the second box, Indian and foreign brands in the third, retail chains and marketplaces in the fourth, families and financiers on the right.

The band row is the summary. The first cell is marked as China and importers, coloured as the rival, sitting under the components station. The two coloured cells marked India listed sit under assembly and under brand and design. The last two belong to the retail chains and to households on EMI.

Read it this way: Indian listed companies hold stations two and three and are squeezed from both sides. On the left they buy from a handful of foreign component makers who set the price. On the right they sell through retailers and dealers who take a fat cut and can push back on price.

Use the geography note too. Electronics clusters around Noida and Greater Noida, ACs and phones around Sri City and Chennai, white goods around Pune and Ahmedabad, jewellery in Hosur and Coimbatore. When a news item mentions a state incentive, a plant fire or a port delay, you can place it on this map at once.

c3.story:
Here is the odd thing about consumer durables demand: most of it is not really about income. Indians do not buy more ACs because they got a raise in March. They buy them because April was brutally hot, because a new flat needs fitting out, because there is a wedding in the family, or because the EMI offer at the store made a big number feel small.

That makes this demand weather, calendar and credit, in roughly that order.

Weather first. The cooling categories, ACs, coolers, fans and fridges, sell most of their year in a few weeks before and during summer. In 2024 a long heatwave sold out ACs across north India and left dealers short of stock. In 2023, and again in 2025, unseasonal rain and an early monsoon left the same dealers sitting on boxes they could not move. Same companies, same products, opposite years.

Calendar next. Weddings and festivals decide jewellery and gifting. A season with fewer auspicious dates is a thinner quarter for Tanishq, regardless of how strong the economy feels. Housing completions decide fans, lights, water heaters and kitchen appliances, a few quarters after the flat is handed over.

Then credit. A huge share of big-ticket purchases runs on consumer-durable loans, so when lending tightens, the festive weekend gets quieter.

Not every customer is a household. Global phone brands such as Samsung, Xiaomi and Motorola buy assembled handsets from Dixon. Walmart, Target and Costco buy Indian towels and bedsheets from Welspun. Supermarkets, pharma companies and data centres buy commercial refrigeration and chillers from Blue Star and Voltas. Schools buy pencils from Doms. Each of these is a different clock.

Watch the sky, the wedding calendar and the EMI book. The results only confirm what they already said.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read each in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

  • The name tells you whose wallet it is: households cooling down, new homes being fitted out, weddings and festivals, global phone brands, aspirational wardrobes, Western retailers, shops and cold chains, schools and offices.
  • The middle line is the product, which also tells you which door serves that customer. Cooling and fitting-out tiles map to the appliance brands; the phone-brand tile maps to contract makers; weddings and wardrobes map to the lifestyle brands.
  • The last line is the useful one. It is your watch list outside the sector: summer heat, housing completions, the gold price and the wedding calendar, smartphone demand and PLI, US retail inventory, data-centre capex.

Now sort the tiles by the kind of driver. Several move with weather or calendar, which you can forecast weeks ahead. Some move with credit and housing, which follow interest rates. A few move with global brands and US retailers, which follow the world economy and tariffs. A company exposed to one tile is a concentrated bet on that driver; a company spread across several is steadier.

Finally, cross-check with the doors. Contract makers often depend on a handful of brand customers inside a single tile, which is why one lost account can reset their year.

c4.story:
Follow a hundred rupees spent on an AC and you discover why this is a hard business to get rich in, even when the product is flying off the shelves.

For a brand owner, the biggest bite goes to raw materials and components. Copper, aluminium, steel and the imported compressor eat roughly two thirds of every sale. Then comes a thick slice for advertising, dealer margins, people and freight, because a brand that stops advertising in summer simply loses shelf space to the one next to it. Depreciation and interest are small, since many brand owners outsource assembly and carry net cash. What survives is a single-digit margin.

For a contract maker, the picture is starker. Almost all of the sale is the bill of materials, passed through from component suppliers and billed on to the brand. The contract maker's own costs are lean, and what is left is a few rupees per hundred. That sounds terrible until you remember that a good contract maker turns its plant over many times a year. A thin margin earned again and again on the same assets can still produce an excellent return on capital.

Three lines trip people up. The first is the commodity lag. Brands set prices for a season, but buy copper by the quarter, so a metal spike hits gross margin before the price hike arrives. The second is working capital. Brands stuff dealers ahead of summer, so a washed-out season leaves stock in the channel that has to be cleared with discounts for the next two quarters. The third is other income: net-cash brand owners earn treasury income that can quietly prop up profit in a bad year.

In this sector the season is the revenue line and copper is the margin line. Everything else is commentary.

Titan has its own quirk. It leases much of its gold rather than buying it outright, so the cost of that lease sits in interest, and a rising gold price can produce inventory gains that flatter a quarter.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, one for appliance brand owners and one for contract manufacturers. Read each from left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is raw materials and components. For brand owners it takes roughly two thirds. For contract makers it takes nearly nine of every ten rupees, because the whole bill of materials flows through their books.
  • The opex bar is ads, dealer margins, people and freight. It is several times larger for the brand owner, which pays for the brand and the dealer, than for the contract maker, which pays for neither.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small and similar in both.
  • The last bar is what is left: high single digits for the brand owner, a few rupees for the contract maker.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list marks which P&L lines matter here. Gross margin, advertising, working capital and capex with asset turn all get a yes. Depreciation, interest and other income are marked sometimes, because each matters for one door and not the others. Tax gets a no; GST sits on the customer's bill.

Then read the so-what: after every summer and every Diwali, look at channel inventory and gross margin together. Clean channel plus stable margin means the next season starts fresh.

c5.story:
Consumer durables runs on two clocks at once, and you need to read both.

The fast clock is the season. The summer quarter decides cooling, and the festive quarter decides televisions, kitchen appliances and gold. One good or bad season can swing the whole year. The slow clock is commodities, interest rates and policy: copper and steel, EMI costs, PLI schemes, import bans and tax slabs.

Here is how the last cycle played out. Covid wiped out the 2020 AC summer, but work-from-home sent families shopping for televisions, laptops and kitchen gadgets. The same year the government banned imports of filled ACs and launched PLI. The 2021 summer was hurt by the second wave, but 2022 was a record, and Dixon and Amber became the market's China+1 darlings. The trouble was that copper and steel were expensive the whole time, and every brand built channel stock for a repeat summer.

Then 2023 arrived with rain in March, April and May. ACs sat in warehouses, dealers demanded discounts, and margins compressed for two quarters. A blistering 2024 heatwave cleared the channel and set records. And then 2025 washed out again, with an early monsoon cutting AC volumes hard.

What happened next is the reason the clock reads the way it does today. Ahead of Diwali 2025, the GST Council moved ACs, large televisions and dishwashers from the top tax slab down to the standard slab. That is one of the biggest single price cuts this category has seen, delivered by the tax man rather than by the companies. Within weeks LG Electronics India launched a large IPO, which tells you how the market felt about the sector's future.

The tax cut reset the price. The summer will decide whether it reset the demand.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each arc are the last cycle: boom across 2021 and 2022, the peak in 2022, the bust in 2023, the bottom running into 2024. The arrow points just past the bottom into the early up-cycle, labelled post-GST restart. Hover any arc to read what defined that phase.

The timeline beside it tells the story year by year from 2019. The colours matter: two boom entries, 2021 to 2022 and then 2024, with a bust year in between. That alternation is the season clock showing through. The latest entry, marked now, describes the tax cut and the clean channel.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Channel inventory: clean, arrow up. The next season starts fresh.
  • Copper and aluminium: elevated, arrow down. This is the hand working against the brand owners.
  • Volume growth after the GST cut: accelerating, arrow up. If it stays strong after the festive season, the cut created demand rather than pulling it forward.
  • Contract makers' asset turns: holding, flat. Rising would mean new plants are filling.

Three hands are friendly and one is not, which is exactly why the so-what says brand owners recover first and contract makers wait for their plants to fill.

c6.story:
The people who decide a consumer durables company's year mostly do not work there. A copper trader in London. A forecaster at the India Meteorological Department. A rate-setter at the RBI. A GST Council meeting in Delhi.

Two dials matter more than the rest combined. The first is copper. It is in every AC's tubing, every fan's motor and every metre of wire. When copper jumps, the brand owner's gross margin shrinks for a quarter or two, because the season's price list is already printed. Price hikes follow, but always late, and sometimes into a weak market that will not take them.

The second is the summer, and specifically its timing. A hot March gets dealers ordering early, which fills the June quarter. A rainy April kills it. No company can hedge this, which is why management commentary in this sector so often begins with the weather.

Then come the two-dot dials. Interest rates move the cost of the EMI, and a lot of big-ticket purchases run on EMI. A weaker rupee raises the price of imported compressors, panels and chips. The gold price is two-faced: a rally lifts the rupee value of each Tanishq bill and creates inventory gains, but it also makes customers buy fewer grams. Housing completions feed the fan, lighting and water-heater categories a few quarters after families move in.

The one-dot dials are smaller pressures. Aluminium and steel add to the input squeeze. Crude raises plastic and freight costs. US tariffs and retail inventories matter mainly for home-textile exporters like Welspun. And the industrial output index for durables is a coincident check on factory volumes, not a forecast.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force, such as copper, summer heat or the rupee.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. This is the most useful column, because it tells you which line of the P&L to check next quarter.
  • A rise does: a green upward arrow means a rise helps, a red downward arrow means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways. In this table most arrows are red, because most dials here are costs. Summer heat, housing and the durables output index are the green ones. Gold carries the diamond.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three dots can make or break the year.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: copper, aluminium, gold, the rupee, Brent crude, the money-market rate, the realty index, durables industrial output and exports. Summer heat has no live series and shows a dash; for that you read the weather forecasts.

Start with the three-dot rows: copper and summer heat. Then glance at the two two-dot cost rows, interest rates and the rupee. If copper and the rupee are both moving against the brands while the summer forecast is soft, you already know the shape of the next quarter before anyone reports it.

c7.story:
Every few years someone pitches Indian durables as the great penetration story: only a small minority of Indian homes own an AC, so the runway is endless. The runway is real. The bottlenecks explain why it is being travelled at a jog rather than a sprint.

The biggest is structural: the imported heart of the machine. India assembles the box, but the compressor, the display panel and the chips mostly come from China and East Asia. That means the costliest part of the product is priced by someone else, in dollars, and India's assembly boom has not yet changed that. The component incentive scheme is the attempt to fix it, but building compressor and panel capacity takes years.

The second structural bottleneck is the channel. Distributors and large-format chains take a fat margin and can return unsold stock. Online marketplaces squeeze further on price. A brand that wants shelf space pays for it, every season.

Contract makers face their own ceiling: a few rupees per unit on a product someone else prices. One lost brand account, or one missed PLI target, changes their year.

Then the recurring surprises. Weather risk is the obvious one: a single rainy April can erase a large part of the year's AC profit. Policy whiplash is the subtler one. Import bans, quality-control orders, revised star labels and GST changes have each reset parts of the market within months since 2020. The commodity lag is cyclical: prices are set for the season, copper is bought for the quarter.

Gold earns its own row because it is two-sided. A sharp rally inflates jeweller sales while cutting grams sold, and mandatory hallmarking since 2021 has steadily pushed buyers from the neighbourhood goldsmith toward organised chains like Tanishq.

The penetration story is true. It is just slower than the investor presentation.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. The severity label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural rows are permanent features: the imported core, dealer and channel power, and thin contract margins. They cap margins across the whole cycle, so they belong in your valuation, not your news feed.
  • Recurring rows come back again and again: weather risk and policy whiplash. These are the headlines that move a stock for a week and a quarter for a year. Set a news alert per company.
  • Cyclical marks the commodity pass-through lag, which bites when metals rise and fades when they settle.
  • Two-sided marks gold and hallmarking: painful for grams sold, helpful for organised jewellers taking share.
  • Slow marks low penetration and slow conversion: a long-term tailwind that moves at the pace of power supply, flat sizes and incomes.

Read the so-what line under the table as the reading order. The first two structural rows, the imported core and the dealer's cut, set the ceiling on margins. The recurring rows, weather and policy, are the quarterly surprises.

One test for any company: which of these rows does it actually escape? A brand owner building its own compressors is chipping at the first row. A lifestyle brand selling through its own stores is escaping the second.

c8.story:
In consumer durables, a notification from Delhi can move demand more than any ad campaign. The clearest proof came in 2025.

Until September 2025, ACs, large televisions and dishwashers sat in the top GST slab, taxed like luxuries. Then the GST Council moved them down to the standard slab before Diwali. In one stroke, the sticker price of an AC fell meaningfully without any company cutting its margin. That is why the rulebook marks the GST Council as new, and why its so-what calls the cut the biggest demand event in a decade. A reversal would be the biggest risk.

Other rules work like tariffs without being called tariffs. BIS quality control orders require ACs, fans, televisions, toys and many components, imported or not, to meet Indian standards. In practice that slows the cheapest imports and favours local assembly. The 2020 import ban on ACs with refrigerant did the same thing more bluntly.

Then there is the rule that built a whole door. The PLI schemes pay cash incentives on incremental output of phones, IT hardware and AC and LED components. Dixon, Amber and PG Electroplast exist at their current size largely because of them. The component scheme is the next leg, aimed at the parts India still imports.

Some rules raise costs slowly. BEE star labels tighten every couple of years, pushing makers toward pricier inverter technology. E-waste rules make brands collect and recycle a growing share of what they sell. The Kigali phase-down will force new refrigerant gases and redesigned compressors from 2028.

And for jewellers, mandatory hallmarking with a unique ID has quietly shifted buyers toward organised chains, while the gold import duty can move demand within a quarter. The July 2024 Budget's sharp duty cut was one such moment.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column is how you prioritise.

  • New: the GST Council's 2025 cut. This is the row that explains the current up-cycle. Any talk of reversing it is the first thing to watch.
  • Live: actively shaping the market today. BIS quality control orders, the PLI schemes, DGFT and customs rules on imports, CPCB e-waste rules and the consumer affairs department's repair and warranty rules all sit here. For contract makers, the PLI row is the one to follow most closely; for brand owners, quality control orders and customs duties shape what the competition can import.
  • Always: permanent fixtures, BEE star labelling and BIS hallmarking with the gold import duty. They rarely make headlines, but each tightening of a star label raises cost per unit.
  • Coming: the Kigali phase-down, which will force a shift to new refrigerant gases and compressors. Slow, but it touches every AC and fridge maker.

Notice how many rows protect local assembly: quality control orders, customs, PLI. That cluster is the policy wall behind the contract makers. Notice too that the costs fall mostly on brand owners: star labels, e-waste, repair rules.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks one question in five ways: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Suppliers can squeeze your input price, customers your selling price, rivals can start a price war, newcomers can crowd in, and substitutes can make you unnecessary.

Run appliance brand owners through it and the weakest spot is rivalry. A dozen Indian, Korean, Japanese and Chinese brands fight for the same dealer shelf, and every summer someone decides to buy share with a discount. Suppliers are powerful too: a handful of compressor and panel makers set the price of the most expensive parts. And dealers and online marketplaces lean on margins and returns.

Contract makers have a different weak spot: the buyer. Their customer is a global brand that writes the specification, dictates the price per unit and can move volumes to a rival plant. Each brand also likes having at least two suppliers, precisely so that no contract maker gets too comfortable. Suppliers squeeze them even harder than they squeeze the brands, because contract makers buy components at scale on someone else's behalf.

Both face steady entry. Reliance, Chinese brands and start-ups keep arriving in appliances; PLI invites a new contract maker every year.

And substitutes? There is no substitute for a fridge. But there is a hidden one: waiting. In a slowdown, families simply keep the old AC running another summer. A longer replacement cycle is the substitute nobody shows on a slide.

The market pays contract makers for growth and brand owners for margins, because each is short of the other.

The lifestyle door is not on the radar, but it would be the smallest shape of all: the customer pays for the name, and nobody else can print it.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts. So a smaller shape is a better business.

Two shapes are drawn: appliance brand owners and contract manufacturers. Look at overall size first. They are similar, both middling, which says neither door has an easy life.

Then look at where they differ, because that is the real lesson.

  • Rivalry: the brand-owner shape reaches further. The dealer shelf is crowded.
  • Supplier: the contract-maker shape reaches further. Component makers squeeze the assembler hardest.
  • Buyer: the contract-maker shape hits the outer ring. A global brand dictates price and can walk. This is the single biggest pressure point on the chart.
  • Entrants: the shapes match. Both doors keep attracting new players.
  • Substitutes: the shapes match at the inner ring. Little substitutes for the products themselves.

The table beside the chart gives each score, from zero for no pressure to three for heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. If you know a company that escapes one pressure, say a brand owner that makes its own compressors, mentally pull its shape in on that spoke. That is how the framework is meant to be used.

c10.story:
A durables results call can bury you in detail: category shares, new launches, plant commissioning, dealer additions, star-rating changes. Eight numbers cut through it.

Start with gross margin. It is the commodity squeeze versus pricing power, and it moves first. Then volume growth by category, which tells you whether the season or the tax cut actually delivered. Value growth can hide a weak season behind price hikes, so always ask for units.

Next, the brand's health. Advertising as a share of sales tells you whether a margin improvement was earned or bought by quietly starving the brand. A brand owner that cuts ads in a bad year looks better this year and worse the next.

Then the two channel numbers, which are where the real story usually hides. Inventory days show whether the summer's stock actually sold through. Receivable days catch dealer stuffing: if receivables jump after a weak season, the company pushed boxes onto dealers to book sales, and those boxes will come back as discounts.

For contract makers, asset turn is the number that matters most. Their margin will always be thin; the question is whether new plants are filling fast enough to earn on it. Then ROCE, which tells you whether either model earns its keep, and capex to depreciation, which tells you whether a company is building, perhaps backward into compressors or components, or coasting.

Gross margin tells you about copper. Receivable days tell you about honesty.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company you own. Notice how many rows are about the channel: inventory days, receivable days and volume growth all exist to catch a stuffed channel or a season that did not sell through.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, and they are rules of thumb. Several split by door: gross margin has one range for brand owners and a much lower one for contract makers; ROCE asks a little more of contract makers than of brands, because high turns should earn it. Asset turn is really a contract-maker metric.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of listed companies in this industry. Advertising share has no median because filings rarely split it out cleanly; you get it from the annual report.

A caution: the median blends brand owners, contract makers and lifestyle brands, so it can sit between the door benchmarks rather than near either one. Compare a company with its own door's good mark first, then with the median.

The best use: after every summer and festive quarter, line up gross margin, inventory days and receivable days for your names. Stable margin with falling inventory is a clean season.

c11.story:
The best early warnings about durables come from outside the sector, and they arrive on very different schedules.

Some speak in the same quarter. Bajaj Finance's consumer-durable loan book moves with purchases as they happen, because so much of the buying runs on EMI. The gold price and the wedding calendar set jewellery grammage within the month.

Others speak a quarter ahead. The weather forecast for March to May is the big one: an early, hot forecast gets dealers stocking up, and the June quarter sells through. Copper and aluminium futures move a quarter before raw-material contracts reset. Shipment guidance from Samsung, Xiaomi and Motorola is effectively Dixon's order book. Walmart and Target talking about destocking is Welspun's next quarter. And a GST or BIS notification moves demand within a quarter of taking effect.

Housing completions speak two quarters out, because families buy fans, lights and kitchen appliances after they take possession.

Put the strongest signals together and you get the three-sign rule. The industry is in a genuine up-cycle when the channel is clean, unit volumes are growing in double digits, and metal prices are stable or falling. Right now two of three are ticking. The channel cleared through the festive season, and the GST cut is lifting volumes. The missing sign is copper, still elevated. That is the shape of an early recovery: demand has turned, but margins have not fully caught up.

Which is exactly what the call says. Brand owners with clean channels and lifestyle brands with pricing power come first. Contract makers remain a volume story, worth owning for PLI growth but not for margins they were never designed to have.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to see the channel through which it reaches earnings.

  • Far left, same quarter: Bajaj Finance durable-loan growth, and the gold price with the wedding calendar. These confirm what is already happening.
  • One quarter ahead: the crowded middle, with the March-to-May weather forecast, copper and aluminium futures, smartphone brand guidance, US retailers' inventory commentary and GST or BIS notifications.
  • Two quarters ahead: housing completions and repainting commentary, the earliest dot on this chart.

Use it as a reading order. Each quarter, check the rightmost dot first, then the one-quarter cluster, then confirm with the left-hand dots. In this industry, most of the useful warning sits a single quarter out, so the time to act is short.

Below the chart is the rule with its three signs. Ticks for a clean channel and double-digit volumes; a cross for metal prices, with the note that copper is still elevated. Two of three means early recovery, as the rule text says.

Then the call box: the headline, the three points behind it, and what would change the call: a third washed-out summer, a copper spike or a sharply weaker rupee that outruns price hikes, or a GST reversal or PLI miss. Treat those three as your alerts.

explainer.one_liner: Defence companies build fighter jets, warships, missiles, radars and the electronics inside them for one customer, the Indian armed forces, and are now being pushed to make at home what India used to import and to sell some of it abroad.

doors.name: State-owned platform primes
doors.sub: Design, integrate and deliver whole aircraft, missiles and electronic systems on multi-year government contracts, paid in milestones with large advances upfront
doors.blurb: A bet on the defence budget, on the government preferring its own factories, and on delivery not slipping

doors.name: Shipyards
doors.sub: Build destroyers, frigates, submarines and patrol vessels over five to ten years each, on fixed-price contracts with big customer advances
doors.blurb: A bet on the navy's fleet plan and on finishing ships early enough to keep the incentive

doors.name: Private electronics and sub-systems
doors.sub: Design and make radar modules, missile electronics, optics and test systems as a supplier to the primes and the research labs
doors.blurb: A bet on the primes outsourcing more, with small order books that double or halve on one contract

doors.name: Aerospace parts and structures
doors.sub: Precision-machine engine parts, tooling, airframe pieces and hangars for Indian and global aircraft makers
doors.blurb: A bet on global aerospace supply chains adding India, more than on the Indian military

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the government's own kitchen that cooks every state banquet. Door two builds the banquet hall itself, one every few years. Door three supplies the spice mixes and the ovens to the kitchen. Door four makes cutlery for restaurants in India and abroad.
explainer.door_so_what: The primes have the orders and the cash, the shipyards have the longest visibility and the slowest conversion, and the private names have the growth and the lumpiness, so the same budget headline moves each door differently.

stations.name: Research and design
stations.what: The government's labs and the primes' design bureaus draw the aircraft, missile or radar; foreign partners supply what India cannot yet design, above all engines
stations.who: DRDO labs, HAL and BEL design centres; GE, Safran and Rolls-Royce for engines; Russia, France and Israel for licensed designs

stations.name: Materials and components
stations.what: Special steels, titanium, composites, chips, optics and seekers come in, much of it imported
stations.who: Midhani for alloys, PARAS for optics, APOLLO and DATAPATTNS for electronics; Israel, the US and Europe for sensors and chips

stations.name: Sub-system making
stations.what: Components become radar modules, missile guidance, sonar, hull blocks, machined engine parts
stations.who: DATAPATTNS, APOLLO, UNIMECH, KRISHNADEF, hundreds of small private vendors around Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune

stations.name: Platform integration
stations.what: Sub-systems are assembled into a fighter, a frigate, a missile battery, a radar network and tested
stations.who: HAL, BEL, BDL, MAZDOCK, COCHINSHIP, GRSE, SWANDEF; the government's quality agencies at every step

stations.name: Delivery, upkeep and export
stations.what: The forces take delivery; the maker supports it for decades and sells spare versions abroad
stations.who: Army, navy and air force; HAL and BEL service depots; export customers in Southeast Asia, Africa and the Gulf

kitchen.rival: Foreign original equipment makers, above all US, French, Russian and Israeli, who still supply engines, sensors and the big-ticket imports
kitchen.note: Bengaluru is the aerospace capital, Hyderabad the missile and electronics hub, and the shipyards sit in Mumbai, Kochi, Kolkata, Visakhapatnam and Goa. The foreign content hides in the engines and sensors, so a fighter stamped Made in India may still depend on a delivery from Ohio.
kitchen.so_what: India has largely nationalised the last two stations; the profit and the delay both come from the first two, where the engine and the sensor still arrive from abroad.

end_markets.name: Indian Air Force
end_markets.buys: Fighters, trainers, helicopters, transport aircraft, radars, missiles
end_markets.moves_with: Squadron shortfalls, the capital budget, engine deliveries from abroad

end_markets.name: Indian Navy
end_markets.buys: Destroyers, frigates, submarines, carriers, patrol craft, sonar and combat systems
end_markets.moves_with: The fleet plan, Chinese naval activity in the Indian Ocean, shipyard capacity

end_markets.name: Indian Army
end_markets.buys: Artillery, tanks and vehicles, anti-tank and air-defence missiles, radios, drones, night vision
end_markets.moves_with: Border tension with China and Pakistan, emergency procurement powers

end_markets.name: Paramilitary, coast guard and police
end_markets.buys: Patrol vessels, small arms, surveillance, communications
end_markets.moves_with: Home ministry budgets, coastal security pushes

end_markets.name: Export customers
end_markets.buys: Missiles, radars, patrol vessels, light helicopters, artillery
end_markets.moves_with: Government-to-government deals, lines of credit, rivals' delivery backlogs

end_markets.name: Space and ISRO
end_markets.buys: Launch vehicle structures, satellite electronics, ground systems
end_markets.moves_with: Launch cadence, the opening of space to private firms

end_markets.name: Global aerospace majors
end_markets.buys: Machined parts, tooling, sub-assemblies for civil and military aircraft
end_markets.moves_with: Airbus and Boeing production rates, supply-chain diversification away from China

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Three services and one ministry make almost every buying decision, so the industry's demand is a policy choice, not a market, and it can be accelerated or frozen by a single committee meeting.

lines.why: The book is the next five to ten years of revenue; a big contract signing is the single most important event in a stock's year
Orders only matter if they turn into delivered aircraft and ships; execution, not demand, is the constraint
Imported kits carry no margin; the more a prime designs and sources at home, the more it keeps
The forces pay a large share upfront; the interest on that cash can be a fifth of a shipyard's profit and flatters margins
Negative for shipyards because of advances; heavy for private suppliers who wait on the primes and the labs to pay
Factories are old and largely depreciated at the PSUs; small for the private names
New production lines for fighters and new dry docks are the capex that unlocks the book; otherwise asset-light
Almost all listed names are debt-free and sit on cash; interest is income, not cost
Late deliveries attract penalties and lost incentives; the shipyards' margin swings on finishing early or late

pnl.analogy: A defence prime is a caterer with one wealthy client who pays half the bill before the wedding, so the caterer earns interest on the client's money while cooking slowly. The risk is not the client leaving; it is the oven, imported, arriving late.
pnl.so_what: Read order book against sales for visibility, revenue growth for execution, and then strip the interest on advances out of the profit to see what the factories actually earn.

clock.is_cyclical: Not a market cycle; a policy cycle. Demand is set by the defence budget, the share of it spent at home and the pace of approvals, with border conflicts as the accelerator and procurement scandals as the brake.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Post-Kargil modernisation money flows, big import deals are signed and the PSU primes grow fat on licensed production

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: The helicopter bribery scandal, blacklisted vendors and a cautious ministry; orders pile up in committees

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Procurement freezes, the fighter tender collapses into a small off-the-shelf buy and the primes list to a cold market; HAL's shares fall below issue

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: A cash crunch at the aircraft prime, then the Galwan clash and the first import-ban lists reset the whole policy toward buying Indian

clock.position_detail: record order books, deliveries lag engines

timeline.what: Balakot air strikes and a fleet of ageing fighters expose the squadron gap. The aircraft prime borrows to pay salaries while waiting on government dues. The stocks are unloved.
The Galwan clash with China changes everything. Emergency buying powers are used, the first list of weapons that may no longer be imported is published and foreign ownership limits are raised.
The big home-built fighter order is signed, a new procurement manual favours Indian design, defence corridors are set up and exports are pushed with a hard target. Order books begin to swell.
Exports hit records, the navy commissions its first home-built carrier, private suppliers list and re-rate, and the sector becomes the market's favourite theme.

Order placement slows into the election and valuations hit extremes; the stocks correct sharply from the peak even as order books stay full. Engine deliveries from the US slip, delaying fighter output.

Operation Sindoor in May proves home-made missiles and air defence in combat and drives emergency orders. A further fighter batch, carrier-borne jets from France and the submarine programme are cleared. The stocks rally back.

Order books at the primes stand at several years of sales, brokers list the primes among their top picks into the results season, and the shipyards hold record advances. The constraint is engines and delivery, not demand.

hands.name: Defence capital budget growth
hands.meaning: Faster growth means more approvals become contracts this year

hands.name: Order book to sales at the primes
hands.meaning: Rising visibility is good only if execution keeps pace

hands.name: Engine and import deliveries
hands.meaning: Late engines mean fighters built but not delivered, which means revenue slips a year

hands.name: Export order wins
hands.meaning: Exports prove competitiveness and loosen the one-customer problem

clock.so_what: An execution-paced boom means revenue, not orders, is the surprise variable, and a stock can fall on a record order book if deliveries slip.

dials.name: Defence capital budget
dials.channel: The money available to sign and pay for contracts
dials.rise_does: lifts orders and advances a year later

dials.name: Border tension and conflict
dials.channel: Emergency procurement and political will
dials.rise_does: pulls orders forward and re-rates the stocks

dials.name: Share of procurement bought at home
dials.channel: The import-ban lists and Buy Indian categories
dials.rise_does: shifts budget from foreign makers to listed Indian ones

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Imported engines, sensors and kits; export earnings
dials.rise_does: raises input costs on fixed-price contracts

dials.name: US and Western export controls and deliveries
dials.channel: Engines and sensors India cannot yet make
dials.rise_does: delays fighters and ships; tighter controls hurt

dials.name: Government fiscal space
dials.channel: Room to grow the capital budget
dials.rise_does: a wider deficit squeezes capital spending

dials.name: Global defence spending
dials.channel: Export demand and competition for the same engines and parts
dials.rise_does: opens export markets, tightens supply chains

dials.name: Interest rates
dials.channel: Income on the advances the primes and yards hold
dials.rise_does: raises other income at cash-rich names

dials.name: Steel and special alloy prices
dials.channel: Hulls, airframes, barrels
dials.rise_does: squeezes shipyard fixed-price margins

dials.name: Crude oil
dials.channel: Government finances and Gulf export customers' budgets
dials.rise_does: hurts the budget, helps Gulf buyers

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track the defence capital budget and the share bought at home; conflict moves the stocks for a month, those two move the earnings for a decade.

bottlenecks.name: Engines from abroad
bottlenecks.why: India does not make a fighter engine, and marine turbines and many helicopter engines are imported too. A late shipment from one US plant stalls a whole fighter line.

bottlenecks.name: One customer, slow decisions
bottlenecks.why: The ministry approves, negotiates and signs on its own clock; a programme can spend years between approval and contract, and a change of minister resets it.

bottlenecks.name: Execution at the primes
bottlenecks.why: Order books of several years of sales mean the factories, not the budget, are the limit; adding a production line takes years and skilled hands.

bottlenecks.name: Shipyard capacity and dry docks
bottlenecks.why: Each yard can build only so many hulls at once; a delayed launch blocks the next keel.

bottlenecks.name: Sensors and chips imported
bottlenecks.why: Seekers, infrared sensors and radar chips come from Israel, the US and Europe; a geopolitical fallout upstream becomes a delivery slip downstream.

bottlenecks.name: Payment delays and fiscal squeeze
bottlenecks.why: The ministry has paid the primes late when its budget ran short, forcing a cash-rich company to borrow for salaries.

bottlenecks.name: Procurement scandals
bottlenecks.why: A bribery allegation can blacklist a vendor and freeze a programme for years; the whole sector has been through this before.

bottlenecks.name: Valuation and retail crowding
bottlenecks.why: The theme attracts retail money in waves; stocks have swung by half on sentiment while order books barely moved.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first and third bottlenecks decide this year's revenue; the second and seventh decide whether the next decade of orders arrives on time.

rulebook.body: Ministry of Defence and the Defence Acquisition Council
rulebook.what: Approves what to buy, in which category and from whom
rulebook.why: Every large order starts as a council approval; the approval-to-contract gap is the sector's clock

rulebook.what: The procurement manual that ranks Buy Indian designed-and-made above everything else
rulebook.why: Steers budget to Indian primes and their Indian supply chains

rulebook.what: Lists of weapons and components that may no longer be imported after set dates
rulebook.why: A guaranteed order shift to domestic makers, year by year

rulebook.body: Department of Defence Production and the quality agencies
rulebook.what: Oversees the PSUs, certifies airworthiness and quality, runs the export licence desk
rulebook.why: Certification delays are delivery delays; export licences gate overseas sales

rulebook.what: The state research body that designs most Indian missiles, radars and the home-built fighter
rulebook.why: Its development timelines are the primes' production timelines; its technology transfers feed the private names

rulebook.what: Automatic route up to a high majority share, full ownership with approval
rulebook.why: Lets foreign majors set up joint ventures that become orders for Indian suppliers

rulebook.what: Two state corridors with land, incentives and clustering for defence manufacturing
rulebook.why: Where the private supplier capacity is being built

rulebook.body: Export promotion and lines of credit
rulebook.what: Government-to-government deals and concessional loans for buyers of Indian arms
rulebook.why: Exports are the only way out of the one-customer problem

rulebook.what: Opens launch, satellite and ground segments to private companies
rulebook.why: A second customer set for the electronics and structures names

why.rivalry: The primes are the government's own and face no domestic rival on platforms; private suppliers bid against each other and against the primes' in-house units
why.supplier: Engines and sensors come from a few foreign makers who set schedules; private names also depend on imported chips
why.buyer: One customer with full power over price, but one that wants its own factories to prosper; private suppliers are squeezed by the primes above them
why.entrants: Nobody can enter platform integration; new private suppliers appear each year as the primes outsource
why.substitutes: The import route is the substitute for a prime's product, and the lists are closing it; private parts face little substitution

forces.so_what: The primes keep the most profit because their customer wants them to; the private names grow faster but keep less and live on the primes' outsourcing mood.

cheat_sheet.tells: Years of visible revenue

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when the capital budget is growing, approvals are turning into signed contracts, and deliveries are keeping pace with the book; three of three is a clean boom, two is a boom with a delivery problem, one is a policy pause.

call.headline: A policy-driven boom with a delivery bottleneck. Prefer primes and shipyards with proven execution and visible advances; treat the private small-caps as single-contract bets and size them accordingly.
points: Order books are at several years of sales and the budget, the import-ban lists and the conflict have all pulled demand forward.
Revenue, not orders, is the swing variable now; imported engines and shipyard capacity set the pace and have slipped.
Valuations have swung by half on sentiment twice in three years, so entry price matters more here than in most industries.
would_change: A procurement scandal or ministerial reset freezing contract signings
Engine and sensor deliveries normalising, which would release a revenue catch-up
A fiscal squeeze that flattens the capital budget or delays payments to the primes

explainer.tell_a_friend: Defence companies build fighters, warships, missiles and radars for one customer, the Indian armed forces. For years that customer preferred imports and took forever to decide, so the state-owned makers were dull, cash-starved stocks; the aircraft prime even borrowed to pay salaries in 2019. Then the 2020 Galwan clash with China changed the policy: lists of weapons that may no longer be imported, a procurement manual that ranks Indian design first, and a hard export target. Order books swelled to several years of sales, exports hit records, and the stocks became the market's favourite theme, overshooting in 2024 and roaring back after the May 2025 conflict proved home-made missiles in combat. The catch is that India still imports the engines and many sensors, so a late shipment from one American plant stalls a fighter line. The companies are debt-free and sit on customer advances, which flatters their profit with interest income. Watch the capital budget, the gap between approvals and signed contracts, and whether deliveries keep pace with the book.

glossary.def: The company that integrates a whole platform, a fighter or a warship, and signs the contract with the forces. In India mostly state-owned.
A complete weapon system such as an aircraft, ship, tank or missile battery, as against a part inside one.
A functional block inside a platform: a radar, a seeker, a sonar, a fire-control computer.
Contracts signed but not yet delivered. At the primes it runs 3–5 years of sales.
The ministry committee, chaired by the defence minister, that approves a purchase in principle. Approval is not yet a contract.
The council's formal approval of a need and a category. The first public step of any order.
The procurement rulebook. Its 2020 edition ranks Indian-designed, Indian-made products highest.
A government list of items that may not be imported after a given date. Several lists cover hundreds of items.
The share of a product's value made in India. Higher content means higher margin and priority in tenders.
Money the forces pay at signing, often 15–20% of a contract. The primes earn interest on it until spent.
Payment released when a stage is reached: a hull launched, a flight test passed.
A penalty written into the contract for late delivery, usually a fixed share per period of delay.
A contract priced at audited cost plus an agreed margin. Common for the PSUs; limits both upside and loss.
A foreign maker handing over designs and know-how so an Indian firm can build the product locally.
Building a foreign design in India under licence, typically with imported kits. Low margin, little learning.
Maintenance, repair and overhaul: keeping delivered platforms flying or sailing for decades. Steady, high-margin revenue.
Fast-track buying powers given to the forces after a crisis, with shorter approvals and smaller lots.
An export or import agreed between two governments directly, skipping an open tender.
A concessional loan India extends to a friendly country to buy Indian equipment.
A basin that can be drained so a ship can be built or repaired. A yard's capacity is counted in docks and slipways.
Defence Research and Development Organisation, the state body that designs most Indian weapons.
Designated zones in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu with incentives for defence factories.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by equity plus debt.

c1.story:
Most industries have thousands of customers. Indian defence has, for practical purposes, one: the Ministry of Defence, buying for the army, the navy and the air force. That single fact shapes everything about the business, from how orders arrive to why the stocks swing the way they do.

Within that one-customer world, there are four very different ways to make money.

The first door belongs to the state-owned primes. Hindustan Aeronautics builds fighters, trainers and helicopters. Bharat Electronics builds radars, communication networks and the electronics of air-defence systems. Bharat Dynamics builds missiles. They design, integrate and deliver whole platforms on contracts that run for years, and the ministry pays a large share upfront as advances. They are, in effect, the government's own factories, and the government wants them to prosper.

The second door is the shipyards: Mazagon Dock in Mumbai, Cochin Shipyard, Garden Reach in Kolkata, and Swan Defence, the old Pipavav yard revived after an insolvency process. They build destroyers, frigates, submarines and patrol vessels, each over five to ten years, on fixed-price contracts with big advances. Cochin Shipyard built INS Vikrant, India's first home-built aircraft carrier. The visibility is the longest in the market; the conversion into revenue is the slowest.

The primes have the orders, the shipyards have the patience, and the private names have the growth.

The third door is the private electronics and sub-system makers: Data Patterns, Apollo Micro Systems, Paras Defence, Krishna Defence. They design and build the radar modules, missile electronics and optics that go inside the primes' platforms. Their order books are small enough that a single contract can double or halve a year.

The fourth door looks outward. Precision engineering firms machine engine parts, airframe pieces and tooling for global aircraft makers. For them, an Airbus production rate matters more than an Indian budget speech.

The same headline, say a big fighter approval, means a decade of revenue for the prime, a possible sub-system order for the private supplier a year later, and almost nothing for the aerospace parts maker.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you the contract shape: multi-year platform contracts with advances, multi-year ship contracts with advances, supplier orders from the primes and labs, or parts orders from global aircraft makers.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. Notice the split: the first two doors are almost all government-owned; the last two are private.
  • The profit bar tells you how much of the value the company keeps. State-owned primes sit at the high end. That surprises people, since their only customer is all-powerful, but the customer wants these factories strong, contracts are often priced on cost plus a margin, and the primes face no domestic rival on platforms. Shipyards sit in the middle, because fixed prices and long builds expose them to cost slips. Private electronics and aerospace parts also sit in the middle: real skills, but squeezed by the primes or by global buyers above them.
  • The last line is the bet. For the shipyards it hides a detail worth knowing: finishing a ship early can earn an incentive, finishing late costs penalties, so the margin swings on the calendar.

Below the tiles, the analogy of the government's kitchen, the banquet hall, the spice supplier and the cutlery maker gives you the four in one breath.

The so-what line is the practical rule: the primes have the orders and the cash, the shipyards the longest visibility and slowest conversion, the private names the growth and the lumpiness. Size a position accordingly.

c2.story:
A fighter rolling out of HAL's Bengaluru hangar looks unmistakably Indian. Follow its parts back through the kitchen, though, and the story gets more international with every step.

Station one is research and design. DRDO, the government's defence research organisation, and the design bureaus inside HAL and BEL draw the aircraft, the missile or the radar. But some things India still cannot design at home, and the most important is the jet engine. The Tejas runs on an American GE engine. Licensed designs from Russia, France and Israel fill other gaps. This is where the foreign original equipment makers stand.

Station two is materials and components: special steels, titanium, composites, chips, optics and missile seekers. Midhani, the state alloy maker, supplies some metals; Paras makes optics; Apollo and Data Patterns build electronics. But much of the sensor and chip content still arrives from Israel, the US and Europe.

Station three is sub-systems, where components become radar modules, missile guidance units, sonar, hull blocks and machined engine parts. This is where India's private defence ecosystem lives: listed suppliers plus hundreds of small vendors around Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.

A fighter stamped Made in India can still be waiting for a box from Ohio.

Station four is platform integration. HAL, BEL, BDL and the shipyards assemble everything into a fighter, a frigate, a missile battery or a radar network, with the government's quality agencies inspecting at every step. Station five is delivery, decades of upkeep, and increasingly exports, to buyers in Southeast Asia, Africa and the Gulf.

Here is the uncomfortable truth the kitchen reveals. India has largely nationalised the last two stations: integration and delivery are firmly Indian. The first two stations, where the engine and the sensor come from, are where both the profit and the delay originate. When GE's engine deliveries for the Tejas slipped, HAL had airframes ready and nothing to put in them. Revenue waited a year on one supplier's production line.
c2.read:
Five station boxes on top, a band row underneath. Read the boxes left to right.

The five boxes run from design on the left to delivery and export on the right. Under each name you get what happens there and who stands there. As you move right, the names shift from DRDO and foreign engine makers, to alloy and electronics suppliers, to private sub-system makers, to the primes and yards, and finally to the armed forces and export customers.

The band row is unusual on this card. Station one is coloured as the rival band, DRDO and foreign OEMs. That is the visual statement that the most critical knowledge, especially engines, still sits outside listed India. Station two is imports and Midhani. Listed India holds stations three and four, sub-systems and integration. Station five belongs to the customer, the armed forces.

So listed defence is a middle-of-the-chain business, just as in many industries, but with a twist: its supplier at station one is often its own government lab, or a foreign company whose government controls export licences.

Read the geography note next. Bengaluru for aerospace, Hyderabad for missiles and electronics, and the shipyards on both coasts. Its last line is the one to remember: the foreign content hides in the engines and sensors.

Use the diagram as a delay tracer. A late engine at station one becomes an undelivered fighter at station four. A sensor export licence held up abroad at station two becomes a missile battery waiting for its seeker. The so-what line sums it up: India has nationalised the last two stations, and both the profit and the delay come from the first two.

c3.story:
In most industries, demand is the sum of millions of choices. In Indian defence, it is the sum of a few committee meetings. Three services and one ministry make almost every buying decision, which means demand is a policy choice, not a market outcome. It can be accelerated by a border clash or frozen by a scandal.

The air force is the biggest-ticket buyer and the one with the most visible problem: too few fighter squadrons as old Soviet-era aircraft retire. That gap is why HAL signed for a large batch of upgraded Tejas fighters in 2021 and a second, bigger batch in September 2025. But the air force's demand runs through a supply bottleneck: imported engines decide how fast those fighters actually arrive.

The navy buys on the longest horizon of all. Its fleet plan, sharpened by Chinese naval activity in the Indian Ocean, keeps destroyers, frigates and submarines flowing to Mazagon Dock, Garden Reach and Cochin Shipyard for a decade at a time. Mazagon built the Scorpene-class submarines with France's Naval Group, and the navy's carrier-borne fighter deal for French Rafales, signed in 2025, adds another layer of demand.

The army is the most event-driven. Border tension with China and Pakistan triggers emergency procurement powers, and artillery, air-defence missiles, radios, drones and night vision are bought quickly. Operation Sindoor in May 2025 was a live demonstration: Indian-made missiles and air defence, including the Akash system built by BEL and BDL, performed in combat, and emergency orders followed.

A border clash moves the stocks for a month. A fleet plan moves the earnings for a decade.

Then come the customers who help solve the one-customer problem. Exports have hit records, led by deals such as the Philippines' purchase of BrahMos missiles in 2022. ISRO and newly private space companies buy launch structures and satellite electronics. And global aerospace majors buy machined parts from Indian suppliers as they diversify away from China. None of these is yet as large as the home market, but each one makes a company less dependent on a single ministry's calendar.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, one per customer. Each has three lines.

  • The name: the buyer.
  • What it buys: tells you which door benefits. Fighters and helicopters point to HAL; ships and sonar to the yards and BEL; missiles to BDL; parts to the aerospace door.
  • What moves it: your watch list. Squadron shortfalls and engine deliveries for the air force; the fleet plan and Chinese naval activity for the navy; border tension for the army; government-to-government deals for exports; launch cadence for space; Airbus and Boeing production rates for the global majors.

Sort the tiles into two groups. The first four, the three services and the paramilitary, are the home budget. They are huge but they share one wallet and one approval process. The last three, export customers, space and global aerospace, are the diversifiers. They are smaller, but they follow different clocks.

Then link each to a door. A prime selling mostly to the air force is tied to engine deliveries. A shipyard is tied to the navy's fleet plan and its own dock capacity. A private electronics name can sit behind several tiles at once, which is one reason its lumpiness can smooth out over time. An aerospace parts maker barely touches the first four tiles at all.

The so-what under the grid warns that a single committee meeting can accelerate or freeze demand. So the best use of this grid is as a map of whose decisions to follow: each tile's moves-with line names the decision-maker or event that will show up in orders a year later.

c4.story:
Picture a caterer with one extremely wealthy client. The client pays half the bill before the wedding. The caterer puts that money in a fixed deposit, earns interest on it, and cooks at a measured pace. The risk is not that the client leaves; there is nowhere else to go. The risk is that the imported oven arrives late. That, roughly, is the economics of an Indian defence prime.

Look at the raw-material line first. A prime spends about half its revenue on materials, components and imported kits. Here is the subtle point: an imported kit carries almost no margin for the prime. If HAL assembles a licensed design from foreign kits, it earns an integration fee. If it designs and sources the parts at home, it keeps far more. Rising indigenous content is not only a patriotic slogan; it is a margin lever.

The shipyards have a heavier raw-material bill, with steel, engines, weapons and sensors bought in, and fixed-price contracts that run for years. So their margins are thinner, and they swing on the calendar. Finish a ship early and you may earn an incentive; finish late and liquidated damages, contractual penalties for delay, eat into profit.

Strip out the interest on the customer's own money, and you see what the factory really earns.

Now the line that flatters everyone. The forces pay large advances, and those advances sit on the balance sheet as cash. Interest on that cash flows into other income. For a shipyard, it can be a fifth of profit. That is real money, but it is treasury income, not manufacturing skill, and it will shrink if rates fall or advances are consumed.

Depreciation and interest barely matter. The PSU factories are old and largely written down, and almost every listed name is debt-free. Capex matters only when it unlocks the order book: a new Tejas production line at HAL, a new dry dock at a yard. And working capital is a tale of two doors: negative for shipyards sitting on advances, painfully positive for private suppliers waiting on the primes to pay.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: on the left a state-owned platform prime, on the right a shipyard.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar, materials, components and imported kits, takes roughly half of a prime's sales and about seven tenths of a shipyard's. That gap is design content: a prime that designs more keeps more.
  • The opex bar, people, testing, power and overheads, is bigger at the prime, roughly a quarter of sales, because design engineers and flight testing are expensive.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a barely visible sliver in both. Old factories, no debt.
  • The last bar is what is left. The prime keeps about a fifth of sales; the shipyard about half that.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount. And note one thing the bars do not show: other income from advances, which sits below them and makes reported profit look better still.

The list below marks which lines matter. Order book and inflow, revenue conversion of the book, gross margin with indigenous content, and other income from advances all get a yes. Working capital, capex and liquidated damages get a sometimes, each with a door-specific reason. Depreciation and interest get a no.

Notice that other income is a yes here, which is rare. In most industries on this page it is noise. In defence it can be a fifth of a shipyard's profit, which is why the so-what line tells you to strip it out to see what the factories actually earn.

c5.story:
Defence does not have a market cycle in the usual sense. Nobody's prices crash because of a glut of frigates. It has a policy cycle: periods when the government wants to buy, buys at home and decides quickly, and periods when it does none of those things.

The last boom came after Kargil. From 2004 to 2010, modernisation money flowed, large import deals were signed and the PSU primes grew fat on licensed production of foreign designs. Then came the brake. Around 2010 to 2012, the VVIP helicopter bribery scandal and a run of blacklisted vendors made the ministry deeply cautious. Files piled up in committees.

The bust from 2013 to 2018 was long and dull. Procurement froze. The marquee fighter tender for over a hundred aircraft collapsed into a small off-the-shelf purchase of Rafales. HAL listed in 2018 into a cold market and its shares slipped below the issue price. By 2019, the aircraft prime was borrowing to pay salaries while it waited for the ministry to clear its dues.

Then two events reset the policy. The Balakot strikes in 2019 exposed the squadron gap. The Galwan clash with China in 2020 changed the politics entirely: the first list of weapons that could no longer be imported was published, foreign ownership limits were raised, and the procurement manual was rewritten to rank Indian design first.

Galwan did for Indian defence stocks what no budget speech ever had: it made buying Indian a strategic necessity.

The boom that followed was spectacular. Big Tejas orders, record exports, the first home-built carrier commissioned, private suppliers listing and re-rating. In 2024 order placement slowed into the election, valuations were extreme and the stocks corrected sharply even as order books stayed full. Then Operation Sindoor in May 2025 proved Indian-made missiles in combat, emergency orders followed, a second Tejas batch and carrier-borne Rafales were cleared, and the stocks rallied back.

Today the constraint is not demand. It is engines, docks and delivery.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. Under each arc sit the years of the last policy cycle: boom from 2004 to 2010, peak around 2010 to 2012, bust from 2013 to 2018, bottom in 2019 and 2020. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled boom, execution-paced: record order books, deliveries lag engines. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase.

The timeline from 2019 is colour-coded. 2019 is a bust year. 2020 is neutral, the hinge year when Galwan reset policy. Then boom entries for 2021 to 2023, a neutral 2024 for the election-year correction, boom again in 2025 after Operation Sindoor, and the now entry for 2026, where order books stand at several years of sales.

The four hands are what you watch.

  • Defence capital budget growth: rising in the low teens, arrow up. More approvals can become contracts.
  • Order book to sales at the primes: several years, arrow up. Good only if execution keeps pace.
  • Engine and import deliveries: slipping, arrow down. This is the one hand pointing the wrong way, and it is the most important: late engines mean fighters built but not delivered.
  • Export order wins: rising, arrow up. Proof of competitiveness and a loosening of the one-customer problem.

Three hands up on demand, one down on supply. That is what an execution-paced boom looks like. The so-what states the consequence: revenue, not orders, is the surprise variable, and a stock can fall on a record order book if deliveries slip.

c6.story:
Most industries on this page are moved by prices: copper, crude, interest rates. Defence is moved by decisions. Three of them carry the heaviest weight, and none has a price chart.

The first is the defence capital budget, the slice of defence spending that buys new equipment rather than paying salaries and pensions. It is the money available to sign and pay for contracts. A rise this year shows up as orders and advances next year. The second is border tension. Conflict pulls orders forward through emergency procurement and stiffens political will for big programmes. The third, and the most important for listed companies, is the share of procurement bought at home. A rupee spent on an imported fighter does nothing for HAL; a rupee shifted onto a positive indigenisation list flows straight to Indian order books.

Conflict moves the stocks for a month. The budget and the share bought at home move the earnings for a decade.

Then come the dials that cost money. A weaker rupee raises the cost of imported engines, sensors and kits on contracts priced in rupees. Western export controls and delivery schedules decide when engines and sensors arrive; tighter controls, or simply a busy American factory, delay fighters and ships.
