And fiscal space matters because a stretched government finds it easier to delay capital spending, or payments to the primes, than to cut salaries.

A few dials are double-edged. Global defence spending is rising, which opens export markets for Indian missiles and radars but also tightens the supply of the very engines and parts India needs. Crude oil hurts the Indian budget but swells the wallets of Gulf export customers.

And one dial runs the opposite way from most industries: higher interest rates help. Because the primes and yards sit on large customer advances in cash, higher rates lift their other income. It is a small effect, but it shows how unusual this industry's balance sheets are.
c6.read:
One row per dial. Read across: the dial, its channel, what a rise does, its weight and today's reading.

  • Channel: the route into profits, from the money available to sign contracts to the interest earned on advances.
  • A rise does: green up arrows on the capital budget, border tension, the share bought at home and, unusually, interest rates. Red down arrows on the rupee, Western export controls, fiscal space and steel. Diamonds on global defence spending and crude.
  • Weight: three rows carry three dots, the most of any industry here: capital budget, border tension and share bought at home. That trio is the whole thesis.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track. Look closely at which ones do: the rupee, a bond proxy for fiscal space, exports, the money-market rate, steel output and crude. Two of the three heaviest dials, the capital budget and the share bought at home, have no live series at all and show a dash; border tension is proxied by the market's volatility index, a rough stand-in. In other words, the dials that matter most for defence are read from budget documents and policy announcements, not from a price screen.

How to use it: after each Union budget, check the capital line and any new indigenisation list. Those two readings will tell you more about the next few years than any quarterly result. Then glance at the red rows to see whether engines and fiscal pressure are slowing delivery and payment.

The so-what line puts it plainly: track the defence capital budget and the share bought at home.

c7.story:
Indian defence has an odd problem for a booming industry. Demand is not the constraint. The government has signed, the order books are full, and the stocks have priced it in. What limits growth is how fast the factories and their foreign suppliers can actually deliver.

The biggest bottleneck is the engine. India does not make a fighter engine. Marine gas turbines and many helicopter engines are imported too. When GE's deliveries of Tejas engines slipped, HAL's fighter line slowed to a crawl, and with it the revenue that analysts had pencilled in. GE and HAL agreed in 2023 to produce a more powerful GE engine in India, but a truly home-grown fighter engine remains years away.

Sensors and chips follow the same pattern. Seekers, infrared sensors and radar chips come from Israel, the US and Europe. A diplomatic chill or a supplier's own backlog upstream becomes a delivery slip downstream.

India has the order books of a superpower and the engine supply of a customer.

Then the factories themselves. When order books hit several years of sales, the production line becomes the limit. HAL has added a production line for the Tejas, but each line takes years and skilled hands to stand up. Shipyards face the physical version: each yard has a fixed number of docks and slipways, and a delayed launch blocks the next keel from being laid.

The customer brings its own frictions. The ministry decides on its own clock; a programme can take years to move from approval to signed contract, and a new minister can reset it. When its budget runs short, it has paid the primes late, which is how HAL ended up borrowing for salaries in 2019. And procurement scandals, from Bofors in the 1980s to the helicopter deal a generation later, can blacklist vendors and freeze programmes for years.

Finally, a market bottleneck: retail money arrives in waves. The stocks have swung by half on sentiment while order books barely moved, which is both a risk and an opportunity.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck: what it is, why it bites, and a severity label.

  • Structural: four rows, engines from abroad, one customer with slow decisions, shipyard capacity and dry docks, and imported sensors and chips. That is a heavy structural load. These do not go away with a good budget; they set the pace of the whole industry.
  • Cyclical: execution at the primes. When order books balloon, factories become the limit; when books normalise, so does this.
  • Recurring: payment delays when the ministry's budget runs short, and procurement scandals. Both have happened before and both freeze activity when they return.
  • Two-sided: valuation and retail crowding. It is the only row about the stock rather than the business. It cuts both ways: crowding inflates prices in a rally and creates bargains in a sell-off.

Now read the so-what line, which pairs the rows in an unusual way. The first and third rows, engines and execution, decide this year's revenue. The second and seventh, slow decisions and scandals, decide whether the next decade of orders arrives on time. So split your attention: a quarterly results watch on engines and execution, and a slower political watch on approvals and probity.

A practical habit: when a defence prime misses revenue estimates, check which row caused it. An engine delay is a timing problem that reverses when shipments resume. A slower approval pipeline is a demand problem that compounds. They look identical in a single quarter and very different over two years.

c8.story:
In defence, the rulebook is not something that happens to the industry. It is the industry. Every order begins as a ministry decision and travels through a procurement manual written by the same ministry.

The starting point is the Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by the defence minister. It approves what to buy, in which category and from whom. An approval is called an acceptance of necessity, and it is the first public sign that a programme is coming. But it is only a first sign. The gap between a council approval and a signed contract, often a year or more of trials, negotiation and cabinet clearance, is the sector's real clock.

The Defence Acquisition Procedure, revised in 2020, is the procurement manual. Its most important feature is a ranking of categories that puts indigenously designed, developed and manufactured equipment at the top. A programme in that category is almost guaranteed to go to an Indian prime with an Indian supply chain.

A positive indigenisation list is the closest thing to a guaranteed order a listed company will ever see.

Then the positive indigenisation lists, first published in August 2020: lists of weapons and components that may no longer be imported after set dates. Each list converts future import spending into domestic orders on a schedule. The government has published several since, covering everything from artillery to small components.

Other rules widen the ecosystem. Foreign investment limits were raised so that global majors can set up joint ventures in India, creating orders for local suppliers. Two defence industrial corridors, in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, offer land and incentives for private manufacturing. Export promotion through government-to-government deals and lines of credit is the only real escape from the one-customer problem.

Underneath it all sit DRDO, whose development timelines become the primes' production timelines, and the quality agencies that certify airworthiness. And at the edge, IN-SPACe and the new space policy are opening launch and satellite work to private companies, a second customer set for electronics and structures makers.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care and its status.

  • Always: three rows, the Ministry of Defence with the Defence Acquisition Council, the Department of Defence Production with the quality agencies, and DRDO. These are the permanent machinery. The council is the one to follow most closely, because every large order starts as one of its approvals.
  • Live: five rows, the Defence Acquisition Procedure, the positive indigenisation lists, foreign investment rules, the defence corridors, and export promotion with lines of credit. These are the policy push that turned the sector around after 2020, and each one is still adding orders.
  • New: one row, IN-SPACe and the space policy. A slow-burn second market rather than a quarter mover.

There are no coming rows, which tells you something. The policy architecture is built. What investors watch now is how fast it is used: how many council approvals convert to contracts, how many new items each indigenisation list adds, how many export licences are cleared.

Read the why column of the first row twice: the approval-to-contract gap is the sector's clock. It links directly to the cross-intelligence card, where council approvals appear as the earliest warning signal of all.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. For defence, look there for council approvals, new lists and signed contracts.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money. Apply them to Indian defence and you get a result that looks wrong at first glance: the company with an all-powerful single customer keeps the most.

Start with the state-owned primes. Rivalry is almost absent. No Indian private company can build a fighter or a missile system at scale, and the government channels platform work to its own factories. Entry is practically impossible for the same reason. The buyer, the ministry, has full power over price in theory. In practice it wants its own factories to prosper, often prices contracts on cost plus a margin, and pays advances. A customer who wants you to succeed is a very different thing from a customer who merely can squeeze you.

The primes' weak spot is suppliers. Engines and key sensors come from a handful of foreign makers who set their own schedules. HAL can have the government's full backing and still wait on one American factory. That is the heaviest spoke in their shape.

The primes' customer is their protector. Their supplier is their bottleneck.

Substitution is the other force with bite for the primes. The substitute for a prime's product is an import. The indigenisation lists are steadily closing that route, but it has not vanished: big-ticket items like the Rafale still come from abroad.

Now the private electronics names. They face real rivalry, bidding against each other and against the primes' own in-house units. Their buyer is not the friendly ministry but the primes and the labs above them, who can and do squeeze suppliers on price and payment terms. New private suppliers appear every year as the primes outsource more. In return, their parts face little substitution, and they depend somewhat less on foreign engines.

The net result is the pattern from the first card. The primes keep the most because their customer wants them to. The private names grow faster but keep less, and their fortunes rise and fall with how generously the primes choose to outsource.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: state-owned platform primes and private electronics and sub-systems. The overall picture is interesting. The prime's shape is not uniformly small: it is tiny on rivalry and entrants, then shoots out to the outer ring on suppliers. The private shape is rounder and more even, moderate on every spoke.

Look for the crossings. There are two. On suppliers, the prime reaches further, three against two: foreign engine and sensor makers set the schedule. On substitutes, the prime reaches further again, one and a half against one: the import route is a substitute for its product. Everywhere else, the prime's shape sits inside the private one.

The table gives the scores and reasons.

  • Rivalry: half against two. No domestic rival on platforms.
  • Buyer: two against two and a half. One powerful customer for both, but the private names face the primes above them.
  • Entrants: half against two. Nobody enters platform integration; new suppliers appear yearly.

How to use it: the supplier spoke is the one to watch for primes. If engine co-production at home becomes real, that spoke shrinks and the prime's shape becomes small almost everywhere. For the private names, watch the buyer spoke: if the primes outsource more generously, it shrinks; if they bring work in-house, it grows.

c10.story:
Defence results calls are full of excitement: new platforms, export enquiries, technology partnerships. Underneath, eight numbers tell you whether the factory is keeping up with the hype.

Start with the order book against trailing sales, which tells you how many years of revenue are already visible. A few years is excellent. Beyond a certain point, though, a bigger book stops being good news and starts being a question about execution: can the factory ever deliver all that? Then order inflow for the year, which tells you whether council approvals actually became contracts.

Sales growth is the execution check. A record book with sluggish sales growth means deliveries are slipping, usually for want of engines or dock space. EBITDA margin tells you about design content and pricing on cost-plus contracts; primes, shipyards and private electronics each have their own normal range.

In defence, a bigger order book is good news until it becomes a question.

Now the number that separates a factory from a treasury: other income as a share of profit. Customer advances earn interest, and that interest can make a mediocre manufacturing year look healthy. If a large share of pre-tax profit is other income, you are partly buying a fixed deposit.

Receivable days tell you whether the ministry is paying on time, which it has not always done. Return on capital tells you what the business earns on the money tied up in it, ideally measured excluding the customer's own cash, which otherwise distorts the picture. And capex to depreciation asks whether new production lines and docks are being built to clear the book. A prime with a book worth many years of sales and no new capacity is telling you, quietly, that it will take a decade to deliver.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the metric, what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: the question to ask of each company.
  • What good looks like: the only column with figures. The EBITDA margin row gives three ranges, for primes, shipyards and private electronics; use the one that matches the door. The order book row has a ceiling as well as a floor: above a certain multiple, execution becomes the question.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest annual filings in our database. Three rows have no median, order book to sales, order inflow and other income as a share of profit, because they come from presentations or need adjusting by hand. Those are the rows where your own homework matters most.

A good reading order: order book and inflow from the investor presentation, then sales growth from the results to judge execution, then other income against pre-tax profit to see how much is treasury, and finally capex to depreciation for whether capacity is being added.

Then compare three things for any company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. Bear in mind the median blends primes, yards and small private suppliers, so its margin will fall somewhere between the door benchmarks.

One special warning for the ROCE row: a debt-free company sitting on customer advances can show an inflated or distorted return on capital. The tells column says it: measure it excluding customer cash.

c11.story:
Defence is the industry where you can see orders coming furthest ahead, because the government announces its intentions in stages. The trick is knowing how long each stage takes.

The earliest signals speak three quarters ahead. A Defence Acquisition Council approval becomes a signed contract and an advance roughly a year later. A new positive indigenisation list converts future imports into domestic orders from its stated date. Both are public, and both tell you about orders that the results will not show for most of a year.

Two quarters ahead come the Union budget's defence capital outlay, foreign engine makers' delivery guidance, export licence approvals and government-to-government talks, the primes' commentary on outsourcing to private vendors, and Airbus and Boeing production rates for the aerospace parts makers. Of these, engine guidance is the one most investors underweight. It sets when fighters actually get delivered, which sets when HAL books the revenue.

And then the same-quarter signal: border incidents and conflict. Emergency orders land within weeks and the stocks move the same day, as they did around Operation Sindoor in May 2025.

Approvals tell you about demand. Engine deliveries tell you about revenue. Confuse the two and you will be surprised every quarter.

These signals feed a three-sign rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when the capital budget is growing, approvals are turning into signed contracts, and deliveries are keeping pace with the book. Three of three is a clean boom; two is a boom with a delivery problem; one is a policy pause. Today the budget is growing in the low teens, a tick. Approvals are converting in a post-conflict rush, a tick. Deliveries are not keeping pace, with engines slipping, a cross.

That gives the call: a policy-driven boom with a delivery bottleneck. Prefer primes and shipyards with proven execution and visible advances, and treat the private small caps as single-contract bets, sized accordingly. Valuations have swung by half twice in three years, so entry price matters more here than almost anywhere.
c11.read:
The chart places outside signals by how far ahead they speak. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

For defence, the dots lean right. Only one sits at the far left: border incidents and conflict, a same-quarter signal. A large group sits at two quarters: the budget's capital outlay, foreign engine delivery guidance, export licences and talks, primes' outsourcing commentary, and Airbus and Boeing rates. Two dots sit furthest right at three quarters: council approvals and new indigenisation lists. This is an industry that warns early, if you read the right documents.

Use it as a reading order. Each quarter, start at the right: what did the council approve, and did a new list appear? Then the two-quarter cluster: is engine guidance improving, are exports clearing, are the primes outsourcing more? The left-hand dot tells you only what has already happened, often already in the price.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs.

  • Capital budget growing: a tick, low teens.
  • Approvals becoming contracts: a tick, post-conflict rush.
  • Deliveries keeping pace: a cross, engines slipping.

Two of three: a boom with a delivery problem.

Finally, the call box with its points and what would change it. Use the last three as alerts. A procurement scandal or ministerial reset would freeze signings. A fiscal squeeze would flatten the budget or delay payments. And engine deliveries normalising is the upside alert: it would turn the cross into a tick and release a revenue catch-up.

explainer.one_liner: E-commerce companies put a shop, a restaurant, a job board or a railway counter inside your phone, take a small cut of every order, and spend enormous sums on riders, warehouses and discounts so that you keep coming back.

doors.name: Delivery marketplaces
doors.sub: A cut of every food or grocery order, plus ads from restaurants and brands, minus the rider and the dark store
doors.blurb: A bet that order frequency rises faster than the cost of the last mile

doors.name: Classifieds and listings
doors.sub: Recruiters, sellers and dealers pay a subscription or a listing fee; the platform owns no stock and delivers nothing
doors.blurb: A bet on a network that is already the default, so every extra rupee is nearly all profit

doors.name: Own-stock vertical retailers
doors.sub: Buy or make the product, sell it online and in stores, keep the full retail margin and carry the inventory
doors.blurb: A bet on a brand and a category, where the website is just the shopfront

doors.name: Toll booths
doors.sub: A tiny fee per ticket, per order or per truck trip on a very large number of transactions
doors.blurb: A bet on volume and on nobody changing the toll

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a dabbawala who also runs the kitchen's advertising. Door two is the newspaper's classifieds page, now on a phone. Door three is a shop that happens to have a very long queue outside its website. Door four is the toll plaza on the highway: small change, every car, every day.
explainer.door_so_what: A delivery name is valued on how fast its losses shrink, a classifieds name on how high its margin already is, a vertical retailer on store economics, and a toll booth on whether anyone can touch the toll, so the same results headline means different things behind each door.

stations.name: Traffic
stations.what: Cheap data, cheap smartphones and UPI bring the customer to the app; ads on Google, Meta and cricket bring them back
stations.who: Jio and Airtel, Google and Meta, NPCI's UPI

stations.name: Supply
stations.what: Restaurants, kiranas, brands, factories, recruiters and dealers list what they sell
stations.who: Millions of small sellers; INDIAMART and JUSTDIAL organise them

stations.name: Platform
stations.what: The app matches buyer and seller, takes payment and keeps a cut or a fee
stations.who: ETERNAL, SWIGGY, MEESHO, NYKAA, NAUKRI, LENSKART, IRCTC

stations.name: Fulfilment
stations.what: Dark stores, warehouses, gig riders and trucks move the parcel in ten minutes or two days
stations.who: Amazon and Flipkart's own networks, Delhivery, gig riders, BLACKBUCK's truckers

stations.name: Customer
stations.what: Urban households order dinner, milk, lipstick and spectacles; small firms order supplies; job seekers apply
stations.who: Metro and Tier-2 households, small businesses, travellers

kitchen.rival: Amazon and Flipkart
kitchen.note: The money is made in the top eight cities, where dark stores sit within a few kilometres of dense, well-off flats; the Tier-2 story is real for ticketing and social commerce but thin for quick commerce. Riders and real estate are the cost lines that geography sets.
kitchen.so_what: Amazon and Flipkart stand at the fulfilment station with foreign balance sheets, so every listed name's margin depends on how hard those two choose to fight in that quarter.

end_markets.name: Urban households
end_markets.buys: Dinner, groceries in ten minutes, beauty, eyewear, baby products, mattresses
end_markets.moves_with: Urban salaried incomes, IT hiring, discretionary mood

end_markets.name: Restaurants and cloud kitchens
end_markets.buys: Orders, delivery and advertising slots
end_markets.moves_with: Eating-out frequency, food inflation, their own margins after the platform's cut

end_markets.name: Brands and FMCG makers
end_markets.buys: Ad slots and shelf space on the app, quick-commerce listings
end_markets.moves_with: Marketing budgets, the shift of grocery spend from kirana to app

end_markets.name: Small sellers and factories
end_markets.buys: Leads, listings and a payment rail
end_markets.moves_with: Small-business confidence, GST compliance, working-capital availability

end_markets.name: Recruiters
end_markets.buys: Job postings and resume database access
end_markets.moves_with: IT services hiring, startup funding, white-collar attrition

end_markets.name: Travellers
end_markets.buys: Train, bus and flight tickets with a convenience fee
end_markets.moves_with: Rail capacity, holidays, fuel prices and airfares

end_markets.name: Car buyers and dealers
end_markets.buys: Used-car listings, auctions and leads
end_markets.moves_with: New-car waiting lists, used-car prices, auto finance rates

end_markets.name: Truck owners
end_markets.buys: Fuel cards, toll payments, loads and GPS tracking
end_markets.moves_with: Freight demand, diesel prices, highway tolls

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Nearly every buyer here is urban and salaried, so an IT hiring freeze or a weak urban-wage print is an e-commerce order-frequency signal a quarter early.

lines.line: Gross order value and take rate
lines.why: Revenue is a cut of what flows through; growth in flow times the cut is the whole top line, and ad income lifts the cut without hurting the seller
What is left after the rider, the packaging and the discount; the first number that turns positive in a delivery business and the one the stock trades on
The dial management turns to buy growth; a quarter of soaring orders with soaring marketing is bought, not earned
Marketplaces collect from the customer today and pay the seller later, so cash arrives before cost; own-stock retailers carry months of inventory instead
Dark stores, warehouses and store fit-outs now sit on the balance sheet; the shift to owning inventory makes this line grow
Dark-store roll-outs are the capex line; a store takes two to three quarters to mature, so a build phase depresses margins while the future improves
A large, non-cash charge that keeps reported profit far below adjusted profit; read both numbers
Almost every listed name is net cash from its IPO; interest is other income, not a cost

pnl.analogy: A delivery platform is a wedding caterer who is paid a fixed cut per plate but pays each waiter per plate carried; the business works only when the hall is full. A classifieds site is the hall owner: once built, every extra booking is nearly pure profit.
pnl.so_what: Read contribution margin per order and marketing spend together: margin up with marketing flat is real operating leverage, margin up with marketing down is harvesting, and margin flat with marketing up is a price war.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, but to the funding cycle rather than the economic one. When global money is cheap, platforms raise, burn and grow; when rates rise, the money stops, the discounts stop and the weakest players fold or sell.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Lockdowns push grocery, food and beauty online; cheap global money funds a listing wave led by Zomato and Nykaa

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Loss-making platforms list at record valuations and every category gets a ten-minute delivery start-up

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Rate hikes end cheap money, platform stocks fall by well over half, the funding winter starts and Zomato buys a distressed Blinkit

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Platforms pivot to profit, food delivery turns positive, discounts fade and the survivors consolidate

clock.position_detail: profits arriving, valuations full, quick-commerce war easing

timeline.what: A tighter FDI press note bars foreign-owned marketplaces from owning stock or favouring sellers, and Amazon and Flipkart restructure around it. Food delivery is a two-horse race funded by discounts.
COVID-19 moves groceries, medicines and dinner onto the phone for good. Cheap global money arrives, Zomato lists in 2021 to a frenzy and Nykaa follows; quick commerce is born as a ten-minute promise.

The bust. Global rates rise, the funding winter sets in, Zomato's stock falls to a fraction of its listing price and it buys Blinkit cheaply. Every platform swaps growth slides for profitability slides.
The bottom. Food delivery turns profitable, Blinkit becomes the surprise growth engine, and the stocks begin a long climb.
A second listing wave starts: Ixigo, FirstCry, Swiggy and Blackbuck list. Quick commerce becomes the hottest category in Indian consumer and dark-store counts double.

Zomato renames itself Eternal and moves Blinkit to owning its own stock after the FDI cap is eased. The quick-commerce war with Zepto and Instamart peaks in losses. Urban Company, Lenskart, Meesho and Wakefit list; a new GST charge lands on delivery services.

Eternal is the year's standout large-cap on narrowing quick-commerce losses and strong food-delivery profit, Nykaa and Meesho hold their IPO gains, and FSSAI is moving to make online food players directly accountable. Valuations are full and the sector trades on execution, not hope.

hands.name: Quick-commerce contribution margin
hands.meaning: Positive means the war is being won on economics; a fresh dip means a new entrant is spending

hands.name: Marketing cost to revenue
hands.meaning: Falling means growth is organic; rising with flat orders means a price war

hands.name: US ten-year yield
hands.meaning: Lower yields re-rate long-duration growth stocks and reopen funding for rivals

hands.name: Dark-store additions
hands.meaning: Slowing means harvesting begins; a renewed surge means another round of burn

clock.so_what: In a listing wave the stocks run ahead of the economics, so the next leg depends on contribution margins keeping their promise while global rates stay kind.

dials.name: US ten-year yield
dials.channel: Discount rate on profits that arrive years from now, and the global funding tap for rivals
dials.rise_does: crushes valuations and dries up competitor funding

dials.name: Urban salaried incomes and IT hiring
dials.channel: Order frequency, basket size and job postings
dials.rise_does: lifts orders, baskets and Naukri billings

dials.name: India policy rate
dials.channel: Consumer credit for big-ticket online purchases and the valuation of growth
dials.rise_does: slows EMIs and discretionary baskets

dials.name: Fuel price
dials.channel: Rider and truck cost per delivery
dials.rise_does: raises last-mile cost and squeezes contribution margin

dials.name: Food inflation
dials.channel: Basket value in grocery, restaurant prices in food delivery
dials.rise_does: fattens order value but trims frequency

dials.name: Risk appetite
dials.channel: Multiples on loss-making and recently listed names
dials.rise_does: widens the premium on growth stocks

dials.name: Rupee against the dollar
dials.channel: Foreign flows into listed platforms and imported devices
dials.rise_does: weaker rupee pushes foreign holders to sell

dials.name: FDI and foreign competition policy
dials.channel: What Amazon, Flipkart and foreign-owned platforms may own and sell
dials.rise_does: tighter rules protect Indian-owned platforms

dials.name: Gig-worker and GST rules
dials.channel: Cost of the rider and the tax on the delivery fee
dials.rise_does: raises last-mile cost per order

dials.name: Smartphone and data penetration
dials.channel: New users from smaller towns
dials.rise_does: adds the next hundred million shoppers

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track the US ten-year yield for the multiple and urban hiring for the orders; together they explain most of the swings since 2021.

bottlenecks.name: Last-mile cost
bottlenecks.why: A human on a bike carries every order, so the cost per delivery falls only with density. Below a certain number of orders per rider per hour, growth adds losses.

bottlenecks.name: Amazon and Flipkart's balance sheets
bottlenecks.why: The two largest rivals are unlisted in India and funded by foreign parents who can lose money for a decade. Price discipline is borrowed, not owned.

bottlenecks.name: Funding-driven competition
bottlenecks.why: Every time global money is cheap a new entrant arrives with discounts; Zepto did it in quick commerce and Rapido is doing it in food delivery.

bottlenecks.name: Policy on foreign ownership
bottlenecks.why: The marketplace versus inventory rule is rewritten every few years, and each rewrite reshuffles who may own stock and who may not.

bottlenecks.name: Gig-worker regulation
bottlenecks.why: State gig-worker welfare laws, the labour codes and GST on delivery fees each add a few rupees per order, which is the whole contribution margin.

bottlenecks.name: Dark-store real estate
bottlenecks.why: The right two thousand square feet near rich flats is scarce and rents rise with every competitor's expansion.

bottlenecks.name: Kirana and dealer pushback
bottlenecks.why: Trader associations lobby against deep discounting and quick commerce, and the government listens before elections.

bottlenecks.name: Stock-option dilution
bottlenecks.why: Large annual option grants quietly transfer a slice of the company from shareholders to employees every year.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two never go away and cap margins for delivery names; the funding cycle decides when the next price war starts, so watch rivals' fund-raises as closely as results.

rulebook.what: Decides whether a foreign-owned platform may hold inventory or must stay a pure marketplace
rulebook.why: Shapes Amazon and Flipkart's business model and gave Indian-owned platforms a structural edge; Eternal's inventory pivot rests on it

rulebook.body: Department of Consumer Affairs and the CCPA
rulebook.what: E-commerce consumer-protection rules, the ban on dark patterns and fake reviews, service-charge rules
rulebook.why: Each rule adds compliance cost and limits nudges that lift conversion

rulebook.what: Antitrust probes into preferential sellers, deep discounting and exclusive launches
rulebook.why: A finding against Amazon or Flipkart changes the competitive rules for everyone

rulebook.what: Tax collected at source on sellers, and GST now charged on local delivery services through platforms
rulebook.why: The delivery-fee tax is paid out of the contribution margin or passed to the customer

rulebook.body: Labour codes and state gig-worker laws
rulebook.what: Social-security contributions and welfare boards for gig riders, starting in Rajasthan and Karnataka
rulebook.why: A levy per transaction lands straight on cost per order

rulebook.what: Hygiene ratings, labelling and now direct accountability for online food players
rulebook.why: A proposed amendment would make platforms liable for what restaurants and dark stores sell

rulebook.body: Ministry of Railways and IRCTC's mandate
rulebook.what: The monopoly on online rail ticketing and the convenience fee
rulebook.why: The fee has been waived and restored before; it is the toll booth's whole profit

rulebook.what: A government-backed open network meant to unbundle the marketplaces
rulebook.why: A slow but real threat to take rates if it ever scales

rulebook.what: A proposed ex-ante law for large digital platforms, on the EU model
rulebook.why: Would restrict self-preferencing and bundling by the biggest players

why.rivalry: Two or three delivery platforms fight for the same flat with the same riders and discounts; a classifieds leader is usually alone in its category
why.supplier: Riders can switch apps mid-shift and restaurants can delist; recruiters and sellers have nowhere else with the same audience
why.buyer: Customers keep two delivery apps and switch for a coupon; a recruiter cannot leave the biggest resume pool
why.entrants: A funded entrant can buy share in delivery within a year; building a classifieds network from scratch has failed repeatedly
why.substitutes: The kirana, the restaurant's own app and ONDC are substitutes for delivery; LinkedIn and job portals of the big IT firms nibble at classifieds

forces.so_what: Classifieds keeps most of the profit because its network is the moat, delivery keeps the least because the rider and the rival set the price, which is why a classifieds name earns high margins at a lower multiple while a delivery leader earns thin margins at a very high one.

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the flow through the platform is still compounding
cheat_sheet.good: Above 25% y/y for quick commerce, above 15% for food delivery

cheat_sheet.tells: How much of each order the platform keeps
cheat_sheet.good: Rising or steady at 18-22% for food delivery; ads above 3% of GOV

cheat_sheet.tells: Unit economics after the rider and the discount
cheat_sheet.good: Above 7% of GOV for food delivery; positive and rising for quick commerce

cheat_sheet.tells: Operating leverage after marketing and tech
cheat_sheet.good: Expanding every quarter; classifieds above 35%

cheat_sheet.metric: Marketing as a share of revenue
cheat_sheet.tells: Whether growth is bought or earned
cheat_sheet.good: Falling as a share while orders grow

cheat_sheet.metric: Monthly transacting users and order frequency
cheat_sheet.tells: The health of the network
cheat_sheet.good: Both rising; frequency above 3 orders a month for food delivery

cheat_sheet.tells: The gap between adjusted and reported profit
cheat_sheet.good: Stock-option charge below 5% of revenue and shrinking

cheat_sheet.tells: How many quarters of war the company can fund
cheat_sheet.good: Net cash of at least 8 quarters of burn, or burn at zero

lead_indicators.name: Rival fund-raises and dark-store announcements
lead_indicators.channel: A funded competitor spends on discounts within a quarter and margins follow

lead_indicators.name: IT services hiring and attrition commentary
lead_indicators.channel: White-collar hiring is Naukri's billings and the urban order budget

lead_indicators.name: US ten-year yield and Nasdaq growth multiples
lead_indicators.channel: Indian platform stocks re-rate with global growth stocks the same month

lead_indicators.name: FMCG companies' quick-commerce commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Brands' channel mix shows where grocery spend is moving before platform results

lead_indicators.name: Fuel prices and rider wage disputes
lead_indicators.channel: Last-mile cost per order rises a quarter later

lead_indicators.name: GST Council and labour-code announcements
lead_indicators.channel: A new levy per order takes a quarter or two to pass through or absorb

lead_indicators.name: Rail passenger volumes and airfares
lead_indicators.channel: Ticketing fees move with tickets sold the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: Used-car prices and auto finance rates
lead_indicators.channel: Dealer demand for listings follows the used-car market

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when contribution margins are expanding, marketing as a share of revenue is falling, and global yields are steady or lower; two of three means the rally rests on fundamentals, one of three means it rests on liquidity.

call.headline: Boom phase with real profits underneath. Prefer the leaders with proven unit economics and the asset-light classifieds names; treat freshly listed loss-makers as execution bets priced for perfection.
points: Food delivery is profitable and quick-commerce losses are narrowing at the leader, so the stock story has moved from hope to delivery.
The listing wave of 2024 and 2025 added a dozen names at full valuations; the market will sort them on contribution margin, not on gross order value.
Regulation is tightening at the edges: GST on delivery, gig-worker levies and FSSAI accountability each shave the margin per order.
would_change: A sharp rise in global yields that re-rates growth stocks and reopens the funding winter
A new, well-funded entrant restarting the quick-commerce discount war
A rewrite of the FDI or digital-competition rules that removes the Indian-owned platforms' edge

explainer.tell_a_friend: E-commerce companies put a shop, a restaurant or a railway counter inside your phone and take a cut of every order. The trick is that someone on a bike still has to carry the parcel, so a delivery platform makes money only when a neighbourhood is dense enough that one rider carries several orders an hour. A job board or a seller directory has no rider at all, which is why it earns fat margins. The sector runs on the global funding cycle rather than the Indian economy: when money was cheap in 2020 and 2021, platforms listed at wild prices and burned cash on discounts. When rates rose in 2022 the stocks collapsed and the survivors learned to make a profit. Food delivery turned profitable in 2023, quick commerce became the new battlefield, and a second wave of listings arrived in 2024 and 2025. Today profits are real but prices are full. Watch contribution margin per order, marketing as a share of revenue, and the US ten-year yield.

glossary.def: The total rupee value of everything bought through the platform. The platform's revenue is a slice of this, not the whole.
The platform's revenue as a share of gross order value: commissions plus ads plus fees, divided by GOV.
Revenue per order minus the direct cost of that order (rider, packaging, discount, payment fee). The first profit line to turn positive.
Operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and the stock-option charge. The number platforms prefer to headline.
A small warehouse closed to walk-in customers, stocked for ten-to-thirty-minute delivery to flats within a two-to-three kilometre radius.
Grocery and essentials delivered within minutes from a dark store: Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto.
The platform connects buyers and sellers and never owns the goods. Foreign-owned platforms in India were long restricted to this.
The platform buys and owns the stock it sells, keeping the full retail margin and the inventory risk.
Government rules on how much a foreign-owned online platform may own and whether it may hold stock; rewritten in 2018-19 and eased in 2025.
A listings business: recruiters, sellers or dealers pay to be found. The platform sells visibility, not goods.
A small fixed charge per ticket booked online. For IRCTC and Ixigo it is most of the profit.
A rider or service professional paid per task through an app, without an employment contract.

glossary.term: Social Security Code and gig-worker laws
glossary.def: Central and state laws requiring platforms to contribute 1-2% of each transaction to a welfare fund for gig workers.
App designs that trick users into paying more or subscribing: fake urgency, hidden fees, basket sneaking. Banned by the consumer-protection regulator in 2023.
Central Consumer Protection Authority, the enforcement arm under the Department of Consumer Affairs.
Competition Commission of India, the antitrust regulator probing preferential treatment and deep discounting by big platforms.
Open Network for Digital Commerce, a government-backed network meant to let any seller reach any buyer app without a single marketplace in between.
Shares granted to staff that vest over years. Charged as an expense, which is why reported profit trails adjusted profit.
The period from 2022 when venture capital dried up after global rate rises, forcing start-ups to cut burn.
The number of distinct customers who placed at least one order in a month.
The final leg from dark store or hub to the customer's door, carried by a rider. The most expensive kilometre.
Cash and investments minus borrowings. For listed platforms, the war chest left from the IPO.

c1.story:
Open your phone's home screen and count the shops on it. A restaurant row, a grocery store that promises ten minutes, a beauty counter, an optician, a railway booking window, a job board, maybe a used-car lot. Indian e-commerce is not one industry. It is a mall where every tenant runs a different business model, and the listed companies in it make money in four very different ways.

The first door is the delivery marketplace: Eternal, which owns Zomato and Blinkit, Swiggy with Instamart, and Urban Company sending a plumber instead of a parcel. It takes a cut of each order and earns ad money from restaurants and brands, but it also pays a human being to carry every single order to your door. That rider is the whole drama of the business.

The second door is classifieds and listings: Naukri for jobs, IndiaMART for factory supplies, Justdial for local services, CarTrade for used cars. These platforms own no stock and deliver nothing. Recruiters and sellers pay a subscription to be seen. Once the network is the default, each extra rupee of revenue is nearly all profit.

The third door is the own-stock vertical retailer: Nykaa, Lenskart, FirstCry, Wakefit. They buy or make the product and keep the full retail margin, which means they also carry the inventory. The website is a shopfront; the real business is a brand and a category, increasingly with physical stores beside the app.

The fourth door is the toll booth: IRCTC, Ixigo, Meesho, Blackbuck. A tiny fee on an enormous number of tickets, orders or truck trips.

The same headline, orders up a lot, means four different things behind four doors.

For a delivery name it may mean losses are about to shrink, or that discounts are buying growth. For a classifieds name it means a margin already high gets higher. For a vertical retailer the question is store economics. For a toll booth the only question that really matters is whether anyone can touch the toll.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, and give the bar the most attention.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how money comes in: a cut of every order minus the rider and the dark store; a subscription or listing fee with no stock and no delivery; the full retail margin on stock the company owns; or a tiny fee per ticket, order or truck trip.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Several of them listed only in 2024 or 2025, which matters later when we get to the cycle.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each rupee the company keeps. Classifieds sit at high: no rider, no warehouse. Vertical retailers and toll booths sit at medium. Delivery marketplaces sit at low, because the last mile and the rival's discounts take most of the order value.
  • The bet line names what you are really wagering on: order frequency outrunning delivery cost; a network already being the default; a brand and a category; volume with nobody changing the toll.

Then read the analogy and the so-what below. The so-what gives you four different yardsticks: how fast losses shrink, how high margins already are, how stores perform, and how safe the toll is. The trap is to compare a delivery name's margin with a classifieds name's margin; they are not the same species.

c2.story:
Every online order, whether it is a biryani, a lipstick or a train ticket, travels through the same five stations. Where the listed companies stand in that chain explains most of their economics.

The first station is traffic. Cheap mobile data after Jio arrived in 2016, cheap smartphones and UPI payments brought hundreds of millions of Indians online. Then the platforms rent their attention back from Google, Meta and the cricket broadcasters through ads. Nobody listed in this sector owns this station; they pay a toll to it.

The second is supply: the restaurants, kiranas, brands, factories, recruiters and car dealers with something to sell. Millions of small sellers, mostly unorganised. IndiaMART and Justdial earn their living by organising them.

The third is the platform itself, the app that matches buyer and seller, takes the payment and keeps a cut. This is where Eternal, Swiggy, Meesho, Nykaa, Naukri, Lenskart and IRCTC stand. It is the only station Indian listed companies clearly own.

The fourth is fulfilment: dark stores, warehouses, gig riders and trucks moving the parcel in ten minutes or two days. Here stand the two giants that are not listed in India, Amazon and Flipkart, with networks built on foreign balance sheets, alongside Delhivery and Blackbuck's truckers.

The fifth is the customer, overwhelmingly an urban household in the big metros, plus small businesses, job seekers and travellers.

The listed names own the matchmaking. The biggest rivals own the trucks.

That geography matters more than it looks. Quick commerce makes money only where a dark store sits within a few kilometres of dense, well-off flats. That is why the top eight cities carry the economics, and why the smaller-town story is real for ticketing and social commerce but thin for ten-minute grocery. And because Amazon and Flipkart sit at the fulfilment station with patient foreign capital, every listed name's margin depends partly on how hard those two choose to fight in a given quarter.
c2.read:
Two layers: the five stations across the top, and the band row underneath that says who holds each.

The five boxes run from traffic on the left to the customer on the right. Under each you get what happens there and who stands there. Read the who lines: telcos, Google, Meta and NPCI's UPI on the left; millions of small sellers next; the listed platforms in the middle; Amazon, Flipkart, Delhivery and gig riders at fulfilment; households on the right.

The band row compresses that into one line. The first two cells, telcos and tech giants then small sellers, are plain. The coloured India listed cell sits only under the platform station. The fulfilment cell is marked Amazon and Flipkart and coloured as the rival. The last cell is urban households.

So the visual story is simple. Indian listed e-commerce is a one-station business. It rents traffic from Google and Meta on the left. On its right, the fulfilment station is where its biggest competitors are strongest, and where delivery names like Eternal and Swiggy have to build their own dark stores and rider fleets to compete.

Use it like this: when news hits any station, trace it along the row. A rise in Google ad prices is a cost shock at station one. A rider strike or a fuel price hike is a cost shock at station four. Amazon announcing a ten-minute service is a competitive shock at station four aimed straight at the delivery door.

c3.story:
Who actually pays these companies? The answer is less obvious than it looks, because the person tapping the app is often not the main customer.

Take a food delivery order. You pay for the biryani and a delivery fee, and since 2023 a small platform fee on top. But the restaurant pays too: a commission on the order, and increasingly money for ads that push it up your feed. On a quick-commerce app, the shampoo brand pays for the banner and the prime slot on the virtual shelf. Advertising is how these platforms raise their cut without raising your bill.

Then look at the classifieds door. Naukri's customer is not the job seeker, who uses it free. It is the recruiter, paying for postings and database access. That makes Naukri's revenue a direct read on white-collar hiring, which in India means largely IT services. When TCS and Infosys freeze hiring, Naukri's billings feel it within a quarter or two. IndiaMART's customer is the small factory paying for leads, which moves with small-business confidence and GST compliance. CarTrade's customer is the dealer, paying to sell used cars, which moves with used-car prices and finance rates.

Toll booths have their own customers. Travellers pay IRCTC a convenience fee per ticket, so rail capacity and holidays decide its volume. Truck owners pay Blackbuck for fuel cards, tolls and loads.

What ties nearly all of them together is that the buyer is urban and salaried. A software engineer in Bengaluru orders dinner, buys skincare, books a train home for Diwali and, eventually, updates a resume.

An IT hiring freeze is an e-commerce earnings warning, delivered a quarter early.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read each in three lines: who pays, what they pay for, and what moves them.

  • The name tells you the payer: urban households, restaurants and cloud kitchens, brands and FMCG makers, small sellers and factories, recruiters, travellers, car buyers and dealers, truck owners.
  • The middle line is what they buy. Notice how many tiles buy attention rather than goods: ad slots, listings, leads, job postings. That is the take-rate engine.
  • The last line is the watch list outside the sector: urban incomes and IT hiring, food inflation, marketing budgets, small-business confidence, rail capacity and airfares, used-car prices, freight demand and diesel.

Now map each tile to a door. Households, restaurants and brands feed the delivery marketplaces and vertical retailers. Recruiters, small sellers and car dealers feed the classifieds door. Travellers and truck owners feed the toll booths.

The pattern to notice is concentration of driver. Several tiles, households, recruiters and to a degree brands, all move with the same thing: the health of urban salaried India. A sector that looks diversified across food, jobs, beauty and travel is, underneath, one large bet on that customer. The tiles that break the pattern, truck owners and small factories, are the ones that move with the real economy rather than with the office.

c4.story:
Follow a hundred rupees of revenue through two very different platforms and you understand why the market treats them like different species.

Start with a delivery marketplace. Roughly half of the hundred goes straight out as delivery cost: the rider, packaging and the dark store that holds the groceries. Another big chunk, almost as large, goes to marketing, technology and people. Depreciation on dark stores and warehouses takes a little more. What is left is a few rupees. That is a profitable delivery platform; for years, the left-over bar was negative.

Now a classifieds site like Naukri or IndiaMART. Its input cost is almost nothing, because it delivers nothing. It spends about half its revenue on sales teams, technology and marketing. And then roughly two fifths of every rupee is left over. Same app-based business, utterly different shape.

The number delivery investors obsess over is contribution margin: what is left from each order after the rider, the packaging and the discount, before head-office costs. It is the first number to turn positive in a delivery business, and the stock trades on it. Zomato's food delivery got there first; Blinkit followed later in quick commerce.

A quarter of soaring orders with soaring marketing is bought, not earned.

Two other lines deserve attention. Employee stock options are a large non-cash charge in this sector, which is why reported profit sits far below the adjusted profit managements prefer to quote. Read both. And depreciation is rising, because the model is shifting: Blinkit moving toward owning its inventory after Eternal restructured to count as Indian-owned under the FDI rules, and vertical retailers opening stores. Owning things puts them on the balance sheet.

Interest, meanwhile, is not a cost here. Almost every listed name sits on IPO cash, so interest shows up as income.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: delivery marketplaces on one side, classifieds and listings on the other. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is goods or delivery cost. For delivery marketplaces it takes roughly half. For classifieds it is a sliver, barely visible.
  • The opex bar is marketing, tech and people. It is large on both charts, a little over half for classifieds and somewhat under half for delivery.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small on both.
  • The last bar is what is left. This is the picture to remember: a few rupees for delivery against roughly two fifths for classifieds.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Gross order value with take rate, contribution margin, marketing and discounts, and employee stock options all get a yes. Working capital, depreciation and capex are marked sometimes: marketplaces collect cash before they pay sellers, while own-stock retailers carry months of inventory. Interest gets a no, since these companies mostly hold net cash.

Then use the so-what as a three-way test each quarter. Contribution margin up with marketing flat is real operating leverage. Margin up with marketing down is harvesting. Margin flat with marketing up is a price war.

c5.story:
Most industries follow the economy. Indian e-commerce follows something else: the price of global money.

When money is cheap, investors fund platforms that burn cash on discounts to grab share, and the public market pays up for growth. When rates rise, the funding stops, the discounts stop and the weakest players fold or sell. The economy can be fine throughout; the cycle runs on the cost of capital.

The last cycle was textbook. Lockdowns in 2020 moved groceries, medicines and dinner onto the phone for good. Global money was nearly free. Zomato listed in July 2021 to a frenzy, Nykaa followed, and every category suddenly had a ten-minute delivery start-up. That was the peak: loss-making platforms at record valuations.

Then 2022. US rates rose fast, the funding winter set in and platform stocks fell by well over half. Zomato's stock sank far below its listing price, and it bought Blinkit, a struggling quick-commerce player, in an all-stock deal. Every platform swapped its growth slides for profitability slides.

The bottom came in 2023. Food delivery turned profitable. Platform fees appeared on your bill. Blinkit, the distressed purchase, turned into the surprise growth engine. The survivors began a long climb.

The best deal of the bust was a business nobody wanted at the time.

Then came a second listing wave: Ixigo, FirstCry, Swiggy and Blackbuck in 2024; Urban Company, Lenskart, Meesho and Wakefit in 2025. Quick commerce became the hottest category in Indian consumer, and the war with Zepto and Instamart peaked in losses in 2025. Today Eternal has been the year's standout large-cap as those losses narrow, and the clock sits in the boom arc: profits are real, but so are full valuations.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last cycle: boom across 2020 and 2021, peak in 2021, bust in 2022, bottom in 2023. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled second listing wave. The detail line says it plainly: profits arriving, valuations full, the quick-commerce war easing. Hover any arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Notice the colours: a boom stretch for 2020 and 2021, a bust entry in 2022, a neutral bottom in 2023, a fresh boom in 2024, then a neutral 2025 when the quick-commerce war peaked and a crowd of companies listed, and the latest entry marked now.

The four hands are how you move the arrow yourself.

  • Quick-commerce contribution margin: turning positive, arrow up. A fresh dip would mean a new entrant is spending.
  • Marketing cost to revenue: falling, arrow up. Growth is becoming organic.
  • US ten-year yield: easing, arrow up. Lower yields support long-duration growth stocks, but also reopen funding for rivals.
  • Dark-store additions: slowing, mixed. Slowing means harvesting; a renewed surge means another round of burn.

Three hands point up and one is mixed. That fits a boom with real economics underneath, where the risk is less the business and more the price.

c6.story:
Here is a slightly uncomfortable fact for anyone who owns Indian platform stocks: the single most important number for their valuation is set in Washington, not Delhi.

The first three-dot dial is the US ten-year Treasury yield. Platform profits are expected to arrive years from now, and the further away a profit is, the more its present value depends on the discount rate. When the US yield rises, long-duration growth stocks everywhere fall, Indian platforms included. The yield also controls the global funding tap: when it is low, venture money flows to rivals, and rivals spend it on discounts. That is why this dial carries a diamond. Lower yields lift your multiple and arm your competitors at the same time.

The second three-dot dial is urban salaried incomes and IT hiring. This one is about orders, not multiples. More software jobs mean more dinners ordered, bigger baskets and more Naukri billings. It is the closest thing this sector has to a demand dial.

The two-dot dials sharpen the picture. Fuel prices raise the cost of every delivery and squeeze contribution margin. Food inflation fattens the rupee value of a grocery basket but trims how often people order. The RBI policy rate shapes consumer credit and the domestic appetite for growth stocks. Risk appetite, which you can watch through India VIX, widens or narrows the premium on recently listed loss-makers. And two rule-shaped dials matter a lot: FDI policy, which has kept Amazon and Flipkart from owning inventory on their marketplaces and so gave Indian-owned platforms an edge, and gig-worker and GST rules, each of which adds a few rupees to every order.

The one-dot dials are slower: the rupee nudges foreign flows, and smartphone penetration keeps adding new users from smaller towns.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the business. This column tells you whether a dial moves the multiple, the order book or the cost per order. The US yield and risk appetite move the multiple; urban incomes, food inflation and the policy rate move orders and baskets; fuel and gig-worker rules move the cost per order.
  • A rise does: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways. The US yield and food inflation carry diamonds here.
  • Weight: one to three dots.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a matching series: the US ten-year yield, the Nifty IT index as a stand-in for IT hiring, the money-market rate, Brent crude for fuel, food CPI, India VIX and the rupee. FDI policy, gig-worker and GST rules and smartphone penetration show a dash; those you follow through the news.

Read the three-dot rows first: the US yield and urban hiring. One sets the price the market pays for these companies, the other sets how many orders they get. If both move against you in the same quarter, as they did in 2022, the stocks fall regardless of execution.

Then scan the red two-dot rows, fuel and gig-worker rules, because they hit contribution margin directly.

c7.story:
Why can't a delivery platform simply grow its way to the margins of a classifieds site? Because of the bottlenecks, and the first one rides a motorbike.

Every order is carried by a human. The cost per delivery falls only with density: more orders per rider per hour, more orders per dark store per day. Below a certain density, every extra order adds losses rather than profit. That is why quick commerce works in dense metro neighbourhoods and struggles almost everywhere else. It is structural; no app update changes it.

The second structural bottleneck is the competition's balance sheet. Amazon and Flipkart, the latter owned by Walmart, are not listed in India and are funded by foreign parents who can lose money here for a decade. Price discipline in Indian e-commerce is borrowed from them, not owned by the listed companies.

Then the cyclical one: funding-driven competition. Whenever global money is cheap, a new entrant arrives with discounts. Zepto did it in quick commerce. Rapido is now doing it in food delivery. Each time, incumbents must choose between matching the discounts and losing share.

The recurring bottlenecks are mostly rules and real estate. The FDI line between marketplace and inventory gets redrawn every few years. Gig-worker welfare laws, starting in Rajasthan in 2023 and then Karnataka, plus the labour codes and GST on delivery fees, each add a few rupees per order, which can be the entire contribution margin. The right dark-store location near rich flats is scarce, and rents climb with every competitor's expansion. And trader associations lobby against deep discounting, with a government that listens before elections.

In delivery, density is the moat and the rider is the meter.

The slow one is stock-option dilution: large annual grants quietly transfer a slice of the company from shareholders to employees, year after year.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each risk belongs.

  • Structural: last-mile cost and Amazon and Flipkart's balance sheets. These cap delivery margins permanently, so they belong in your valuation. Notice both hit the delivery door far harder than classifieds, which has no rider and no foreign giant in most of its categories.
  • Cyclical: funding-driven competition. This one tracks the US yield dial from the wiring diagram. When money gets cheap, expect a new discounter within a year.
  • Recurring: foreign-ownership policy, gig-worker regulation, dark-store real estate and kirana pushback. These are the headlines that hit a quarter. Each one shaves rupees off the cost per order or changes who may own stock.
  • Slow: stock-option dilution, a quiet annual leak rather than an event.

Read the so-what under the table as a reading order. The first two rows set the ceiling for delivery margins. The funding row tells you when the next price war starts, which is why the so-what says to watch rivals' fund-raises as closely as results.

One practical test: for each company you own, count how many of these rows apply. A classifieds name may face only the stock-option row. A quick-commerce name faces nearly all of them.

c8.story:
Indian e-commerce has been shaped by its rulebook more than almost any other consumer sector, and one rule built the whole competitive landscape.

That rule is the FDI policy on e-commerce. Foreign-owned platforms may run a marketplace, but may not own the inventory they sell. A tightened press note issued in 2018, which bit from February 2019, also barred them from favouring sellers they had stakes in. Amazon and Flipkart had to restructure around it. Indian-owned platforms face no such limit, which is precisely why Eternal capped its foreign shareholding in 2025 so it would count as Indian-owned and controlled, letting Blinkit own its own stock. One policy, and a large company rearranged its shareholder register.

Then the rules that nibble at the margin. Since January 2022, food delivery platforms have collected and paid the GST on restaurant food themselves. From the 2025 GST changes, delivery fees through platforms carry GST too, paid either from the contribution margin or by the customer. State gig-worker laws and the labour codes ask platforms to fund rider welfare through a levy per transaction. FSSAI is moving to make online food players directly accountable for what restaurants and dark stores sell.

Consumer rules limit the tricks that lift conversion: the CCPA's 2023 guidelines against dark patterns, rules against fake reviews. The Competition Commission has investigated Amazon and Flipkart over preferred sellers and exclusive launches.

And then the toll booth's whole profit. IRCTC's convenience fee was waived after demonetisation in 2016 and restored in 2019. In October 2021, the railway ministry ordered IRCTC to share half of it; the stock crashed, and the order was withdrawn the next morning.

When your profit is a fee, the person who can waive it is your biggest risk factor.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column sets your priorities.

  • Always: the DPIIT's FDI policy on e-commerce and the railway ministry's mandate for IRCTC. These are foundations, not news, but when either changes, a business model changes with it. The FDI row is the one that gave Indian-owned platforms their edge.
  • Live: the consumer affairs department and CCPA, the Competition Commission and ONDC. These shape behaviour today: dark-pattern bans, antitrust probes, and an open network that could pressure take rates if it ever scales.
  • New: the GST Council and CBIC row, with GST now charged on delivery services through platforms. This one lands directly on cost per order.
  • Coming: labour codes and state gig-worker laws, FSSAI accountability for online food, and a proposed ex-ante digital competition law on the EU model. These are the rules to prepare for. Two of the three raise cost per order; the third could restrict self-preferencing by the biggest players.

Notice which door each row hits. Most land on the delivery marketplaces. The railway row is entirely about one toll booth. Classifieds barely appear, which is part of why that door keeps the most profit.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces boils down to a question every platform investor should ask: once the order comes in, who gets to keep the money?

Run a delivery marketplace through it and it struggles on almost every spoke. Rivalry is maximal: two or three platforms fight for the same flat, with the same riders and the same discounts. Buyers are fickle: most urban households keep two delivery apps and switch for a coupon. Suppliers have options: riders can switch apps mid-shift, and restaurants can delist or push their own ordering. Entrants keep coming, because a well-funded newcomer can buy share in delivery within a year. And substitutes are real: the neighbourhood kirana, the restaurant's own app, and ONDC.

Now run Naukri through the same test. Rivalry is low because a classifieds leader is usually alone in its category. Recruiters have nowhere else with the same pool of resumes, and job seekers go where the recruiters are. That is a network effect: each side attracts the other, and the leader gets stronger simply by being the leader. Building a rival classifieds network from scratch has failed repeatedly in India. LinkedIn and the big IT firms' own job portals nibble at the edges, but they nibble.

A delivery app rents its customers. A classifieds leader owns its market.

That contrast explains a paradox in how the market prices these businesses. Classifieds earn high margins at a lower multiple, because their growth is steady and their market is mature. Delivery leaders earn thin margins at a very high multiple, because investors are paying for the possibility that density and scale eventually tame the forces that squeeze them today.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: delivery marketplaces and classifieds and listings. This is one of the starkest contrasts on any industry page. Look at the overall size first: the delivery shape is far larger than the classifieds shape in every direction. The classifieds shape hugs the centre.

  • Rivalry: delivery hits the outer ring; classifieds sits near the centre. This is the widest gap on the chart.
  • Buyer: delivery reaches well out, because customers switch for a coupon. Classifieds stays modest; a recruiter cannot leave the biggest resume pool.
  • Supplier: delivery sits in the middle, riders and restaurants can walk; classifieds sits near the centre.
  • Entrants: delivery in the middle, classifieds near the centre.
  • Substitutes: the closest the two shapes come. Both face some substitution: the kirana for one, LinkedIn for the other.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a one-line reason. Vertical retailers and toll booths are not drawn, but you can place them yourself: a toll booth like IRCTC would have a tiny shape everywhere except one spoke, the regulator behind the supplier and buyer lines.

c10.story:
An e-commerce results release can run to dozens of slides of gross order value, cohorts, cities and dark-store maps. Eight numbers tell you most of what matters, and they are designed to catch the classic tricks.

Gross order value growth comes first: the total value flowing through the platform, before the platform's cut. It shows whether the network is still compounding. Then the take rate, how much of that flow the platform keeps, including ads. A rising take rate driven by ads is the healthiest kind, because the customer's bill does not change.

The heart of the matter is contribution margin per order: what is left after the rider, the packaging and the discount. This is where unit economics live or die. Then adjusted EBITDA margin, which adds head office, marketing and tech. Expanding every quarter means operating leverage is real.

Marketing as a share of revenue is the honesty check. If orders soar while marketing soars, growth was bought. Monthly transacting users and order frequency tell you about the network itself: more users ordering more often is the dream.

Then two numbers managements prefer you skip. Employee cost including stock options is the gap between the adjusted profit in the headline and the reported profit in the accounts. And net cash against quarterly burn tells you how many quarters of war a company can fund before it needs the market's help.

Adjusted EBITDA is what the company wants you to see. Stock options are what it costs you to see it.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to put to each company. Several rows exist to separate earned growth from bought growth: take rate, contribution margin, marketing share.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, as rules of thumb. Several are door-specific: gross order value growth has separate bars for quick commerce and food delivery; adjusted EBITDA has a high bar for classifieds; order frequency is a food-delivery measure.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of listed companies. Only three rows have one: sales growth, EBITDA margin and employee cost. The rest, take rate, contribution margin, marketing share, users and frequency, net cash against burn, are operating metrics found in investor presentations rather than in filings, so they show a dash.

A caution on the medians: they blend loss-making delivery names, very profitable classifieds and steady toll booths. The EBITDA median in particular can sit between doors and describe none of them well. Always compare a company with its own door's good mark first.

The best routine: each quarter, put contribution margin, marketing share and stock-option cost side by side for your names. That trio tells you whether growth is earned and whether the profit is real.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings in Indian e-commerce rarely come from the platforms themselves. They come from venture-funding headlines, IT company hiring calls, FMCG results and bond markets on the other side of the world.

Some signals arrive in the same quarter. The US ten-year yield and Nasdaq growth multiples move Indian platform stocks the same month, whether or not anything changed in Indian ordering. Rail passenger volumes and airfares move IRCTC's and Ixigo's fees as tickets are sold.

Most useful signals speak one quarter ahead. A rival's fund-raise or dark-store announcement means discounts within a quarter, and margins follow. IT services hiring and attrition commentary is next quarter's Naukri billings and the urban order budget. When FMCG companies talk about how much of their sales now go through quick commerce, they are telling you where grocery spend is moving before the platforms report. Fuel prices and rider wage disputes raise last-mile cost a quarter later. Used-car prices and auto finance rates lead CarTrade's dealer demand.

The furthest dot is policy: GST Council and labour-code announcements take a quarter or two to pass through or be absorbed.

Combine the big ones and you get the three-sign rule. The rally rests on fundamentals when contribution margins are expanding, marketing as a share of revenue is falling, and global yields are steady or lower. Right now all three are ticking, though the yield tick carries a note to watch for a reversal.

Three ticks is a boom with real profits under it. It is also the moment the market stops forgiving misses.

That is why the call favours leaders with proven unit economics and the asset-light classifieds names, and treats freshly listed loss-makers as execution bets priced for perfection.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to see its channel into earnings.

  • Same quarter, far left: the US ten-year yield with Nasdaq multiples, and rail passenger volumes with airfares. These describe what is happening now.
  • One quarter ahead: the crowded middle. Rival fund-raises and dark-store announcements, IT hiring and attrition commentary, FMCG companies' quick-commerce commentary, fuel prices and rider wage disputes, used-car prices and auto finance rates.
  • Two quarters ahead: GST Council and labour-code announcements, the earliest warning on this chart.

Use it as a reading order. Check the policy dot on the right first, then sweep the one-quarter cluster, paying most attention to rival fund-raises, because a funded competitor is the fastest way for a delivery name's margins to reverse. The left-hand dots are for confirmation.

Below the chart is the rule with three signs. All three carry ticks: contribution margins expanding as quick commerce turns positive, marketing share falling as discounts fade, and global yields easing, with a note to watch for a reversal. Three of three is the rule's strongest reading.

Then the call box: the headline, three points, and what would change the call: a sharp rise in global yields, a new well-funded quick-commerce entrant, or a rewrite of the FDI or digital-competition rules. Make those three your news alerts.

explainer.one_liner: FMCG companies sell the small things every Indian household buys every week, a cigarette, a packet of tea, a bottle of cooking oil, a bag of atta, and make money by doing it a billion times through a million kirana shops.

doors.name: Tobacco cash machines
doors.sub: Cigarettes sold at a price the brand sets, under a heavy excise tax, with almost no competition from new brands
doors.blurb: A bet on the tax rate: volumes barely grow, but pricing power and cash flow are unmatched

doors.name: Branded staples and foods
doors.sub: Tea, salt, atta, spices, packaged foods and branded oil sold through distributors and kiranas at a modest margin
doors.blurb: A bet on distribution reach and on brands moving buyers from loose to packed

doors.name: Commodity processors and traders
doors.sub: Crush, refine, pack or trade edible oil, rice, sugar, seafood and pulses on a thin spread
doors.blurb: A bet on a commodity spread and on volume, not on a brand

doors.name: Farm-input sellers
doors.sub: Branded pesticides and fertiliser sold to farmers through dealers, filed under FMCG for their distribution model
doors.blurb: A bet on the monsoon, the sowing season and dealer credit

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the toll road the government taxes heavily but nobody can build a second one. Door two is the trusted kirana brand your mother asks for by name. Door three is the wholesale mandi trader who lives on the gap between buying and selling. Door four is the village seed-and-pesticide shop that watches the sky.
explainer.door_so_what: This industry label hides four very different businesses, so a tobacco name trades on tax news, a staples brand on volume growth, a processor on commodity spreads and a farm-input name on the monsoon; never compare their margins directly.

stations.name: Farm and import sourcing
