explainer.tell_a_friend: Insurers collect small premiums from many people and pay the few who die, fall sick or crash, and they invest the money in between. Life insurers sell protection and long savings plans, mostly through banks in the same group, and their profit is a promise spread over decades, so look at value of new business, not reported profit. General and health insurers sell one-year covers, and their profit is premium minus claims minus costs, plus interest on the float. Covid made India buy cover in 2020. Then from 2023 the rules kept changing: a tax on big policies, expense limits, higher surrender values, and in 2025 GST removed on retail life and health. Each change squeezed margins and the stocks de-rated. Now volumes are growing again on a lower margin base. The best names own their bank channel and sell protection, not savings dressed up as insurance.

glossary.def: The price of an insurance policy, paid once or every year.
Claims paid as a share of premium earned. 70% means ₹70 of claims for every ₹100 of premium.
Claims ratio plus expense ratio. Below 100% means underwriting profit; above 100% means the insurer relies on investment income.
Premium collected but not yet paid out as claims, invested in the meantime.
Annualised premium equivalent: regular premiums plus one tenth of single premiums. The standard life sales number.
Value of new business: today's value of the future profit from policies sold in the period. Margin = VNB divided by APE.
Net worth plus the value of future profits from policies already sold. Life insurers are valued as a multiple of it.
The share of policies still paying premium after a set time, such as 13 or 61 months.
Available capital divided by the capital the regulator requires. The minimum is 150%.
Unit-linked insurance plan: a life policy whose savings part is invested in market funds.
Participating plans share profits as bonuses; non-participating plans promise fixed returns and keep more margin for the insurer.
Pure life cover with no savings element. The highest-margin product.
A product that turns a lump sum into a monthly income for life.
Selling insurance through a bank's branches, usually a bank in the same group.
What a customer gets back on quitting a policy early. The 2024 rules raised it from the first year.
IRDAI's cap on an insurer's total commission and operating cost as a share of premium, in force since April 2023.
GST paid on costs that a business can offset against GST it collects. With no GST on premiums since September 2025, insurers lost this offset.
Compulsory cover for damage or injury you cause to others; the price is set by the government.
Insurance bought by insurers to pass on part of their big risks. GIC Re gets the first offer by law.
A coming rule that sets required capital by the actual riskiness of each insurer's book, instead of a flat formula.
The new insurance accounting standard that spreads profit over the life of a policy.
An IRDAI-backed online marketplace for buying, servicing and claiming insurance.
Point of sales person: a lightly trained agent allowed to sell simple products.
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, the government's crop insurance scheme, launched 2016.

c1.story:
Insurance is the strangest business on the market. A factory knows its costs before it sets a price. An insurer sets the price first and finds out its costs years later, when the claims come in. A life insurer may not know whether a policy was profitable until the policyholder turns eighty.

That one oddity splits the industry into doors that behave nothing alike. Life insurers, LIC, SBI Life, HDFC Life, ICICI Prudential Life, sell protection against dying too early and savings plans that run for ten, twenty or thirty years. Their profit is a promise: it trickles in over the life of each policy, so the market values them on how much future profit each year's sales lock in, a number called value of new business, rather than on this year's reported earnings.

General insurers, ICICI Lombard, Go Digit, New India Assurance, sell one-year covers for cars, factories, crops and company health plans. Their profit shows up every quarter as the gap between premiums and claims, plus the interest earned on premiums before claims are paid. Standalone health insurers, Star Health and Niva Bupa, are a specialised version selling only retail health, where the claims are hospital bills and the enemy is medical inflation. And at the back sits the reinsurer, GIC Re, which insures the insurers: it takes a share of their big risks, the factory fire, the cyclone, the flood, for a share of their premium.

A life insurer sells a promise and books it over decades. A general insurer sells a year and finds out by Diwali whether it priced it right.

All four tiles carry the same medium or low profit bar, and that is worth pausing on. Insurance is not a business where anyone keeps a fat, easy margin. The regulator caps expenses, the banks that sell the policies take their cut, and claims are, by design, most of the premium. The winners are the ones that do the ordinary things slightly better for a very long time.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you what is sold and how profit arrives: slowly over a policy's life for life insurers, quarterly as underwriting plus float income for general insurers, as hospital bills against premiums for health insurers, and as a share of other insurers' risks for the reinsurer.
  • The tickers are listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. LICI sits with the private life names even though it is state-owned; it is still the largest life insurer by policies.
  • The profit bar is medium for the first three doors and low for the reinsurer. Life insurers keep a fair share because retail buyers rarely shop on price, but banks and the regulator take their cut. General and health insurers keep a fair share when they price with discipline. The reinsurer keeps the least: it takes the lumpiest risks, faces global competitors on price and has the least control over what it insures.
  • The bet line names the one variable each door depends on: new-business profit for life, underwriting discipline for general, out-running hospital inflation for health, and a quiet catastrophe year for the reinsurer.

The so-what line under the analogy is the most practical sentence here. A life insurer's profit is a value number published with results; a general or health insurer's is the quarterly gap between premium and claims. So the same quarter can look great for one door and poor for another for reasons that have nothing to do with management. Before comparing two insurers, check they sit behind the same door.

c2.story:
Follow a policy from idea to claim and you pass through five stations. The interesting part is that the insurer stands at only some of them, and the most powerful station is one it often does not own.

The first station is product and pricing. Actuaries, the mathematicians of the trade, design the cover and price it from mortality tables, claims history and interest rates. Since 2022 the regulator has let insurers launch most products without prior approval, a regime called use and file, which made this station faster.

The second station is distribution, and this is where the power sits. Most private life insurance and much general insurance in India is sold across a bank counter, very often by a bank in the same group: SBI sells SBI Life, HDFC Bank sells HDFC Life, ICICI Bank sells ICICI Prudential Life and ICICI Lombard, Axis Bank sells Axis Max Life. LIC has its famous army of agents. Online aggregators and point-of-sale agents fill the gaps. Every one of them takes a commission, and the bank's choice of whose policy to push can make or break an insurer's year.

The third station is underwriting and capital: accepting the risk and holding enough capital behind it to stay above the regulator's solvency floor. The fourth is reinsurance. Big or lumpy risks are passed on in part, by law first to GIC Re, which receives a slice of every general policy, then to foreign reinsurers such as Swiss Re and Munich Re through their Indian branches.

The last station is where the money finally moves: premiums invested in government bonds and shares until claims fall due, and claims settled through hospitals, garages, surveyors and third-party administrators. A health insurer's fate is decided here, in thousands of hospital billing counters it does not control.

In Indian insurance, whoever owns the bank counter owns the growth. Everything else is execution.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right: a policy is designed, sold, underwritten, partly reinsured, and finally paid out.

  • Each box names the station, what happens there and who stands there. Look at the second box: it names the parent banks, LIC's agents and online aggregators, not the insurers. That is the distribution point from the story.
  • The first band row shows who holds each station. Stations one and three are in the Indian colour: product design and underwriting are the insurers' own work. Station two, banks and agents, is uncoloured, because the seller is a different company, even when it shares a group name. Station four is in the rival colour: GIC Re stands there by law, alongside foreign reinsurers. Station five, hospitals and garages, is uncoloured too.
  • The second band row shows where the rival stands: foreign reinsurers and insurers, now allowed to own an Indian insurer outright. The rival label stretches across the first four stations. That is the change the new law brings: a foreign group can now design, sell, underwrite and reinsure in India on its own account, rather than as a junior partner. Only the last cell, the local hospital and garage network, is left to the wider world.

Then read the note: banks own the customer, LIC still leads individual life by policies, and the state general insurers lose share every year. The so-what turns that into a rule for the stock. A bank parent pushing a rival product, or a regulator capping what the bank can earn, moves an insurer more than any ad campaign. When you study an insurer, study its distribution mix first.

c3.story:
Who buys insurance in India, and why? The honest answer, for much of the industry's history, was that people bought it to save tax, or because a bank manager suggested it with a loan, and only occasionally because they actually wanted protection. That is changing, slowly, and the change is the investment case.

Start with salaried families. They buy term cover, savings plans and retail health. For decades the push came from the tax deduction for insurance premiums. The new income tax regime, made the default in 2023, offers no such deduction, so the tax reason is fading. What replaced it, at least briefly, was fear: Covid in 2020 and 2021 made millions of families realise what a hospital bill or an early death could do to them, and term and health sales jumped.

Bank customers buy policies bundled with accounts and loans. When you take a home loan and the bank suggests a cover to protect it, you are this tile. It is volume that rises and falls with bank credit growth and branch sales targets, and the regulator watches it closely for mis-selling.

Employers buy group health and group term cover for staff. This is enormous volume and thin margin, because companies shop their renewals every year and state insurers have historically priced for share. Vehicle owners buy motor cover, of which the third-party part is compulsory by law and priced by the government. Businesses buy fire, property, marine and engineering cover, priced off global reinsurance rates. Farmers buy crop insurance through the national scheme, with governments paying much of the premium, sometimes late. And retirees buy annuities that pay a monthly income for life.

Notice how different the motives are. Some buy out of fear, some because the law says so, some because the bank asked, some because their employer did it for them.

Retail is where the margin is and group is where the volume is. Growth built on the second is worth less than it looks.
c3.read:
Each tile is a customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who buys.
  • The second line is what they buy: term, savings, health, bundled covers, group plans, motor, property, crop, annuities.
  • The third line is what moves them, your watch list outside insurance: income growth and tax rules, bank sales targets and loan growth, hiring and medical inflation, vehicle sales and the third-party price, the capex cycle and global reinsurance prices, the monsoon and state payments, and bond yields for annuities.

A helpful way to read the grid is to sort the tiles by who decides. In salaried families and retirees, the buyer decides, and these are the high-margin tiles. In bank customers, the bank decides. In employers and businesses, a procurement team decides, on price. In vehicle owners and farmers, the law or the government decides.

Then match the tiles to the doors. Life insurers draw on salaried families, bank customers and retirees, and the margin depends on how much is pure protection versus savings. General insurers draw on employers, vehicle owners, businesses and farmers. Standalone health insurers live in the retail part of the first tile, which is why they carry the most medical-inflation risk.

The so-what line gives the warning: a quarter of fast growth built on group or credit-linked business is worth less than it looks. When an insurer reports strong premium growth, check which tile it came from. Retail protection growth is the real thing; a burst of group renewals at keen prices is volume borrowed at the cost of margin.

c4.story:
An insurer's accounts look upside down to anyone used to reading a manufacturer's. The customer pays first. The insurer delivers, by paying a claim, later, sometimes decades later. In between, it holds the customer's money and invests it. That pile of money is called the float, and it changes everything about how profit works.

Start with general and health insurance, where the picture is clearest. Premiums come in; claims and expenses go out. Add the two as a share of premium and you get the combined ratio. Below a hundred per cent, the insurer made money on underwriting itself. Above it, the insurer paid out more than it took in. Here is the surprise: many general insurers run combined ratios slightly above a hundred and still make a decent profit, because the float earns bond interest in the months between premium and claim. Losing a little on every policy and making it up on the float is a legitimate business model, as long as rates stay high enough and the losses stay small.

In health, the claims ratio has a built-in creep. Hospital tariffs rise faster than consumer prices year after year, so a health insurer that does not reprice every year sees its margin erode automatically. In motor, the third-party piece is priced by the government, while court awards for accident victims keep rising.

Life insurance is a different animal again. Reported profit is a poor guide, because the cost of acquiring a policy, the commission and the setup, lands in the first year, while profit trickles in for decades. So life insurers publish value of new business, the present value of future profits from this year's sales, and embedded value, the present value of the whole book plus net worth.

The line that ties them all together is solvency: the capital held above the regulator's floor. Fast growth eats capital, and an insurer close to the floor must either slow down or sell shares.

An insurer is paid to wait. The skill is in pricing the risk; the profit is often in what the money earns while waiting.
c4.read:
The two charts walk a hundred rupees of premium down to profit for life and general insurers. Read bar by bar, and notice what the charts leave out.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of premium.
  • The input bar is claims, benefits and reserves set aside. It takes roughly three quarters of premium for life insurers, which includes money reserved for future maturities and deaths, and about seven of every ten rupees for general insurers.
  • The opex bar is commissions, people and branches. It takes a little under a fifth for life, and more than a quarter for general, where every one-year policy must be sold again next year.
  • The third bite, depreciation and interest, is a sliver in both charts. Insurers own no plant and carry little debt.
  • The last bar is what is left from underwriting. Life keeps a modest slice. General keeps almost nothing: that thin bar is the combined ratio sitting just under a hundred.

Now the key point. These walks show premium only. They do not show investment income on the float, which is where a general insurer actually makes most of its profit, and they cannot show a life insurer's future profits, which is what value of new business measures. That is why the so-what says: read value of new business for life, the combined ratio for general and health, because reported profit hides both. These are illustrative shapes; hover a bar for the amount.

The lines below mark claims, commissions, float income and solvency as yeses, and depreciation, capex, working capital and interest as noes. Working capital is a no for a happy reason: customers pay first.

c5.story:
Insurance is not cyclical the way steel or cement is. People do not stop dying or getting sick in a recession. Demand grows with incomes, quietly, year after year. So why did listed insurers soar after 2020 and then spend two years de-rating? Because in this industry the cycle is written in rulebooks and budget speeches, not in commodity prices.

The boom began with Covid. For the first time, millions of Indian families saw, close up, what an early death or a hospital stay could cost. Term and health sales jumped. Then the second wave in the first quarter of FY22 brought a flood of death and hospital claims, and global reinsurers raised the rates they charged Indian life insurers for term cover. Still, the market loved the penetration story, and listed insurers traded at rich multiples of embedded value.

The peak arrived in 2022 and early 2023. LIC listed in May 2022 in what was then India's biggest share sale, and promptly traded below its issue price. Private life margins hit records. Then the February 2023 budget announced that maturity proceeds from traditional policies with annual premiums above five lakh rupees would be taxed from April. Buyers rushed to beat the deadline, and Q4 FY23 sales spiked. After it, high-ticket savings sales slumped.

The bust was a series of rule changes landing one after another. New expense limits replaced commission caps from April 2023. From October 2024, surrender values rose, so customers who quit early got more of their money back, cutting margins on savings plans. Each change was defensible; together they reset the economics.

The bottom came in 2025: commissions renegotiated, margins reset lower but steady, and in September GST on individual life and health premiums was removed, cheaper for buyers, though insurers lost their input tax credit. Now retail protection and health volumes are responding.

In insurance, the bust did not come from customers walking away. It came from the regulator rewriting the menu.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last cycle: the Covid boom of 2020 to 2022, the LIC-listing and pre-tax-change peak of 2022 and 2023, the rule-change bust of 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 bottom. The arrow sits just short of the top, at the very end of the bottom arc and about to cross into boom: early up-cycle. Hover an arc to read its story. Keep the explainer's own verdict in mind: this cycle is mild, and it is driven by rules more than by demand.

The timeline runs from 2019. A neutral 2019, a boom-coloured Covid stretch, a neutral 2022 for the LIC listing and the reform push, a bust-coloured 2023 and 2024 for the tax, expense and surrender changes, a neutral 2025 for GST removal and full foreign ownership, and 2026 marked now.

The four hands:

  • Value of new business margin: reset lower and stabilising, a mixed arrow. Rising would mean the mix is shifting to protection; falling would mean a rule is biting again.
  • Retail protection and health sales: strong after the GST cut, arrow up. The question is whether this is real penetration or a one-off price effect.
  • Health and motor combined ratio: slightly above breakeven, red arrow down. This is the weak hand. Above a hundred means claims and costs exceed premium.
  • Bond yields: drifting lower, mixed. Good for bond portfolios today, but lower yields cut the margin on guaranteed plans tomorrow.

The so-what below tells you who benefits first: insurers with a retail and protection mix. Names that grew on bank-led savings plans must first show margins have stopped falling.

c6.story:
Two dials with three dots each sit at the top of this table, and they could not be more different. One is a regulator's circular. The other is the stock market.

The first is the insurance regulator's rulebook. IRDAI sets how much an insurer may spend on commissions and expenses, how much a customer gets back on surrender, which products may be launched and how much capital must be held. Since 2023 almost every margin reset in this industry began with an IRDAI circular. The direction is one-way for the shareholder: tighter rules cut margins, usually starting the following quarter.

The second is equity markets. When the Nifty is rising, savers buy unit-linked plans, policies whose value tracks a market fund, and life insurers' embedded value rises with the shares they hold. A good market year flatters life insurers twice: more sales, and a richer book.

Then come the two-dot dials. Government bond yields are two-faced. Higher yields mean more income on the float and make annuities more attractive, but they also mark down existing bond holdings in the short term. Medical inflation pushes health claims up, because hospital bills rise faster than general prices. Income tax rules decide whether savings policies still carry a tax reason to buy; every break removed means fewer sold. Natural catastrophes, floods in Chennai in 2015 and Kerala in 2018, cyclones on the east coast, hit property and crop claims for general insurers and the reinsurer.

The one-dot dials are smaller but real. Short-term rates and fixed-deposit rates make savings plans look worse when they rise. Vehicle sales bring new motor policies. Bank credit growth brings credit-linked covers sold alongside loans.

What is missing is almost as telling. There is no commodity, no currency, no China. Insurance is one of the most domestic businesses on the market.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches insurer profits: through rules, sales, investment income or claims.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, and a diamond means it cuts both ways. Equity markets, vehicle sales and bank credit are green. The regulator's rules, short-term rates, medical inflation, tax rules and catastrophes are red. Bond yields are the diamond.
  • Weight: one to three dots. The two three-dot rows are the regulator and the stock market.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a series: the Nifty, a government bond fund for yields, the money market rate, the health component of consumer prices, the auto index and the bank index. The regulator, tax rules and catastrophes show a dash, because no price series captures them; for those, the news is the series.

Notice that most of the green rows are about sales and most of the red rows are about margins. That is the industry's tension in one table: volume depends on markets and banks, margin depends on regulators and hospitals.

Use it door by door. For a life insurer, read the regulator, the Nifty, bond yields and tax rows. For a health insurer, read medical inflation above all. For a general insurer and the reinsurer, read catastrophes and vehicle sales. The so-what gives the short version: watch the regulator's circulars and the equity market; one sets the margin, the other sets the mood of the savings buyer.

c7.story:
India is famously under-insured. Insurance premiums as a share of the economy are well below the global average, and for twenty years every insurer's investor presentation has opened with that gap. So why has the gap closed so slowly? The bottlenecks answer that, and they explain why insurance stocks have rewarded patience less than the penetration story promised.

The first is that the banks hold the customer. Most private life insurers sell the bulk of their policies through one or two banks, often a group parent. That is a superb channel while it lasts. But a bank answers to its own shareholders. When the regulator allowed banks to tie up with many more insurers in 2022, a bank could suddenly sell several insurers' policies from the same counter. An insurer that loses its place at the counter can see growth halve overnight.

The second is that the rules keep changing the economics. Tax, expenses, surrender values and GST have each reset margins since 2023, and two more are already announced: risk-based capital and a new insurance accounting standard. The third is trust. Savings plans sold as investments, claims rejected on technicalities, policies lapsing after a year: all of these keep buyers wary and the regulator watchful.

For health insurers, the defining bottleneck is hospital bills. Hospital tariffs rise faster than consumer prices, and India has no national price standard for procedures, so every year the same surgery costs more. A health insurer must reprice every year just to stand still.

India's insurance gap is real. So is the reason it closes slowly: the customer trusts the bank more than the policy.

Then come the smaller bottlenecks: a government-set motor third-party price that rarely keeps up with court awards, the constant need for fresh capital at fast growers, state general insurers underpricing to keep share, and floods and cyclones that strike the same coastal cities again and again.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each risk belongs.

  • Structural: bank partners holding the customer, low trust and mis-selling, and hospital bill inflation. Three permanent features, and they cap the returns of the whole industry. They belong in your valuation.
  • Recurring: rules changing the economics, and public-sector pricing. The first is the one that has moved these stocks most since 2023; the second is why group health and fire rates stay thin.
  • Slow: the regulated motor third-party price, an old grievance that moves at the pace of government.
  • Cyclical: capital hunger. Smaller insurers need fresh capital in growth phases, which dilutes shareholders.
  • Two-sided: catastrophe concentration. Floods and cyclones hit property books hard, but a bad catastrophe year is also what lets general insurers and reinsurers push prices up afterwards.

The so-what line narrows eight rows to three. For life insurers, the first two rows, the bank counter and the rulebook, decide growth and margin. For health insurers, the fourth row, hospital inflation, decides profit.

A practical way to use the table: for each insurer you own, write down which row would hurt it most. A bank-led life insurer fears the first row. A savings-heavy one fears the second. A standalone health insurer fears the fourth. Then make sure your news alerts cover that row specifically.

c8.story:
If you want to understand why insurance stocks did what they did since 2023, read IRDAI's circulars, not the companies' results. Almost every reset in this industry started with a rule.

The regulator's big shift was from caps on commissions to a cap on total expenses as a share of premium, from April 2023. Insurers gained freedom to pay distributors what they liked, within an overall ceiling. In practice, the banks and large distributors used that freedom to ask for more, and the ceiling became the battleground.

Then came surrender values. From October 2024, a customer who stops paying early must get back much more of their money. That is plainly fairer to the customer. It also cut the margin insurers had earned on early quitters, and insurers responded by deferring commissions so that distributors share the pain when a policy lapses.

The GST change of September 2025 cut both ways. Individual life and health premiums were exempted, so a policy became cheaper overnight for the buyer. But an exempt product cannot claim input tax credit, so the GST insurers paid on commissions, rent and services became a pure cost. Volumes rose; margins took a hit.

In December 2025 Parliament allowed foreign insurers to own an Indian insurer outright. That opens the door to fresh capital, to foreign partners buying out their Indian joint-venture partners or exiting, and to more competition, especially in health.

Two more are on the horizon. Risk-based capital will tie solvency to the actual risks an insurer carries, rather than a flat formula. A new accounting standard will report profit over the life of the policy. And Bima Sugam, a regulator-backed online marketplace, could one day let customers buy and claim without a bank or broker in between, which would shift power away from the channel that holds it today.

In this industry, the regulator is not a background condition. It is the second management team.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who or what, what it does, why it matters, and the status.

  • Always: IRDAI itself, and the motor third-party price set with the road transport ministry. Note the IRDAI row's reason: every margin reset in this sector started with an IRDAI circular.
  • Live: expense limits, surrender value rules and the income tax regimes. These are shaping margins and demand today. The tax row matters more each year, as more taxpayers move to the new regime, which gives no deduction for premiums.
  • New: the GST exemption on retail life and health, and full foreign ownership. Both arrived in 2025, and their effects are still working through: one on volumes and margins, the other on ownership and competition.
  • Coming: risk-based capital with the new accounting standard, and Bima Sugam. These are the rules to prepare for, and they are why the rule on card eleven shows a cross for no new rule shock.

The quickest way to use this table is to read the coming rows as a list of possible future margin resets. Risk-based capital could free capital for well-diversified insurers and demand more from concentrated ones. The new accounting will change reported profit patterns without changing the cash. Bima Sugam would, if it works, lower distribution costs and weaken bank power, good for insurers with weak channels, less so for those whose moat is the bank counter.

Dated regulatory news for insurance, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. IRDAI exposure drafts are the documents to read, because a draft today is a rule in a year.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Insurance gives a surprising answer. The biggest threat is not a rival insurer. It is the seller.

Take life insurance first. The supplier is not a raw-material vendor; it is the bank or agent who supplies the customer. A large bank that sells most of an insurer's policies can and does bargain hard on commissions, and since the 2022 rule letting banks partner with more insurers, it has more leverage than ever. That is why the supplier spoke is the longest for life insurers.

The buyer, by contrast, is weak. A family buying a term policy or a savings plan rarely compares prices across insurers; it trusts the bank manager or the agent. That weakness is the life insurers' quiet advantage, and it is what lets a bank-backed life insurer keep a decent margin despite a powerful channel.

General and health insurance flips the buyer story. An employer renewing group health for thousands of staff runs a tender every year. A fleet owner shops motor rates. And the state general insurers have a history of pricing group health and fire to keep market share, which drags rates down for everyone. So rivalry and buyer power are both higher.

New entrants are a growing force, especially in health. Insurance licences need large capital, but full foreign ownership and fresh licences are bringing newcomers, and Go Digit showed in a few years that a digital-first general insurer can scale fast.

Substitutes split the doors cleanly. A savings plan competes with mutual funds, fixed deposits and gold, and in recent years it has often lost. Nothing substitutes for health or motor cover. You cannot buy a mutual fund to pay a hospital bill.

A savings plan has many rivals. A hospital bill has none.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, life insurers and general plus health insurers, and they cross. Neither is simply smaller.

  • The life shape reaches further on supplier, the bank and agent channel, and on substitutes, the funds, deposits and gold that compete with savings plans.
  • The general and health shape reaches further on rivalry, buyer and new entrants: many players, state insurers pricing for share, employers and fleet owners shopping every year, and new licences arriving.

Look at the shortest spoke on the chart: buyer power for life insurers, at the low end. That is the life insurers' moat drawn as a line: retail buyers rarely shop on price. The shortest spoke for general and health is substitutes, also near the low end: nothing replaces a health or motor cover.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. Use it to adjust for a specific company. A life insurer whose parent bank sells only its policies deserves a shorter supplier spoke; one dependent on an open-architecture bank deserves a longer one. A health insurer selling mostly retail through its own agents deserves a shorter buyer spoke than one heavy in group business. The so-what line puts the conclusion simply: life insurers with a captive bank keep the most, and general insurers keep profit only when they refuse to chase state-insurer pricing.

c10.story:
Insurance results are notoriously hard to read. Reported profit tells you little for a life insurer, premium growth can be bought with keener pricing, and the accounting is full of reserves and adjustments. Eight numbers cut through it, and they differ by door.

For life insurers, start with value of new business, the present value of future profits from this period's sales, and its margin, value of new business divided by sales. This is the single best measure of whether a life insurer is selling profitably. Then annualised premium equivalent, a way of counting new sales that treats a regular annual premium and a one-off single premium on a like-for-like basis. Then product mix: protection and non-linked plans earn the most, unit-linked plans the least. A rising share of protection is the best sign you can see in a life insurer's presentation.

Then persistency, the share of customers still paying after a year, and after five. This is the honesty test. A policy sold properly keeps being paid; a mis-sold one lapses. High persistency means the sales were genuine.

For general and health insurers, the key number is the combined ratio, claims plus costs as a share of premium. Below a hundred per cent means underwriting profit before any float income.

For all of them: the solvency ratio, the capital cushion above the regulator's floor, which tells you whether growth will require a share sale; premium growth against the market, which tells you about share gains; and return on embedded value or equity, which tells you whether growth earns more than capital costs.

For a life insurer, persistency is the polygraph. Customers who keep paying were sold the right policy.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • The first four rows are life-insurer numbers: value of new business and its margin, annualised premium equivalent, product mix and persistency. Read them as a chain: sales volume, then what kind of sales, then whether they stick, then what they are worth.
  • The fifth row, the combined ratio, is for general and health insurers. Note its two benchmarks: below a hundred overall, and lower still for retail health.
  • The last three rows apply to everyone: solvency, premium growth and return on embedded value or equity.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Persistency carries two marks, early and late; the gap between them shows how many customers drop off over the years.
  • Today's industry median shows a value only for premium growth, from the listed insurers' latest annual filings. Every other row shows a dash, because standard filing lines do not carry insurance metrics like value of new business or the combined ratio. Those come from each insurer's public disclosures and investor presentation.

Use the table as a checklist, door by door. For a life insurer, fill in the first four rows plus solvency and return on embedded value. For a general or health insurer, the combined ratio, solvency, premium growth and return on equity. Then read the premium growth median with care: it averages life and general insurers, so it shows the industry's direction rather than a benchmark for any one company.

c11.story:
Insurance is one of the few industries where much of the quarter's sales is published before the quarter ends. Life insurers' new-business premiums are released monthly through the industry council; general insurers' premiums are published monthly too. So the same-quarter dots on this chart are not guesses; they are the quarter's volume, almost line by line, weeks before results. Vehicle registrations, which bring new motor policies, and catastrophe claims from floods and cyclones also land in the same quarter.

One quarter ahead sit two signals. IRDAI circulars and consultation papers: a paper today is next year's margin, and a final rule hits the quarter it applies. And the Nifty's trailing return, because good markets lift unit-linked plan sales a quarter later.

Two quarters ahead are the slowest, most powerful signals. A Union Budget tax change creates a rush before it takes effect and a slump afterwards, as the 2023 budget did with high-ticket savings plans. And hospital tariff hikes show up in health claims within two quarters, before premiums can be repriced.

Put them together and the rule has three signs. Insurers are in an up-cycle when retail sales are growing in double digits, life margins and health combined ratios are stable or improving, and the regulator is not changing the economics. Today the first two hold: retail sales are strong after the GST removal, and margins, reset lower, are now holding. The third does not: risk-based capital and the new accounting standard are pending.

Two of three, which the rule calls early recovery. That is why the call prefers private life insurers with a protection-heavy mix and disciplined retail health insurers: they benefit most from the volume recovery and are least exposed if the next rule bites.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by lead time. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel.

  • Far left, same quarter: four dots. Monthly life new-business data, monthly general insurance premium data, vehicle registrations, and floods and cyclones. This cluster is unusually large, which is the good news about this industry: you can see the quarter as it happens.
  • Middle, one quarter ahead: IRDAI circulars and the Nifty's trailing return.
  • Right, two quarters ahead: Union Budget tax changes and hospital tariff hikes.

Read the chart from right to left each quarter. The budget and hospital dots set the quarter after next; the regulator and the market set the next one; the monthly data confirm the current one.

Below the chart, the rule shows three signs. Retail sales growing in double digits: a tick, strong after the GST removal. Margins and combined ratios stable: a tick, reset lower and now holding. No new rule shock: a cross, with risk-based capital and the new accounting pending. Two ticks, so early recovery by the rule's own definition.

The call box then gives the view, its points and what would change it: a new commission or surrender rule, health claims rising faster than repricing, or a bank partner moving its counter to a rival. Map each to the chart. The first is the IRDAI dot. The second is the hospital tariff dot, two quarters out. The third has no dot at all; it arrives as a company announcement, so it needs a news alert for each insurer you own.

explainer.one_liner: Steel companies melt iron ore with coking coal, or melt scrap with electricity, roll the hot metal into sheets, bars and pipes, and sell it to the people building cars, houses, bridges and machines.

doors.name: Integrated flat-steel majors
doors.sub: Blast furnaces fed by their own or bought iron ore and imported coking coal, selling hot-rolled coil, cold-rolled and coated sheet to autos, appliances and engineering
doors.blurb: A bet on the steel spread: coil price minus ore and coking coal

doors.name: Secondary and long-steel producers
doors.sub: Sponge iron, induction and electric furnaces making rebar, wire rod and billets for construction, often with captive power and pellets
doors.blurb: A bet on construction demand and on owning the raw material, especially iron ore

doors.name: Stainless and specialty
doors.sub: Stainless flat steel, alloy wire, ropes and recycled metals sold for what they do, not by the tonne of carbon steel
doors.blurb: A bet on a niche with its own price, though nickel and Chinese stainless still set the ceiling

doors.name: Pipes, tubes and wire converters
doors.sub: Buy coil or wire rod, shape it into pipes, tubes and wire, and charge a conversion margin on orders
doors.blurb: A bet on an order book from water, gas, oil and power projects, not on the steel price

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a big flour mill that buys wheat from the world market and sells flour by the sack. Door two is a local chakki that owns its own wheat field. Door three bakes cakes. Door four buys flour and makes biscuits to order for a hotel chain.
explainer.door_so_what: An integrated major is a bet on the global coil price and the coking coal bill, a secondary producer is a bet on construction and on its ore, and a converter is a bet on its order book, so the same steel price headline means different things for each.

stations.name: Iron ore and coal
stations.what: Iron ore is mined in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka; most coking coal comes by ship from Australia, with Russia rising
stations.who: NMDC, the state miners, captive mines of Tata Steel, SAIL and LLOYDSME; Australian coking coal

stations.name: Pellets and sponge iron
stations.what: Fine ore is rolled into pellets or turned into sponge iron with gas or thermal coal
stations.who: LLOYDSME, GPIL, SHYAMMETL, JINDALSTEL, plus many unlisted units

stations.name: Melting
stations.what: Blast furnaces or electric furnaces turn iron into liquid steel
stations.who: JSWSTEEL, TATASTEEL, SAIL, JINDALSTEL, NSLNISP, AM/NS India; secondary mills for longs

stations.name: Rolling and finishing
stations.what: Slabs and billets become coil, sheet, rebar, wire, pipe and stainless
stations.who: The majors' rolling mills, JSL for stainless, JINDALSAW, RATNAMANI, BANSALWIRE, USHAMART

stations.name: Users
stations.what: Builders, carmakers, appliance makers, railways and pipeline projects buy and use the steel
stations.who: Construction and infra contractors, autos, capital goods, oil and water utilities

kitchen.rival: China
kitchen.note: The steel belt runs through Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka because that is where the iron ore is; coking coal arrives at east-coast ports. China makes about half the world's steel and exports the surplus, so its export price is the ceiling on Indian coil.
kitchen.so_what: India is rich in ore and poor in coking coal, so an Australian coal spike or a Chinese export surge hits Indian spreads within a quarter.

end_markets.name: Construction and real estate
end_markets.buys: Rebar, wire rod, structurals, the biggest slice of Indian steel
end_markets.moves_with: Housing starts, cement volumes, interest rates

end_markets.name: Infrastructure
end_markets.buys: Structurals, plates, rails, pipes
end_markets.moves_with: Government capex, railway and highway budgets

end_markets.name: Automobiles
end_markets.buys: Cold-rolled and coated flat steel, special bar
end_markets.moves_with: Car, two-wheeler and truck sales

end_markets.name: Capital goods and engineering
end_markets.buys: Plates, alloy steel, forgings
end_markets.moves_with: Private capex, defence and power equipment orders

end_markets.name: Consumer durables
end_markets.buys: Coated sheet and stainless for appliances and utensils
end_markets.moves_with: Urban consumption, festive season

end_markets.name: Oil, gas and water pipelines
end_markets.buys: Large-diameter pipe, seamless tube, ductile iron pipe
end_markets.moves_with: Jal Jeevan funding, gas grid build-out, refinery capex

end_markets.name: Exports
end_markets.buys: Hot-rolled coil and semis to Europe, the Gulf and Asia
end_markets.moves_with: Chinese export prices, EU safeguards and the carbon border tax

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Construction and infra take well over half of Indian steel, so the government's capex budget matters more to volumes than the car cycle does.

lines.why: Profit per tonne shipped; the spread in one number, and it swings by half across a cycle
The biggest imported cost for blast furnaces, priced in dollars and swinging hard with Australian weather and Chinese demand
The domestic coil and rebar price after discounts; follows Chinese export prices with a lag
Large plants, steady charge; jumps when a new blast furnace starts
Every major is building capacity; a new blast furnace takes years and lots of borrowed money, and the cycle may turn before it fills
Coal and ore inventories swell when prices spike; converters carry receivables from government projects
Integrated majors carry heavy debt from expansions and acquisitions; debt to EBITDA decides who survives a bust
Tata Steel's European plants and JSW's American ones have swung group profit for years

pnl.analogy: A steel mill is a mithai shop that buys sugar and milk at world prices and sells sweets at a price set by a giant shop next door, China. Some months the sugar is cheap and the neighbour is busy, and the shop prints money; other months the neighbour floods the street with cheap sweets.
pnl.so_what: Watch EBITDA per tonne against the coking coal price and the Chinese export price; the gap between the two is the next quarter's earnings.

clock.is_cyclical: Deeply. Steel profits follow the spread between steel prices and raw-material costs, and both are set mainly by China's construction cycle and its exports. India's own demand is the steadiest in the world, but it cannot set the price.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Global stimulus and China's restraint send coil prices to records; Indian majors earn their best margins ever and cut debt

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Coking coal spikes after the Ukraine war, the government imposes an export duty, and margins roll over

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: China's property crash pushes its surplus abroad at any price; Indian imports from China, Japan and Korea surge and coil prices fall to multi-year lows

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: A safeguard duty on flat imports puts a floor under prices; coking coal eases; margins begin to rebuild

clock.position_detail: duty floor, coal cheap, capacity rising

timeline.what: Slowdown. Auto and real-estate demand weak, prices fall, margins thin.
After the COVID-19 lockdown, stimulus around the world and Chinese restraint send coil prices to records. Indian mills earn record profit per tonne and pay down debt.
Coking coal more than doubles after the Ukraine war. The government slaps an export duty in May to cool domestic prices, then withdraws it in November. Margins fall from the top.

China's property crash leaves it with surplus steel that it exports at any price. Imports into India hit records and domestic coil falls to its lowest in years. Margins shrink even as Indian demand grows strongly.
A safeguard duty on flat steel imports arrives in April and prices firm. Coking coal is cheap. The majors push ahead with expansions and green-steel plans.

Early up-cycle. The safeguard duty is extended, Indian demand grows faster than any large economy, and the majors are adding capacity. China's exports remain the cap. The EU carbon border tax now charges on exports to Europe.

hands.name: Chinese steel export price
hands.meaning: Rising means the ceiling on Indian prices lifts; falling means a new dumping wave

hands.name: Domestic hot-rolled coil price
hands.meaning: Rising faster than coking coal means spreads widen

hands.name: Coking coal price
hands.meaning: A spike squeezes blast-furnace margins a quarter later

hands.name: Steel imports into India
hands.meaning: Falling imports mean the duty works; a rebound means leakage through other countries

clock.so_what: In an early up-cycle behind a duty wall, the trade is domestic volume and spread; the risk is that the wall is only as good as the next government review.

dials.name: Chinese steel exports and prices
dials.channel: The ceiling on every Indian steel price
dials.rise_does: a rise in Chinese prices lifts Indian spreads

dials.name: Coking coal price
dials.channel: The largest imported input for blast furnaces
dials.rise_does: squeezes integrated margins a quarter later

dials.name: Government capital spending
dials.channel: Rebar, structurals, rails and pipes
dials.rise_does: lifts long-steel and pipe volumes

dials.name: Trade protection
dials.channel: Safeguard and anti-dumping duties on imports
dials.rise_does: raises the floor under Indian prices

dials.name: Domestic steel output
dials.channel: The official monthly volume read
dials.rise_does: confirms demand before results

dials.name: Iron ore price
dials.channel: Cost for non-integrated mills, income for captive miners
dials.rise_does: hurts buyers, helps ore owners

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Coking coal import bill and export realisation
dials.rise_does: raises coal costs, helps exporters

dials.name: Auto production
dials.channel: Cold-rolled and coated flat demand
dials.rise_does: lifts flat-steel premium grades

dials.name: Interest rates
dials.channel: Debt-heavy balance sheets and housing demand
dials.rise_does: raises interest cost, slows building

dials.name: EU carbon border tax
dials.channel: Cost of exporting to Europe
dials.rise_does: makes Indian blast-furnace steel dearer in Europe

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track the Chinese export price and the coking coal price; between them they explain most quarters of the last decade.

bottlenecks.name: Chinese overcapacity
bottlenecks.why: China makes about half the world's steel and its home demand is shrinking; the surplus goes abroad and caps prices everywhere.

bottlenecks.name: Coking coal dependence
bottlenecks.why: India has little good coking coal and imports most of it, so a shock in Queensland lands straight on Indian costs.

bottlenecks.name: Iron ore mining leases
bottlenecks.why: Leases expired and were auctioned in 2020, with high premiums to the state; owning ore is now a big advantage for a few names.

bottlenecks.name: Debt-funded capex
bottlenecks.why: Every major is building, and steel capex funded by debt has bankrupted Indian mills before, in the bust of the last decade.

bottlenecks.name: Policy swings
bottlenecks.why: The government has imposed export duties to cool prices and safeguard duties to protect them within a few years; either can move margins overnight.

bottlenecks.name: Carbon intensity
bottlenecks.why: Indian blast furnaces emit more carbon per tonne than most; Europe's border tax and India's own carbon market make that a cost line.

bottlenecks.name: Rail and port logistics
bottlenecks.why: Moving ore, coal and finished steel needs rakes and berths that run short in peak season.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: China and coking coal set the ceiling and the floor of margins, while policy swings and debt decide which company is still standing at the bottom of the cycle.

rulebook.what: Policy, PSU ownership, the national steel policy and the green-steel taxonomy
rulebook.why: Sets the capacity ambitions and the definition of green steel that future buyers will pay a premium for

rulebook.what: Safeguard and anti-dumping duties on imported steel
rulebook.why: The safeguard duty on flat steel is the floor under today's prices; its renewal is the big date

rulebook.what: Mandatory standards on steel products, including imports
rulebook.why: Blocks substandard imports and works like a tariff

rulebook.what: The government can tax steel and ore exports, as it did in 2022
rulebook.why: Used to cool domestic prices when they spike; a cap on the boom

rulebook.body: Ministry of Mines and the mining law
rulebook.what: Iron ore and coal block auctions and premiums
rulebook.why: Decides who owns ore and at what cost

rulebook.what: Payments for making high-grade alloys and coated steel in India
rulebook.why: Supports specialty capacity and import substitution

rulebook.what: Charges the carbon in imported steel from 2026
rulebook.why: Raises the cost of exporting to Europe, a key outlet for Indian coil

rulebook.what: Emission intensity targets for steel plants
rulebook.why: A domestic carbon price that rewards electric furnaces and penalises old blast furnaces

why.rivalry: Producers fight Chinese imports and each other on price; converters compete on bids for project orders
why.supplier: Coking coal comes from a few Australian sellers; converters buy coil from the same few majors
why.buyer: Carmakers and big contractors negotiate hard; converter buyers need certified suppliers and fewer can qualify
why.entrants: A blast furnace needs billions and ore; a pipe or wire plant is cheaper to build
why.substitutes: Little replaces steel in a building or a car; aluminium and plastics nibble in autos and pipes

forces.so_what: Producers with their own ore keep the most of the cycle's profit, converters keep a steadier slice through order books, and the importer of coking coal is always partly working for Queensland.

rule.text: Steel is in an up-cycle when Chinese export prices are rising, domestic spreads are widening over coking coal, and imports are falling; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a duty-propped rally.

call.headline: Early up-cycle behind a duty wall. Prefer names with their own iron ore and low debt, and the converters with long project order books, over debt-heavy pure blast-furnace growth.
points: Indian demand is growing faster than any large economy's, and the safeguard duty keeps Chinese steel at bay for now.
Captive ore is the biggest cost edge since the 2020 lease auctions, which is why the market pays up for ore-rich names.
Pipe and wire converters earn a conversion margin on orders, so they ride infra spending without betting on the coil price.
would_change: The safeguard duty lapsing or being cut while Chinese exports stay high
A coking coal spike from Australian supply problems
A slowdown in government capex after a budget squeeze

explainer.tell_a_friend: Steel is made by melting iron ore with coking coal in a blast furnace, or melting scrap and sponge iron with electricity. India has lots of ore but little good coking coal, so it imports the coal from Australia. The price of steel, though, is set by China, which makes about half the world's steel and dumps its surplus abroad when its own construction slows. So an Indian mill's profit is the gap between a Chinese-set price and an Australian-set cost. From 2020 to 2021 that gap was huge. In 2023 and 2024 China's property crash flooded the world with cheap steel and Indian margins shrank. In 2025 India put a safeguard duty on imports and prices firmed. Indian demand is the strongest of any big economy because of roads, railways and housing. The best-placed companies own their iron ore and do not carry too much debt. Watch the Chinese export price, the coking coal price and any news on the duty.

glossary.def: A plant that makes steel from iron ore through a blast furnace, then rolls it, all on one site.
A tall furnace where iron ore and coking coal react to make liquid iron.
Furnaces that melt scrap or sponge iron with electricity; cheaper to build and lower carbon.
Direct reduced iron: ore turned into iron with gas or thermal coal, without melting. Feeds electric furnaces.
Fine iron ore rolled into balls and baked so a furnace can use it.
A special grade of coal that turns into coke, the fuel and chemical agent in a blast furnace. India imports most of it.
The benchmark flat steel product, sold in big rolls; its price is the industry's headline price.
HRC rolled thinner and coated with zinc or paint for cars and appliances; earns a premium.
Ribbed steel bars that reinforce concrete in buildings and bridges; the main long product.
Flat is sheet and coil for autos and appliances; long is bars and sections for construction.
Operating profit divided by tonnes sold; the steel spread in one number.
Steel price minus the cost of ore and coking coal needed to make it.
Iron ore from the company's own mine, cheaper and more secure than buying it.
A temporary tariff on a surge of imports to protect domestic industry; India imposed one on flat steel in 2025.
A tariff on imports sold below fair price, after a DGTR investigation.
Directorate General of Trade Remedies, the body that investigates dumping and import surges.
Steel with chromium and often nickel, so it does not rust; priced partly off nickel.
Pipe made without a weld, for high-pressure oil, gas and boiler uses.
Steel made with much lower carbon emissions, through scrap, electric furnaces, gas or hydrogen.
The EU's carbon border tax, charging the carbon in imported steel from 2026.
Plants under construction, not yet earning or depreciating.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.

c1.story:
Every Indian growth story eventually becomes a steel story. The metro line outside your office, the expressway you drove last weekend, the car in its parking slot, the washing machine at home, the gas pipeline running under a field in Gujarat: all of it is steel, rolled, bent, welded or coated. India is now the world's second-largest steel producer, behind only China, and it is the one large economy where steel demand is still growing at a brisk clip year after year.

So owning a steel stock should be simple, right? Buy the demand story and wait. Not quite. The phrase steel company covers four businesses that make money in four different ways, and they react to the same headline in very different ways.

The first door is the giant integrated mill: Tata Steel at Jamshedpur and Kalinganagar, JSW at Vijayanagar, SAIL at Bhilai and Bokaro, Jindal Steel at Angul. These melt iron ore with coking coal in blast furnaces the height of a high-rise and sell flat steel, coils and sheets, to carmakers and appliance makers. The second door is the secondary producer in the mineral belt of Chhattisgarh and Odisha: sponge iron, induction furnaces, rebar for construction, often with its own power plant and, in the best cases, its own iron ore. Lloyds Metals with its mine at Surjagarh in Gadchiroli is the textbook example of how much owning the rock can be worth.

The third door is stainless and specialty: Jindal Stainless, Usha Martin's wire ropes, Gravita's recycled metals. These sell metal for what it does rather than what it weighs. And the fourth door does not make steel at all. Jindal SAW, Ratnamani and Bansal Wire buy coil or wire rod and turn it into pipes, tubes and wire against orders, charging a fee for the conversion.

A steel price headline is good news, bad news or no news, depending on which door you are standing behind.

When Chinese coil prices jump, door one celebrates, door two shrugs, door three watches nickel, and door four mostly checks whether its customers will delay orders.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four business models. Read each tile from top to bottom, then compare the bars across the row.

  • The name and the line under it describe the furnace and the customer: blast furnaces and flat steel for the majors, sponge iron and rebar for the secondary mills, stainless for the specialists, and order-based conversion for the pipe and wire makers.
  • The tickers are listed names that sit mostly behind that door. Click any of them to open its stock page. Notice that JINDALSTEL sits with the majors while LLOYDSME sits with the secondary producers, even though both are really ore stories at heart.
  • The profit bar is the one to stare at. Three of the four doors show medium, which is unusual: in most commodity industries the producers sit at low. Steel producers keep a middling share because India's demand is strong and a duty wall now shields them, but they still hand a lot back to Queensland coal sellers and to Chinese price-setters. The converters show high, because once a pipe maker is certified for a gas pipeline or a refinery, the customer rarely shops around on price alone.
  • The bet line tells you what you are really buying: a spread, a construction cycle plus ore, a niche price, or an order book.

Before you read anything else about a steel name, place it on one of these tiles. A company that straddles two, say a mill with a big pipe arm, should be valued as two businesses.

c2.story:
Picture a kitchen that starts in the red earth of Odisha and ends on a construction site in Pune. At station one, iron ore is dug out of the ground in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka. India is blessed with ore. What it lacks is the other ingredient, good coking coal, and so the second half of station one arrives by ship from Australia, with Russian cargoes growing in recent years, landing at Paradip, Dhamra, Gangavaram and Vizag on the east coast.

Station two prepares the iron. Fine ore is rolled into pellets and baked, or turned into sponge iron with gas or thermal coal. This is where a lot of the secondary producers earn their living, and where many unlisted units in Raipur and Rourkela crowd in alongside them.

Station three is the dramatic one: melting. Blast furnaces turn ore and coke into liquid iron, which becomes steel; electric and induction furnaces do the same with scrap and sponge iron. Station four rolls and finishes: slabs become coil, billets become rebar, coil becomes pipe, stainless becomes a sink. Station five is the customer, a builder, a carmaker, a railway, a city gas company.

Now notice the shape of India's position. Indian listed companies dominate the middle three stations. The trouble is at both ends. Upstream, a few Australian mines and the state ore miner NMDC set the price of the inputs. Downstream, the final price of the product is set not in India but in China, which makes about half the world's steel.

That is why steel in India is a sandwich business. In 2021, when coal was fine and Chinese prices were high, the filling was thick. In 2022, coking coal more than doubled after Russia invaded Ukraine and the sandwich got thin from below. In 2023 and 2024 China's property crash pushed its surplus abroad and the bread got squeezed from above.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the station boxes left to right, then the two rows of bands underneath.

The five boxes run from the mine on the left to the user on the right. Each box tells you what happens there and who does it. Watch how the cast changes: NMDC, the state miners, captive mines and Australian coal on the left; pellet and sponge iron makers next; then the big melters; then the rolling mills and converters; and the builders and carmakers at the end. The boxes coloured as Indian listed are stations two, three and four.

The first band row tells you who holds each station. The first cell is marked as a rival, Australian coal and NMDC: that is the industry admitting that it does not control its own most important cost. The next three cells say India listed. The last cell, builders and autos, is the customer.

The second band row shows China standing at the producing stations alongside Indian companies, with the word World under the customer station. That row is the reason a steel price in Mumbai moves with a steel price in Tangshan: China does not need to sell in India to set the price here, it only needs to be able to.

The practical use: trace any news item to its station. A Queensland cyclone or a coal-export ban hits station one, and you should expect blast-furnace margins at station three to feel it within a quarter. A Chinese export surge hits the price at station four and five. A new rebar order from a highway project starts at station five and flows backwards.

c3.story:
Ask who buys Indian steel and the instinctive answer is carmakers. They are important, and they buy the fanciest grades, the cold-rolled and galvanised sheet that becomes a door panel. But they are not the biggest customer. That title belongs to the humble construction site, which takes well over half of Indian steel through rebar, wire rod and structural sections.

This matters because construction demand marches to a different drummer. A car sale depends on a household's mood and a loan rate. A rebar order depends on whether a builder has launched a tower, whether a state has paid its highway contractor, whether the railway has released funds for a new line. Since the pandemic, the government's own capital spending has been the single most important engine of Indian steel demand: roads, railways, metro systems, ports, airports and the water pipes of the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019 to bring a tap to every rural household.

Pipes are a mini-story of their own. The Jal Jeevan Mission was a bonanza for ductile iron and spiral-welded pipe makers. The national gas grid and city gas networks need large-diameter line pipe. Refineries and power plants need seamless and stainless tubes that can take heat and pressure. That is why the converters' fortunes are tied to project pipelines rather than to the coil price.

And then there are exports, the release valve. When Indian demand is soft, mills push hot-rolled coil to Europe, the Gulf and Southeast Asia. When Chinese prices are low, that valve is shut, and when Europe's carbon border tax bites, a slice of it stays shut for good.

In India, the finance minister's capex line moves more steel than the car showroom does.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read it in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

  • Construction and real estate and Infrastructure sit first for a reason: together they are the bulk of demand. Their third lines read housing starts, cement volumes, interest rates, and government capex. If you watch nothing else, watch these.
  • Automobiles and Consumer durables buy the premium flat products. They are smaller in tonnes but bigger in margin per tonne, which is why the flat-steel majors care about them more than the tonnage suggests.
  • Capital goods buys plates and alloy steel, and moves with private capex and defence orders.
  • Oil, gas and water pipelines is the converters' tile. Its third line, Jal Jeevan funding, the gas grid, refinery capex, is effectively the order book of door four.
  • Exports is the valve. Its third line names the two forces that open and close it: Chinese export prices and European rules.

One way to use the grid: map each company you own onto the tiles. A long-steel producer is almost entirely on the first two. A flat-steel major spreads across autos, durables, capital goods and exports. A pipe maker sits on one tile. Then cross-check with the so-what line underneath: if construction and infra are well over half of demand, the Union Budget's capex number is a steel earnings indicator.

c4.story:
Strip a steel mill to its bones and it is a spread business. It buys ore and coking coal, it sells steel, and it lives in the gap between the two. Analysts compress that gap into one number, EBITDA per tonne: operating profit, before depreciation, interest and tax, divided by tonnes shipped. It is the steel industry's pulse, and across a cycle it can swing by half.

Here is how it moves. The selling side, realisation per tonne, follows Chinese export prices with a lag of a few weeks to a quarter, because Indian buyers can always threaten to import. The cost side is dominated by coking coal for blast-furnace mills, priced in dollars off Australian benchmarks and notoriously jumpy. A cyclone in Queensland, a mine flood, a surge in Chinese buying, and the coal bill can double in months, as it did in 2022. Because coal bought today is melted next quarter, there is always a lag, and that lag decides whether a quarter looks like a feast or a famine.

Then come the lines that separate survivors from casualties. Interest is a big one. Indian steel has a painful memory here: in the bust of the last decade, Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel and several others collapsed under debt and went through the insolvency courts, ending up with ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel, Tata Steel and JSW. Debt-funded capacity built at the top of a cycle is how steel companies die. Depreciation jumps when a new blast furnace is lit, and capex is enormous because every major is expanding at once.

Finally, overseas subsidiaries. Tata Steel's European plants, bought with Corus in 2007, have swung group profits for most of the time since, and the shutdown of its Port Talbot blast furnaces in Wales in 2024 is a reminder that a foreign acquisition can be a decade-long earnings story of its own. JSW's American plants have played a similar, smaller role.
c4.read:
The two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, first for an integrated major, then for a pipe and wire converter. Read each chart left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is iron ore and coking coal for the major, and bought coil or wire rod for the converter. The major's input bite is a little over half its sales; the converter's is roughly two-thirds. That surprises people: the converter pays more for its raw material because its raw material is someone else's finished steel.
  • The opex bar is power, people and freight. The major spends more here, a quarter of sales, because running a blast furnace, a coke oven and a rolling mill is a power-hungry, people-heavy affair.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the business models really part ways. The major's bar is far taller, because a steel plant is a mountain of capital and usually of debt. The converter's is small: a pipe mill is cheap by comparison.
  • The last bar is what remains. In these mid-cycle shapes the two end up with about the same slice, a tenth of sales, but they get there by opposite routes: the major pays less for inputs and more for its plant, the converter the reverse. And the converter keeps its slice more reliably, because its margin is a conversion fee and not a bet on the coil price.

These are illustrative shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below, the line list shows what to watch. EBITDA per tonne, coking coal cost, realisation, capex and interest all carry a yes. Depreciation, working capital and overseas subsidiaries are sometimes: big when a furnace starts, a price spikes or Europe has a bad year, quiet otherwise.

c5.story:
Steel is one of the most honestly cyclical industries in the market, and the last six years have been a textbook cycle squeezed into fast-forward.

Start in 2019: a sluggish Indian economy, weak autos and real estate, thin margins. Then the pandemic, and the most violent upswing in living memory. Governments everywhere spent on recovery, China held back its own output and exports, and coil prices ran to records. Indian mills earned their best profit per tonne ever, and they did something unusual with the money: they paid down debt instead of immediately building new furnaces.

The peak arrived in 2022. Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent coking coal more than doubling. In May, the government slapped an export duty on steel to cool domestic prices, cutting off the export valve just as costs spiked. It withdrew the duty in November, but by then margins had rolled over.

Then came the bust of 2023 and 2024, and it came from China. Its property sector, the single biggest steel consumer on the planet, was in a slow-motion collapse after the Evergrande default. Chinese mills did not cut output to match; they exported the surplus at whatever price cleared. Imports into India hit records, domestic coil fell to its lowest in years, and margins shrank even though Indian demand was growing strongly. That is the cruel part of steel: you can have the best demand in the world and still lose money if your neighbour has nowhere to put his.

The turn came through policy. A provisional safeguard duty on flat steel imports arrived in April 2025, and at the end of that year the finance ministry made it definitive for three years, stepping down a little each year. Prices firmed, coking coal was cheap, and the clock moved into an early up-cycle. The wall is the support, and also the risk.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline beside it, and the four hands below.

The clock has four arcs running clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each arc are when the last cycle passed through that phase: boom in 2020 and 2021, peak in 2022, bust across 2023 and 2024, bottom in 2025. The arrow from the centre points to today. For steel it sits just short of twelve o'clock, at the very end of the bottom arc, tipping into the boom arc: an early up-cycle. Hover any arc for what defined it.

The timeline retells the cycle year by year, colour-coded by tone. Notice the rhythm: a bust year in 2019, the boom, a neutral peak, the long bust, a neutral bottom, and the latest entry marked now. The now entry lists the three supports of today's position: the extended safeguard duty, India's demand, and new capacity, with China's exports named as the cap.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Chinese steel export price: low and stable, with no arrow. This is the missing ingredient. If it rises, the ceiling lifts and the cycle is turning for real.
  • Domestic hot-rolled coil price: firm behind the duty, arrow up.
  • Coking coal price: moderate, no arrow. A spike here would squeeze blast-furnace margins a quarter later.
  • Steel imports into India: falling, arrow up for the industry, because the duty is working. Watch for a rebound through countries not covered by the duty.

Two good hands, two neutral ones: that is what early up-cycle looks like in practice.

c6.story:
An Indian steel mill's quarter is decided by a surprisingly international cast. A property developer in Guangdong deciding not to start a tower. A coal planner in Queensland watching the cyclone forecast. A trade official in Delhi drafting a duty notification. A budget officer in North Block deciding how much the railways get.

Four dials carry the heaviest weight, and they are worth understanding as a set. Chinese export prices are the ceiling: no Indian mill can charge much above the landed price of Chinese coil for long. Coking coal is the floor of costs for every blast furnace. Government capital spending is the volume engine for long steel and pipes. And trade protection, the safeguard and anti-dumping duties, decides how far below the Chinese ceiling the Indian price is allowed to fall. When all four point the right way, as they did in 2021, steel mills print money. When the first two turn against you at once, as in 2022 and 2023, no amount of Indian demand saves the quarter.

Then there are the two-faced dials. A higher iron ore price is a cost for a mill that buys its ore and income for one that mines its own; this is why the market has re-rated the ore-owning names so sharply since the 2020 lease auctions. A weaker rupee raises the coal import bill while making exports more competitive.

And the slow dials. Interest rates matter for balance sheets that carry heavy debt. Europe's carbon border tax, which started charging in 2026, quietly makes Indian blast-furnace steel dearer in one of its key export outlets. It is a small dial today, but it is the one that could grow.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and the weight.

  • Channel is how the dial reaches profits. For steel the channels sort neatly into price ceiling, input cost, volume and protection.
  • A rise does carries an arrow. Green up means a rise helps: Chinese prices, government capex, trade protection, domestic output and auto production. Red down means a rise hurts: coking coal, interest rates and the EU carbon tax. The diamond means it cuts both ways: iron ore and the rupee, where the answer depends on whether the company owns ore or exports.
  • Weight runs from one to three dots. Four rows carry three dots, more than most industries: Chinese prices, coking coal, government capex and trade protection. That tells you steel has more than one master.

The latest column shows a live reading where the dial maps to a series we track. Several steel dials use proxies: the Nifty Metal index stands in for Chinese prices, the Nifty Infra index for government capex, the core-sector steel and iron ore indices for output, the Nifty Auto index for car demand. Proxies are imperfect, so treat them as a direction check. Coking coal and trade protection show a dash: follow those through the news and the companies' quarterly commentary.

The fastest way to use this table is to scan the three-dot rows first, then check whether the green and red arrows among them are currently pointing for or against the industry.

c7.story:
If Indian steel demand is so strong, why don't Indian steel companies simply grow forever? Because seven things get in the way, and two of them never leave.

The first is Chinese overcapacity. China built a steel industry sized for a property boom that has now ended. Its home demand is shrinking, its mills are reluctant to close because they employ whole towns, and the surplus goes abroad. As long as that surplus exists, every Indian price has a lid on it. The second permanent problem is coking coal. India has plenty of coal, but very little of the right kind for blast furnaces, and what it has is high in ash. So the most important input for most Indian steel arrives on a ship, priced in dollars, from a handful of Australian mines.
