doors.sub: Licences, annual maintenance and cloud subscriptions sold to banks and large companies worldwide; a deal takes a year to close and a decade to leave
doors.blurb: A bet on sticky contracts and the dollar, paid for slowly in deal wins

doors.name: Platforms paid per transaction
doors.sub: A toll on every ad shown, every message sent, every card swiped; revenue grows with the customer's volume, not with a sales call
doors.blurb: A bet on India's digital volumes and on the toll rate not being squeezed

doors.name: Consumer internet
doors.sub: Sold to households, one subscription or one in-app purchase at a time; marketing is the biggest cost
doors.blurb: A bet on user growth turning into profit before the cash runs out

doors.name: Product-plus-services and hardware
doors.sub: Engineering services wrapped around a product, or a device sold with its software and maps
doors.blurb: A bet on execution and client budgets, priced like a product but earned like a service

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a landlord with ten-year leases to big tenants. Door two owns the toll booth on a busy road. Door three runs a cinema that must fill seats every week. Door four is a contractor who also sells a kit of his own.
explainer.door_so_what: Ask which door a stock is behind before reading its growth number, because a toll booth and a cinema can both report the same growth and deserve very different multiples.

stations.name: Idea and intellectual property
stations.what: A problem is chosen, a product designed, and code written that the company owns outright
stations.who: Indian listed product companies, with Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai and Hyderabad engineering teams; the global rival is American SaaS

stations.name: Cloud and infrastructure
stations.what: The product runs on rented servers; hosting, data residency and security certificates are bought here
stations.who: Amazon, Microsoft and Google clouds; Indian data centres for localisation

stations.name: Build, test and compliance
stations.what: Engineering, quality, security audits and regulatory certificates such as payment and signature licences
stations.who: Indian engineers at PERSISTENT, INTELLECT, NEWGEN, EMUDHRA; the regulators who certify them

stations.name: Go to market
stations.what: Sales teams, channel partners, app stores and telcos put the product in front of the buyer
stations.who: The companies themselves abroad; Google and Apple stores, telcos and system integrators as gatekeepers

stations.name: Customer and renewal
stations.what: Onboarding, support, upsell, renewal; the subscription is earned again every year
stations.who: Banks, airlines, hotels, brands, merchants and students, in India and abroad

kitchen.rival: United States software and cloud majors
kitchen.note: The engineering sits in Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai and Hyderabad, but the customer for the biggest names sits in New York, London, Dubai and Singapore, so a large share of revenue is in dollars while nearly all cost is in rupees. The cloud bill and the app-store cut are the two rents paid to foreigners.
kitchen.so_what: The money is made at the first and last stations, owning the code and keeping the customer, and lost at the middle ones, where clouds, app stores and sales partners take their cut.

end_markets.name: Banks and insurers worldwide
end_markets.buys: Core banking, lending, treasury, risk and document software
end_markets.moves_with: Bank technology budgets, core-system replacement cycles, dollar rates

end_markets.name: Brands and advertisers
end_markets.buys: Mobile ad delivery, loyalty programmes, customer messaging
end_markets.moves_with: Digital ad spend, festive season, new-app launches

end_markets.name: Merchants and fintechs
end_markets.buys: Card terminals, payment gateways, buy-now-pay-later rails
end_markets.moves_with: Card and UPI volumes, RBI fee rules, consumer spending

end_markets.name: Hotels, airlines and travel
end_markets.buys: Pricing, distribution and revenue-management tools
end_markets.moves_with: Travel demand, hotel room rates, airline capacity

end_markets.name: Broadcasters and streamers
end_markets.buys: Cloud playout, channel delivery and ad insertion
end_markets.moves_with: Streaming launches, connected-TV ad budgets

end_markets.name: Students and parents
end_markets.buys: Test-prep courses, offline centres, textbooks and apps
end_markets.moves_with: Exam calendars, household income, offline centre openings

end_markets.name: Government and defence
end_markets.buys: Digital signatures, maps, drones, surveillance software
end_markets.moves_with: Budget cycles, Make in India tenders, border tension

end_markets.name: Automakers and logistics
end_markets.buys: Navigation, fleet tracking and geospatial data
end_markets.moves_with: Car sales, delivery volumes, connected-vehicle mandates

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Most of these buyers are abroad or are themselves large companies, so this industry is less about Indian consumption and more about foreign technology budgets, with edtech and payments as the domestic exceptions.

walk.opex_label: Cloud hosting, marketing, partner and platform fees

lines.line: Employee cost as a share of sales
lines.why: The main cost line for a product company; it falls as a share of sales when the product scales, and rises when the company is really a services firm in disguise
For platforms, the headline revenue includes money handed to telcos, ad networks or banks; the margin after that pass-through is the real business
Enterprise deals are billed in milestones and banks pay late; rising receivable days ahead of revenue is the first warning sign
Some companies book engineer salaries as an asset instead of an expense; it flatters profit today and shows up as amortisation later
Low for pure software, but acquired products and capitalised code amortise over a few years; a sudden impairment is how an overpaid acquisition confesses
Light for software, heavy for edtech centres and drone factories; a product company that suddenly needs capex has changed business
Most names carry net cash; interest only matters for the rare leveraged acquirer
Treasury income on large cash piles props up profit at some names; a special economic zone tax holiday ending changes the net margin

pnl.analogy: A software product is a textbook written once and sold every year to a new class. Writing it costs a fortune up front, printing another copy costs almost nothing, and the publisher's only fear is a better textbook or a teacher who stops prescribing it.
pnl.so_what: Read employee cost and capitalised development together: a true product company shows the first falling as a share of sales without the second rising.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, but the cycle is in the share price more than in the business. Revenue moves with technology budgets, which are slow, while valuation moves with US interest rates and with whatever the market believes about artificial intelligence, which is fast.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Covid forces every business online, cheap money chases growth, Indian SaaS unicorns multiply and listed names trade at record multiples

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Record venture funding, a rush of listings, edtech valued like infrastructure, growth at any price

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: US rates jump, software multiples collapse worldwide, Indian startups face a funding winter and the largest edtech implodes

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Profits replace growth as the yardstick, cost cuts restore margins, and a cautious listing window reopens

clock.position_detail: multiples reset, deal wins continuing

timeline.what: Indian SaaS is still a private story. The listed set is small: a handful of banking-software names and services companies with products on the side.
Covid moves banks, shops, schools and advertisers online at once. Venture money floods in, a string of product names list, and profits matter less than growth.
US rate hikes crush software multiples worldwide. Indian startups enter a funding winter, the largest edtech collapses under debt and governance questions, and listed names fall by half or more.
Cost discipline restores margins. Banking-software deal wins pick up, generative AI becomes the buzzword in every call, and a few product names return to record highs.

A heavy listing season: a coaching giant, a payments firm, a cloud-broadcast company and a loyalty platform all go public within weeks. The real-money gaming ban forces write-offs at gaming investors. Data-protection rules are notified.

Global fear that AI agents will replace seat-based software hits every product stock, in India too. By autumn the panic fades, IT stocks lead a relief rally and the question becomes who sells AI rather than who is replaced by it.

hands.name: US software multiples
hands.meaning: Indian product names re-rate a month or two behind their US peers

hands.name: Large deal wins at banking-software names
hands.meaning: Deal flow today is licence and implementation revenue for the next two years

hands.name: Platform volumes: ads, messages, swipes
hands.meaning: Volume is revenue for the toll-booth door; a slowdown here shows before any contract is lost

hands.name: Edtech unit economics
hands.meaning: Consumer names turn profitable only if marketing cost per student keeps falling

clock.so_what: At a valuation bottom the enterprise and platform doors recover first because their revenue never fell; consumer names need their own proof of profit.

dials.name: US technology sentiment
dials.channel: The multiple investors pay for growth
dials.rise_does: re-rates Indian product names within weeks

dials.name: US interest rates
dials.channel: Discount rate on far-off profits
dials.rise_does: compresses software multiples everywhere

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Export revenue in dollars, cost in rupees
dials.rise_does: widens margins for exporters

dials.name: Global bank technology budgets
dials.channel: Core-banking and lending software demand
dials.rise_does: fills the enterprise order book

dials.name: Indian digital ad spend
dials.channel: Ad-tech and messaging volumes
dials.rise_does: lifts platform revenue in step

dials.name: Card and UPI spending
dials.channel: Payment-platform transaction fees
dials.rise_does: raises take-rate revenue

dials.name: AI pricing anxiety
dials.channel: Belief that AI agents replace per-seat software
dials.rise_does: derates seat-based names, favours usage-based ones

dials.name: Venture funding flows
dials.channel: Competitor subsidies and hiring wages
dials.rise_does: raises wage bills and discounting by rivals

dials.name: Household incomes and exam demand
dials.channel: Edtech enrolments and fee levels
dials.rise_does: lifts coaching enrolments

dials.name: US visa and tariff policy
dials.channel: Onsite delivery cost for product-plus-services names
dials.rise_does: raises delivery cost for onsite work

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track US software multiples and global bank technology budgets; the first sets the price, the second sets the earnings.

bottlenecks.name: Few large Indian buyers
bottlenecks.why: Indian companies pay little for software, so every serious product company must sell abroad, which means long sales cycles and foreign competition from day one.

bottlenecks.name: Talent war with global captives
bottlenecks.why: Foreign companies' Indian development centres pay more for the same engineers, pushing up wage bills and attrition at listed product names.

bottlenecks.name: Platform gatekeepers
bottlenecks.why: App stores take a cut of consumer revenue, telcos set messaging terms, and ad platforms change rules without notice; a toll-booth business pays its own toll upstream.

bottlenecks.name: Services dressed as products
bottlenecks.why: Many listed names earn most of their revenue from implementation and customisation, which is billed by the hour; the market pays a product multiple until it notices.

bottlenecks.name: Regulatory switch-offs
bottlenecks.why: A single rule can erase a business: the real-money gaming ban in 2025 did it to gaming portfolios, and payment fee rules can do it to merchant acquiring.

bottlenecks.name: AI as rival and tool
bottlenecks.why: AI cuts the cost of writing code, which helps builders and threatens anyone whose moat was cheap engineers; usage-based platforms are safer than per-seat licences.

bottlenecks.name: Listing-wave supply
bottlenecks.why: A dozen large product listings within a year absorb a lot of investor appetite and lock-in expiries weigh on prices for a year after.

bottlenecks.name: Data localisation and compliance
bottlenecks.why: Payment data must stay in India and the new data-protection law adds consent and breach duties; compliance cost is fixed and favours the large.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first and third bottlenecks explain why margins are lower than American SaaS; the fourth and fifth are the ones that blow up individual stocks.

rulebook.body: Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its Board
rulebook.what: Consent, storage, breach reporting and penalties for personal data; the Board became operational in late 2025
rulebook.why: Compliance cost for every consumer app and ad platform; consent rules can shrink ad-targeting data

rulebook.body: RBI payment aggregator and data localisation rules
rulebook.what: Licences for payment platforms and a requirement that payment data stay in India
rulebook.why: A licence is a moat; a fee cap or a zero-charge rule can delete a revenue line overnight

rulebook.body: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025
rulebook.what: Bans real-money online games and sets up a regulator for the rest
rulebook.why: Wiped out real-money gaming investments and their ad spend; esports and casual gaming survive

rulebook.body: TRAI commercial messaging and spam rules
rulebook.what: Blockchain-based registration of senders and templates for business SMS
rulebook.why: Compliance platforms earn from it, but every tightening cuts message volumes

rulebook.body: MeitY IT Rules and CERT-In directions
rulebook.what: Intermediary duties, takedown timelines, incident reporting within hours
rulebook.why: Fixed compliance cost; a takedown dispute can become a headline

rulebook.what: Licenses digital-signature certificate issuers
rulebook.why: A licence business with few holders; eMudhra lives here

rulebook.what: Freed Indian firms to collect and sell map data, with limits on foreign players
rulebook.why: The regulatory moat under domestic mapping

rulebook.body: DGCA drone rules and the drone PLI scheme
rulebook.what: Certification of drones and incentives for Indian makers
rulebook.why: Defence and survey tenders flow to certified Indian makers

rulebook.what: Higher fees on skilled-worker visas and the threat of tariffs on services
rulebook.why: Raises onsite delivery cost for product-plus-services names

why.rivalry: Enterprise deals are fought among a handful of global vendors on reference and trust; platforms and consumer apps fight on price and marketing spend
why.supplier: Engineers and cloud providers are the suppliers; both have pricing power, more so when venture money is flowing
why.buyer: A bank cannot switch its core system without years of pain; an advertiser or a student can switch next month
why.entrants: A certified banking product takes a decade to build; a new app, ad network or coaching channel takes a year
why.substitutes: AI-written software and in-house builds threaten both doors; bundled offerings from the cloud majors threaten the platform door most

forces.so_what: The enterprise door keeps the profit because the buyer is locked in; the platform door keeps some while volumes grow; the consumer door keeps little until marketing stops being the biggest cost.

cheat_sheet.metric: Recurring revenue growth, in constant currency
cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the installed base is growing without one-off licence deals
cheat_sheet.good: 15-25% a year for enterprise; 25%+ for platforms

cheat_sheet.metric: Employee cost as a share of sales
cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the company scales like a product or bills like a service
cheat_sheet.good: Falling towards 40-50% of sales; above 60% is a services firm

cheat_sheet.tells: The real margin of a platform once telco, bank and ad-network costs are netted
cheat_sheet.good: Above 60% for software; 25-40% for payment and messaging platforms

cheat_sheet.tells: Operating leverage arriving, or marketing eating it
cheat_sheet.good: Expanding every year; 20%+ for enterprise, 15%+ for platforms

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether banks and brands are paying on time and whether revenue is being pulled forward
cheat_sheet.good: Under 90 days and stable; a jump of 20+ days is a warning

cheat_sheet.metric: Capitalised development as a share of research spend
cheat_sheet.tells: How much engineer cost is parked on the balance sheet
cheat_sheet.good: Under a quarter of total research spend, and stable

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether existing customers spend more each year
cheat_sheet.good: Above 110%; below 100% means churn is winning

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the cash pile and acquisitions earn their keep
cheat_sheet.good: 25%+ for asset-light names; falling ROCE after an acquisition is the tell

lead_indicators.name: US software earnings and guidance season
lead_indicators.channel: Sets the multiple and signals enterprise budgets a quarter before Indian names report

lead_indicators.name: Global bank technology spending commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Core-banking and lending deals are decided two quarters before licences are booked

lead_indicators.name: Indian festive digital ad budgets
lead_indicators.channel: Ad-tech volumes follow brand budgets set a quarter earlier

lead_indicators.name: Card and UPI transaction counts
lead_indicators.channel: Payment-platform revenue moves with the month's swipe count

lead_indicators.name: RBI and TRAI rule notifications
lead_indicators.channel: A fee cap or a spam rule changes volumes the quarter it lands

lead_indicators.name: US ten-year yield
lead_indicators.channel: Rates move multiples first and funding for rivals next

lead_indicators.name: Venture funding into Indian startups
lead_indicators.channel: Funded rivals raise wages and discount products two quarters later

lead_indicators.name: Exam enrolments and coaching-centre openings
lead_indicators.channel: A student enrolled now is revenue through the next two quarters

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when US software multiples are rising, enterprise deal wins are growing year on year, and employee cost is falling as a share of sales; two of three means recovery, one of three means a trading bounce.

call.headline: A valuation bottom after the AI scare, not an earnings bottom: revenue never fell. Prefer enterprise names with growing deal wins and usage-priced platforms over per-seat licences and consumer apps still buying growth.
points: Multiples reset in early 2026 while recurring revenue kept compounding, so the gap between price and earnings has narrowed in the investor's favour.
Usage-based platforms, ads, messaging and payments, are structurally safer from AI seat-replacement than per-user licences, and their volumes are still growing.
The late-2025 listing wave adds supply and lock-in expiries through 2026, so stock selection matters more than the sector call.
would_change: Another leg down in US software multiples if AI agents visibly cut seat counts at large customers
A payment or messaging fee rule in India that caps platform take-rates
Rising receivable days or capitalised development at the enterprise names, signalling revenue pulled forward

explainer.tell_a_friend: Indian software product companies write a program once and rent it out many times: core systems to banks abroad, ad delivery to brands, card machines to shops, coaching to students. The best of them sell abroad in dollars and pay engineers in rupees, and a bank that installs their system stays for a decade. The worst are services firms wearing a product badge, or consumer apps that must spend on marketing every month to keep growing. The business itself is slow and steady, but the stock price is not: it follows US software multiples, which follow US interest rates and whatever the market believes about artificial intelligence that month. In 2020 and 2021 the stocks boomed, in 2022 and 2023 they halved, in 2024 they recovered, and in early 2026 a scare that AI agents would replace software knocked them down again even as revenue kept growing. Watch deal wins, employee cost as a share of sales, and the ratio of real product revenue to billable hours.

glossary.def: Software as a service: a program hosted on the vendor's cloud and rented by subscription instead of installed and bought outright.
The yearly value of subscriptions in force today. The sector's one big number: it recurs unless the customer leaves.
The old model: a one-time licence fee plus a yearly maintenance charge, typically a fifth of the licence, for updates and support.
The slice of each transaction a platform keeps, such as a share of each card swipe, ad shown or message sent.
Money a platform collects but hands straight to a telco, bank or ad network. Headline revenue includes it; the real margin excludes it.
This year's revenue from last year's customers, as a share of what they paid last year. Above 100% means customers are spending more.
Customers leaving. The enemy of recurring revenue.
Booking engineer salaries as an asset to be amortised later rather than as today's expense. Legal, but it flatters current profit.
Spreading the cost of an intangible asset, such as acquired software or capitalised code, over several years.
A write-down of an asset's value, often an acquisition that turned out to be worth less than was paid.
Charging per user. The model most exposed if AI agents let a customer do the same work with fewer people.
Charging per transaction or per unit consumed. Grows with the customer's volume and is less exposed to AI seat cuts.
The software that keeps a bank's accounts, loans and payments. Replacing one takes years, which is why vendors are hard to fire.
An RBI-licensed firm that collects payments on behalf of merchants. Pine Labs holds such a licence.
Communications platform as a service: sending business SMS, WhatsApp and voice messages for companies, through telcos.
TRAI's blockchain-based register of SMS senders and templates, meant to stop spam.
Technology that buys, targets and shows mobile and web ads, paid when a user installs or buys.
Education delivered through apps and online classes, increasingly paired with offline coaching centres.
Games where players stake money, such as fantasy sports and online rummy. Banned in India in 2025.
A period when venture investors stop writing cheques, forcing startups to cut costs or shut.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, India's privacy law, with rules notified in 2025.
The RBI requirement that payment data be stored only on servers in India.
A foreign company's own technology office in India. Competes for the same engineers as listed product names.
What investors pay per rupee of sales or profit. Software multiples swing with US interest rates.

c1.story:
Here is an odd fact about the country that runs the world's software. For three decades, most of the code written in India belonged to someone else. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune built and maintained systems that an American bank or a German carmaker owned. Software product companies are the exception: they write a program once, own it outright, and rent it out again and again. It is the dream business model of the internet age, and the listed Indian version comes in four very different flavours.

The first door is the enterprise landlord. Oracle Financial Services Software, born as i-flex in Mumbai, sells its Flexcube core-banking system to banks across continents. Intellect Design Arena, Newgen, RateGain, Amagi and Capillary sell banking, document, hotel-pricing, broadcast and loyalty software to big companies worldwide. A deal takes a year to close. Leaving takes a decade, because ripping out a bank's core system is closer to a heart transplant than a software upgrade.

The second door is the toll booth. Every time your bank texts you a one-time password, a messaging platform like Tanla probably carried it. Every time an ad on your phone turns into an app install, Affle gets paid. Every time a shopkeeper swipes your card on a Pine Labs terminal, a tiny fee drops into the till. Nobody calls a salesman; revenue grows with the customer's volume.

The third door is the cinema: consumer internet. PhysicsWallah, which grew out of Alakh Pandey's YouTube physics lessons, and Nazara in gaming must win households one subscription or one purchase at a time, and marketing is their biggest bill.

The fourth door is the contractor with a kit of his own: Persistent's engineering services wrapped around products, MapmyIndia's maps and devices, eMudhra's digital signatures, ideaForge's drones.

Ask three questions of any software stock: who pays, how often, and how much it hurts to leave. The answers sort the doors.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from the top down, then compare the bars across them.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the money arrives: licences and subscriptions from big companies, a toll on every transaction, household purchases one at a time, or a mix of project work and product.
  • The tickers are listed names behind that door; click one to open its stock page. The enterprise tile is the most crowded, which tells you where most of India's listed product depth sits: banking and business software sold abroad.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company keeps. Enterprise sits at high because a locked-in bank pays every year with little extra cost to serve. The toll booths sit at medium: volume is great, but telcos, banks and ad networks take a cut first. Consumer internet sits at low because every new user has to be bought with marketing. The hybrid door sits at medium, earning like a services firm.
  • The last line is the bet. Note the consumer tile's: user growth turning into profit before the cash runs out. That is a race, not an annuity.

Then read the analogy under the tiles: landlord, toll booth, cinema, contractor. It is worth keeping in your head, because the so-what line is the key practical rule on this page: a toll booth and a cinema can post the same growth number and deserve very different multiples. Always identify the door before you read the growth rate.

c2.story:
Follow one piece of software from idea to invoice and you will see where the money is made and where it leaks.

It starts with an idea and a team. A product manager in Chennai notices that mid-sized banks in Africa and Southeast Asia are stuck on ageing core systems, and an engineering team writes a modern replacement that the company owns outright. This first station is where Indian listed product companies stand, and it is where all the value is created: the code, the patents, the know-how.

Then the code needs a home. Almost all modern software runs on rented servers from Amazon, Microsoft or Google. That cloud bill is the first rent paid to a foreigner, and it grows with every customer. For payments and personal data, Indian rules add a twist: since the RBI's data-localisation directive of 2018, payment data must stay on servers in India, so some of that home has to be local.

Next comes the quiet, expensive middle: building, testing, security audits and certificates. A bank will not touch a product without them, and a digital-signature or payments licence is itself a moat. Indian engineers do this well and cheaply.

Then the hardest part, getting in front of the buyer. Enterprise names need sales teams in London, Dubai and Singapore, and often a big system integrator to implement the product. Consumer apps live on Google's and Apple's stores, which take their cut. Messaging platforms need the telcos. These are the gatekeepers, and every one of them charges a toll on the toll booth.

Finally the customer, who must be earned again every year at renewal. A happy bank adds modules; an unhappy one starts a multi-year exit.

The money is made owning the code and keeping the customer. It leaks in the middle, to clouds, stores and partners.
c2.read:
The five boxes run left to right from idea to renewal. Read the top line of each box, then look at who stands there.

  • Idea and intellectual property: Indian listed product companies, with engineering in Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai and Hyderabad.
  • Cloud and infrastructure: the American clouds, plus Indian data centres where localisation demands it.
  • Build, test and compliance: Indian engineers again, and the regulators who certify them.
  • Go to market: the companies' own sales teams, but also app stores, telcos and system integrators acting as gatekeepers.
  • Customer and renewal: banks, airlines, hotels, brands, merchants and students.

Now the band row. Notice the pattern: India listed, rival, India listed, gatekeepers, customers. The Indian coloured cells appear twice, at the first and third stations, with the rival band, US clouds, sitting between them. Unlike most industries on this page, where India holds one contiguous stretch, here India's stations are interrupted by a foreign landlord.

The so-what line tells you how to read that: money is made at the first and last stations and lost in the middle. When you look at a company's accounts, the cloud bill, app-store fees and partner commissions are those middle stations showing up as cost.

The geography note adds the currency angle: engineering in Indian cities, the biggest customers in New York, London, Dubai and Singapore. Dollar revenue against rupee cost, minus two rents to foreigners, the cloud and the app store, is the whole margin story in one sentence.

c3.story:
Who actually pays an Indian software product company? Mostly not Indians. That is the first surprise in this card, and it shapes everything else.

The biggest buyers are banks and insurers around the world. A bank in Nairobi or Riyadh replacing its core system, a European insurer digitising claims, a lender automating loan documents: these are the deals that fill the order books of Oracle Financial Services, Intellect and Newgen. They move with bank technology budgets and with the slow rhythm of core-system replacement, which happens once in a generation per bank. That is a feature: one win is a decade of maintenance revenue.

Then the brands and advertisers, who buy mobile ad delivery, loyalty programmes and customer messaging. Their budgets swell around the festive season and new app launches, which is why ad-tech and messaging quarters can look lumpy. Hotels and airlines buy pricing and distribution tools and move with travel demand; RateGain's fortunes rose and fell with hotel room rates through the pandemic and after. Broadcasters and streamers buy cloud playout and ad insertion, the business Amagi built.

The domestic exceptions are where things get interesting. Merchants and fintechs buy card terminals and payment rails, and they move with card and UPI volumes. But UPI itself carries no merchant fee by government mandate since 2020, so payment firms earn on cards, devices and services around the free rail. Students and parents buy test preparation, and they move with exam calendars and household income rather than with any boardroom.

Government and defence buy digital signatures, maps and drones, in budget cycles and in bursts around border tension. Automakers and logistics firms buy navigation and fleet tracking.

This is an export industry with two domestic side doors: payments and coaching.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, eight buyer groups. Each tile has three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves their spending. The third line is the one to copy into your watch list.

Sort the tiles into three groups as you read:

  • Foreign corporate budgets: banks and insurers worldwide, brands and advertisers, hotels and airlines, broadcasters and streamers. Their third lines talk about technology budgets, ad spend and travel demand. This group is the bulk of the industry and moves with the global economy and the dollar.
  • Indian consumers, at one remove: merchants and fintechs, and students and parents. Their third lines mention UPI volumes, RBI fee rules, exam calendars and household income. This is the domestic engine.
  • Indian state and industry: government and defence, automakers and logistics. Budget cycles, tenders and car sales move these.

The so-what line under the grid makes the key point: this industry is less about Indian consumption and more about foreign technology budgets, with edtech and payments as the exceptions. That is the opposite of most consumer-facing Indian sectors.

Then link the tiles back to card one. The enterprise door sells mainly into the first tile and the travel and broadcast tiles. The toll-booth door sells to brands and merchants. The consumer door is students. The hybrid door covers government and automakers. A company whose tiles are all foreign is a dollar story; one whose tiles are all domestic is an India digital story, and they will not move together.

c4.story:
The explainer's analogy is the right one: a software product is a textbook written once and sold every year to a new class. Writing it costs a fortune; printing one more copy costs almost nothing. So the profit and loss of a true product company should get better as it grows, because each new customer brings revenue without bringing much extra cost. That is operating leverage, and it is what the market pays a product multiple for.

For the enterprise door, the big cost is people: engineers who build and maintain the product, salespeople who chase year-long deals, support staff who keep banks happy. If the company is a real product business, that people cost falls as a share of sales over time. If it stays stubbornly high, the company is probably billing hours for customisation, a services firm wearing a product badge.

The platform door looks completely different. A messaging company that sends a bank's OTPs pays the telco for every message. An ad platform pays publishers for the space. A payment firm pays banks and networks. All of that sits inside the headline revenue and flows straight out again. So platforms show huge revenue and thin margins, and the only honest measure is the gross margin after those pass-through costs.

For a platform, headline revenue is a vanity number. The margin after pass-through is the business.

Two accounting lines deserve suspicion. Capitalised development cost lets a company park engineer salaries on the balance sheet as an asset rather than expensing them, which flatters today's profit and returns later as amortisation. And receivables: enterprise deals are billed in milestones, banks pay slowly, and receivable days rising ahead of revenue is often the first sign that revenue is being booked faster than cash is arriving. Interest rarely matters, since most names hold net cash, but treasury income on that cash can quietly prop up the bottom line.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: global enterprise products on the left, platforms paid per transaction on the right. These two shapes are almost mirror images, which is the point of the card.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • People: engineers, sales and support is the input bar. In the enterprise chart it takes roughly half of every rupee: this is a business of brains. In the platform chart it takes only about a fifth.
  • Cloud hosting, marketing, partner and platform fees is the opex bar, and here the charts flip. The enterprise chart spends about a quarter. The platform chart spends well over half, because the fees it passes on to telcos, ad networks and banks sit in this bar.
  • Depreciation and interest is a sliver in both: asset-light either way.
  • What is left lands in the low twenties for enterprise and the mid teens for platforms.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list of lines tells you what to read. Four get a yes: employee cost share, gross margin after pass-through, receivables, and capitalised development. Depreciation, capex and other income get a sometimes, each with a specific trap: impairments, edtech centres and drone factories, and treasury income. Interest gets a no. The so-what line gives the one test to run on any name: employee cost falling as a share of sales, without capitalised development rising to hide it.

c5.story:
The business of selling software to banks and brands is slow and steady. The price of the shares is anything but. In this industry the cycle lives in the multiple far more than in the revenue, and the multiple takes its orders from US interest rates and from whatever the market believes about technology that month.

The boom of 2020 and 2021 had two engines. Covid pushed banks, shops, schools and advertisers online at once, so demand was real. And near-zero interest rates made investors willing to pay almost anything for growth far in the future. Freshworks, born in Chennai, listed on Nasdaq in 2021; Indian SaaS unicorns multiplied; listed product names traded at record multiples, and edtech was valued like infrastructure.

Then the Federal Reserve raised rates hard in 2022, and every distant profit got discounted more heavily. Software multiples collapsed worldwide. Indian startups entered a funding winter, Byju's went from India's most valuable startup to a cautionary tale of debt and governance, and listed names fell by half or more. The revenue of most enterprise names barely flinched. The prices did.

By 2024, cost discipline had restored margins and banking-software deal wins picked up. In 2025 the listing window flung open: PhysicsWallah, Pine Labs and a string of other product names came to market, while the online gaming ban forced write-offs and data-protection rules arrived.

And then early 2026. When Anthropic released plugins for its Claude Cowork agent, investors around the world asked whether AI agents would replace the software sold per user seat. Product stocks everywhere fell, India's included, even as their recurring revenue kept compounding. By autumn the panic had faded and the question had shifted from who is replaced by AI to who sells it.

Revenue climbed the stairs. The share price took the lift, in both directions.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. On this card, remember that the clock describes valuations more than the businesses themselves.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under them are the last full cycle: the boom of 2020 and 2021, the peak of 2021, the bust of 2022 and 2023, and the bottom of 2023 and 2024. The arrow points at the bottom arc again, labelled an AI-scare bottom. So the industry went round once, started climbing in 2024, and got knocked back to the bottom by the 2026 scare. That second dip is in the price, not the order book, which is why the label says multiples reset, deal wins continuing.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: the boom years, the bust years, then neutral entries for 2024 and 2025 despite all the noise, and the 2026 entry marked now.

The four hands:

  • US software multiples: recovering off lows, an up arrow. Indian names follow their US peers with a lag of a month or two.
  • Large deal wins at banking-software names: steady, flat. Today's deals are licence and implementation revenue for the next two years.
  • Platform volumes: ads, messages and swipes still growing, an up arrow.
  • Edtech unit economics: improving but thin, a mixed reading.

Two hands up, one flat, one mixed: the price side is healing first. The so-what line tells you who benefits: enterprise and platform doors first, because their revenue never fell, while consumer names still owe the market proof of profit.

c6.story:
Two dials set the share price, one sets the earnings, and the rest add colour.

The price setters are US technology sentiment and US interest rates. A software company's value rests on profits far in the future, so the rate used to discount those profits matters enormously. When the US ten-year yield jumped in 2022, a profit ten years out suddenly looked much smaller in today's money, and multiples collapsed everywhere from San Francisco to Pune. Sentiment works the same way faster: when American software stocks rally, Indian product names re-rate within weeks, whether or not anything changed in their own business.

The earnings setter is global bank technology budgets. For the enterprise door, the decision of a bank in Nairobi or Manila to replace its core system is the order book. Those decisions are slow and lumpy, and they matter more than any macro data point.

US rates decide what the market pays for a rupee of software profit. Bank budgets decide how many rupees there are.

Then the two-weight dials. A weaker rupee widens margins for the exporters. Indian digital ad spend lifts ad-tech and messaging volumes in step. Card and UPI spending raises payment-platform fees. And the newest dial, AI pricing anxiety, cuts against any business that charges per user seat: if an AI agent can do the work of ten users, why pay for ten seats? Usage-based platforms, which charge per ad, message or swipe, are far less exposed.

The light dials round it out. Venture funding is two-faced: it raises the market's appetite for tech, but it also funds rivals who pay engineers more and discount their products. Household incomes move coaching enrolments. And US visa and tariff policy raises onsite costs for the product-plus-services names, which still send engineers to client sites.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial: the outside force, the channel by which it reaches profits, what a rise does, its weight in dots, and today's reading where we track a series.

  • The arrow: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways.
  • The dots: three means the dial can make or break a year.

Start with the three-dot rows: US technology sentiment, US interest rates and global bank technology budgets. Notice that two of the three are about valuation, not business. That is unusual, and it is the clock card's point again: in this industry the price moves more than the revenue.

Next, the reading column. Seven of the ten rows map to a series we track. Some map directly, like the US ten-year yield and the rupee. Others are stand-ins and deserve a lighter touch: the Nifty IT index stands in for US tech sentiment, the Nifty Media index for ad spend, consumer non-durables output for card and UPI spending, India VIX for venture risk appetite, and education inflation for coaching demand. Use those as direction checks, not precise gauges. Bank budgets, AI anxiety and visa policy show a dash; you read those in earnings calls and the news.

Finally, count the reds: US rates, AI anxiety, and visa and tariff policy. Two of them are about the US, one about technology itself. The only diamond is venture funding.

The so-what line distils the table: track US software multiples for the price and global bank technology budgets for the earnings.

c7.story:
Why is there no Indian Salesforce? Plenty of Indian engineers built Salesforce. The bottlenecks on this card explain why the listed Indian product sector is smaller and thinner-margined than its American cousin, and why some of its stocks blow up.

The first is the home market. Indian companies spend little on software and haggle hard over what they do buy. So any serious Indian product company has to sell abroad from almost the first day, which means long sales cycles, foreign sales teams and global competitors. Zoho and Freshworks, both from Chennai, made that leap; many others never could.

The second is gatekeepers. A toll-booth business pays tolls of its own: app stores take a cut of consumer revenue, telcos set the terms for business messaging, and Google and Meta can change ad rules overnight. These two together, a stingy home market and rent-seeking gatekeepers, explain most of the margin gap with American SaaS.

The third is AI, which is both rival and tool. It cuts the cost of writing code, which helps product builders. But it threatens any company whose moat was simply cheap engineers, and it threatens per-seat pricing.

Then the two stock killers. Services dressed as products: many listed names earn most of their revenue from implementation and customisation, billed by the hour, and the market pays a product multiple until the day it notices. And regulatory switch-offs: in 2025 the ban on real-money online games wiped out a whole category overnight, forcing gaming investors, Nazara among them through its stake in a poker platform, into write-downs.

In this sector one rule can delete a business model between Friday and Monday.

Rounding out the list: a talent war with foreign captive centres that pay more for the same engineers, a listing wave whose lock-in expiries weigh on prices, and data-localisation rules whose fixed costs favour the big.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck with its reason and a severity label. The labels group the risks into three kinds.

  • Structural: few large Indian buyers, platform gatekeepers, and AI as rival and tool. Three permanent rows, more than most industries carry. The so-what line singles out the first and third rows of the table, the home market and the gatekeepers, as the reason Indian margins trail American SaaS. These belong in your valuation.
  • Two-sided and recurring: services dressed as products, regulatory switch-offs, and the talent war. The so-what line calls the fourth and fifth rows, services in disguise and regulatory switch-offs, the stock killers. They are what to check name by name: read the revenue split between licence, subscription and services, and know which regulator can switch off the core product.
  • Cyclical and slow: listing-wave supply and data localisation. The first is a temporary drag on prices after a heavy listing year; the second a fixed compliance cost that slowly favours scale.

The useful habit is to run each company you own down the table. An enterprise name exports, so the first row has already been solved; its risk is the fourth. A payments platform worries about the fifth. A consumer app lives with the gatekeeper row every day. Different doors, different rows.

c8.story:
Software looks like the least regulated business imaginable: no factories, no pollution, no licences to make a spreadsheet. In India, that impression is dangerous. For half the doors in this industry, the rulebook decides whether the business exists.

Take payments. The RBI licenses payment aggregators, and since 2018 it has required payment data to be stored in India. A licence is a moat, because getting one is slow and expensive. But the RBI and the government also decide what a payment can cost. When UPI and RuPay debit payments were made free for merchants from 2020, an entire fee line disappeared for the industry by notification. Every payments investor now lives with the knowledge that a fee cap is one circular away.

Take gaming. In 2025 the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act banned real-money online games outright. Esports and casual games survived, but the real-money businesses, and the ad budgets they spent, vanished.

Take messaging. TRAI's rules require every business sender and message template to be registered on blockchain-based ledgers run by the operators. Platforms like Tanla earn from building that compliance plumbing, yet every tightening of anti-spam rules also cuts message volumes.

For a platform, the regulator can be your best customer and your biggest risk in the same year.

Some rules are pure moats. The Controller of Certifying Authorities licenses digital-signature issuers, a club of few members that includes eMudhra. The geospatial guidelines of 2021 freed Indian firms to collect and sell map data while limiting foreign players, the ground MapmyIndia stands on. Drone certification and a ban on importing foreign drones steer defence orders to Indian makers like ideaForge.

And over everything sits the new data protection law, whose Board started work in late 2025, adding consent and breach duties to every consumer app and ad platform.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule: what it does, why you care, and its status. The why column is where this card earns its keep, because in this industry it often names the company affected.

Read by status:

  • New: the data protection Act and its Board, and the online gaming Act of 2025. Both landed recently and both are still being absorbed: the first as a compliance cost and a possible squeeze on ad-targeting data, the second as a business that no longer exists.
  • Live: RBI payment-aggregator and localisation rules, TRAI messaging rules, the geospatial guidelines, and drone rules with their incentive scheme. These shape revenue now. Two are moats (maps, drones), two are double-edged (payments, messaging).
  • Always: MeitY IT rules with CERT-In directions, and the certifying-authority licence. Permanent fixtures: a fixed cost for most, a franchise for the licence holders.
  • Coming: US visa fees and tariffs, relevant to the product-plus-services names that still put engineers onsite.

A practical way to use the table: for each company you hold, find its row. A payments platform's row is the RBI one, and its risk is a fee cap. A messaging platform's row is TRAI's. A mapping or drone name has a moat row. If you cannot find a row for a company, its regulatory risk is mostly foreign: bank regulators abroad and data rules in its customers' countries.

Dated regulatory news for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money. In software, the answer depends almost entirely on one question: how painful is it for the customer to leave?

For the enterprise door, the answer is very painful. A bank that has run its loans, deposits and payments on one core system for years has woven it into every branch, every regulatory report and every staff habit. Switching means a multi-year project, a huge bill and the career risk of a failed migration. So the buyer, however large and tough, has surprisingly little power at renewal. Entry is just as hard: a core-banking product that regulators and auditors trust takes a decade to build, and the global shortlist, Oracle's Flexcube, Temenos, Finastra, FIS, Infosys's Finacle and a few others, rarely grows.

For platforms and consumer apps, the answer is not painful at all. An advertiser can move its budget next month. A student can leave one coaching app for another, or for a YouTube teacher. A merchant can swap a card terminal. And a new app, ad network or coaching channel takes a year to launch, not a decade. So rivalry turns into a fight on price and marketing spend, the kind that funded rivals love and shareholders hate.

Lock-in is the whole moat. Everything else is a marketing budget.

Two forces press on everyone. Suppliers, meaning engineers and cloud providers, have pricing power, especially when venture money is flowing and captives are hiring. And substitutes are real for both doors: AI-written software and in-house builds threaten enterprise products, while bundled offerings from the cloud majors threaten platforms. That is the one spoke where the two doors score the same.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: global enterprise products, and platforms with consumer combined. The picture here is unusually clean. The platform-and-consumer shape is bigger on every spoke but one. It reaches the outer ring on rivalry and sits well out on suppliers, buyers and entrants. The enterprise shape is small and tucked in, smallest of all on entrants and buyers.

Look at the spokes in order of the gap between them:

  • Entrants shows the biggest gap: a decade to build a certified banking product, a year to launch an app.
  • Buyer and rivalry come next: a locked-in bank against a footloose advertiser or student.
  • Supplier is close: engineers and clouds squeeze both.
  • Substitutes is a tie, the one spoke where the shapes meet. AI and in-house builds threaten everyone equally.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Read the buyer row's reason in particular; it is the whole investment case for enterprise software in one sentence.

The so-what line maps the shapes to profit: enterprise keeps it, platforms keep some while volumes grow, consumer keeps little until marketing stops being the biggest cost. If a consumer name you follow shows marketing falling as a share of sales, mentally shrink its rivalry spoke; that is the shape starting to change.

c10.story:
Product companies love metrics. Investor decks fill with monthly active users, annual recurring revenue, logos added and adoption curves. Eight numbers are enough to tell a real product business from a good presentation.

Start with recurring revenue growth in constant currency. One big licence deal can flatter a quarter; recurring revenue, subscriptions and maintenance, tells you whether the installed base is actually growing. Then employee cost as a share of sales, the single best test of whether a company scales like a product or bills like a service. A product company's ratio falls as it grows. A services firm's stays put, however many times the word platform appears in the annual report.

For platforms, the gross margin after pass-through is the number that matters, because headline revenue includes money that flows straight out to telcos, ad networks and banks. EBITDA margin then shows whether operating leverage is arriving or marketing is eating it.

A product company's employee cost falls as a share of sales. If it does not, you own a services firm with a better brochure.

Then the honesty checks. Receivable days: a jump means banks are paying slowly or revenue is being recognised ahead of cash. Capitalised development as a share of research spend: how much engineer cost is being parked on the balance sheet rather than expensed. If that share creeps up while employee cost falls, the improvement may be accounting, not scale.

Finally the two that measure the moat. Net revenue retention asks whether last year's customers spend more this year; above a hundred per cent means the base grows by itself, below it means churn is winning. And return on capital employed tells you whether the cash pile and the acquisitions bought with it earn their keep. Falling ROCE after a big acquisition is often the first confession of an overpayment.
c10.read:
Eight rows: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest annual filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company you follow.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Several rows give separate marks per door: enterprise and platforms have very different healthy gross margins, because platforms pass so much through. Always apply the mark for the right door.
  • Today's median is the typical listed company. Two rows, capitalised development share and net revenue retention, show a dash: they come from notes to accounts and investor decks rather than the filing lines we hold. Dig those out yourself for the names you own.

Read the medians with three cautions. The growth median is reported revenue growth, not recurring revenue in constant currency, so a big licence deal or a currency swing can move it. The gross margin median comes from filings that do not always separate pass-through costs cleanly, so a platform's figure may look worse than its true business. And the median mixes all four doors, from banking software to coaching to drones, so it describes the industry, not any one model.

The best use of the table is a three-way comparison for each company: its own number, the median, and the good mark for its door. Pay most attention to the employee cost row: of the eight, it is the one that most directly separates the product companies from the services companies in disguise.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings for Indian software products are written in other people's results.

The loudest is the US software earnings season. When American software companies report and guide, two things happen: their multiples move, and Indian product names follow within weeks, and their commentary on enterprise budgets tells you what the banks and brands are planning. That arrives a quarter before Indian names report. The US ten-year yield speaks on the same horizon, moving multiples first and funding for rivals next. And Indian brands set their festive digital ad budgets a quarter ahead, which is when ad-tech volumes are really decided.

Two quarters out sit the slower voices. Global banks' commentary on technology spending tells you which core-banking and lending deals will be signed, since licences are booked well after decisions. Venture funding into Indian startups tells you whether funded rivals will soon be raising wages and discounting. And exam enrolments and new coaching centres tell you about edtech revenue across the next two quarters.

Some signals land the same quarter: the month's card and UPI counts for payment platforms, and any new RBI or TRAI rule, which changes volumes the quarter it lands.

Put the big signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when US software multiples are rising, enterprise deal wins are growing year on year, and employee cost is falling as a share of sales. Today the first two are ticking: multiples are in a relief rally off the AI-scare lows, and banking-software deal wins are steady. The third is not: wage pressure keeps employee cost flat. Two of three, by the rule's own wording, means recovery.

A valuation bottom, not an earnings bottom: the revenue never fell, only the price did.

That is the call: prefer enterprise names with growing deal wins and usage-priced platforms over per-seat licences and consumer apps still buying growth, and let stock selection do the work while listing-wave supply clears.
c11.read:
The lead-time chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks; the further right, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter: card and UPI transaction counts, and RBI and TRAI rule notifications. These tell you what is happening to platform revenue right now.
  • One quarter ahead: US software earnings and guidance, Indian festive ad budgets, and the US ten-year yield. This cluster drives the share price as much as the earnings.
  • Two quarters ahead: global bank technology commentary, venture funding into Indian startups, and exam enrolments with coaching-centre openings.
  • Three or more: empty here. The slow-burning drivers, core-system replacement cycles, do not have a clean public signal.

Notice that each door has its own dots. Bank commentary is the enterprise door's early warning; card counts and rule notices are the platforms'; enrolments are the consumer door's. Read the dots for the doors you own.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs: two ticks, for US multiples rising and enterprise deal wins growing, and a cross for employee cost share, which is flat with wage pressure persisting. Two of three is the rule's definition of recovery, so the sign to watch is the crossed one: when employee cost starts falling as a share of sales, the recovery moves from price to earnings.

The call box then gives the view, three points and what would change it. Treat the would-change list as alerts: another leg down in US software multiples, an Indian fee cap on payments or messaging, or rising receivables and capitalised development at the enterprise names.

explainer.one_liner: Telecom companies buy airwaves from the government, hang radios on towers, lay fibre to homes and offices, and charge more than a billion Indians a monthly rent for calls and data.

doors.name: Integrated operators
doors.sub: Monthly prepaid and postpaid plans for mobile and home broadband; revenue is subscribers times what each pays per month
doors.blurb: A bet on tariffs going up in a market with only two and a half players

doors.name: Towers and fibre landlords
doors.sub: Rent charged per tenant per tower, with power passed through; long contracts, little growth, lots of cash
doors.blurb: A bet on the tenants staying solvent and the dividends continuing

doors.name: Enterprise and data networks
doors.sub: Connectivity, cloud links, undersea cables and managed services sold to companies on multi-year contracts
doors.blurb: A bet on corporate digital budgets rather than on the Indian consumer

doors.name: Equipment and fibre makers
doors.sub: Routers, radios, optical fibre cable and satellite kit sold to operators and to government networks in lumpy orders
doors.blurb: A bet on the next capex wave and on Chinese vendors staying banned

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the housing society collecting monthly maintenance from every flat. Door two owns the land the society stands on and collects ground rent. Door three wires up office parks. Door four sells the cables and switches to all of them, and starves between projects.
explainer.door_so_what: An operator stock moves on tariffs, a tower stock on its tenants' health, and an equipment stock on order flow, so the same telecom headline can be good for one door and bad for another.

stations.name: Spectrum and licences
stations.what: The government auctions airwaves and charges a yearly licence fee on revenue
stations.who: Department of Telecommunications; operators bid, and the Vodafone Idea dues became government equity

stations.name: Equipment
stations.what: Radios, core network, optical fibre and routers are bought
stations.who: Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung for radios; TEJASNET, HFCL and VINDHYATEL for Indian gear and fibre; Chinese vendors are shut out

stations.name: Towers and fibre
stations.what: Steel towers, rooftops, diesel and grid power, and fibre to every site
stations.who: INDUSTOWER, ALTIUSINVIT, RAILTEL and Jio's own tower arm

stations.name: Network operations
stations.what: Running the network, billing, retail recharge and customer care
stations.who: BHARTIARTL, Jio, IDEA, BHARTIHEXA, TTML

stations.name: Customer
stations.what: Prepaid recharges, postpaid bills, home fibre, enterprise links
stations.who: More than a billion mobile users, a few tens of millions of broadband homes, and corporate India

kitchen.rival: Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung on equipment; Starlink and satellite broadband as the coming substitute
kitchen.note: The costly stations are the first two: spectrum paid to the government and radios bought from foreign vendors in dollars. The Indian listed value sits in the middle, in towers and the network, and the biggest single player, Jio, was unlisted until its 2026 IPO.
kitchen.so_what: When the rupee weakens or an auction is held, cost rises at the first two stations and can only be recovered at the fifth, by raising tariffs, which is why tariff hikes follow auctions.

end_markets.name: Prepaid mobile users
end_markets.buys: Monthly recharges for calls and data
end_markets.moves_with: Tariff hikes, rural incomes, smartphone prices

end_markets.name: Postpaid and premium users
end_markets.buys: Family plans, bundled streaming, international roaming
end_markets.moves_with: Urban incomes, upgrades from prepaid, content bundles

end_markets.name: Home broadband
end_markets.buys: Fibre to the home with TV and streaming bundles
end_markets.moves_with: Housing construction, work from home, cable-TV decline

end_markets.name: Enterprises
end_markets.buys: Leased lines, cloud connectivity, security and messaging platforms
end_markets.moves_with: Corporate IT budgets, data-centre build-out, global trade

end_markets.name: Government networks
end_markets.buys: BSNL's network, railway and defence fibre, rural broadband
end_markets.moves_with: Budget allocations, Make in India rules, election cycles

end_markets.name: Other operators
end_markets.buys: Tower tenancies, fibre leases, roaming
end_markets.moves_with: Rival capex plans and solvency, network sharing deals

end_markets.name: Machines and devices
end_markets.buys: SIM connections for cars, meters, payment terminals
end_markets.moves_with: Smart-meter rollouts, connected-car sales, UPI terminal growth

explainer.end_markets_so_what: The prepaid mass market is where the money is and where tariff hikes are tested, so watch whether users downgrade plans or drop a SIM after each hike.

walk.input_label: Network cost: tower rent, power, licence and spectrum fees

lines.why: The single number the sector trades on; a tariff hike shows here two quarters later as users recharge
Spectrum and network are written off over decades; the charge is enormous and sits between a healthy EBITDA and a thin net profit
Spectrum bought on instalments is debt owed to the government; interest decides whether an operator makes a profit at all
Each generation of network is a fresh capex wave; the cash flow story begins when capex falls after a rollout

lines.line: Licence fee and spectrum usage charge
lines.why: A fixed slice of revenue goes to the government before anything else
Prepaid users pay in advance, which helps operators; tower companies carry receivables from stressed tenants, which hurts
Diesel and grid power at towers; mostly passed through to tenants, but a rising share is being locked into fixed-energy contracts
Years of losses left large tax credits; cash tax is small for most names

pnl.analogy: A telecom operator is a toll road built with borrowed money. Once the road is laid, every extra car is almost pure profit, but the interest and the government's cut are due whether or not the cars come, and every ten years the road must be rebuilt to a new standard.
pnl.so_what: Read average revenue per user against capex to depreciation: rising revenue per user with capex falling below depreciation is the free-cash-flow phase, which is where telecom stocks make their money.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, but it is a competition cycle, not an economic one. A new entrant or a price war sets off a bust that lasts years; consolidation and tariff hikes set off a recovery that also lasts years. Technology generations add a capex cycle on top.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Data takes off, a dozen operators chase subscribers, and stocks rise on volume growth

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Record spectrum auction, Jio launches with months of free service, and the market has more operators than it can feed

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Tariffs collapse, Vodafone and Idea merge, smaller players exit or go bankrupt, and the Supreme Court's AGR ruling adds a mountain of back dues

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Three private operators left, the first tariff hike in years, a government moratorium on dues, and Jio and Airtel raise fresh equity

clock.position_detail: tariffs rising, capex falling, cash arriving

timeline.what: The Supreme Court rules that adjusted gross revenue includes non-telecom income, landing enormous back dues on operators. In December the three private operators raise tariffs together for the first time in years.
Covid makes data essential and lockdowns lift usage. The government offers a moratorium on dues and lets operators convert interest into equity. A second round of tariff hikes lands in late 2021.
The first 5G auction. Jio and Airtel buy heavily and begin a nationwide rollout at record capex. Vodafone Idea cannot keep up, and the government becomes its largest shareholder.
5G rollouts complete in the big cities, Vodafone Idea raises fresh equity, and a third round of tariff hikes lands in mid 2024, roughly a fifth higher. Airtel's revenue per user climbs steadily.

Capex falls as the 5G build matures and free cash flow jumps. Starlink wins its licence. The government moves to ease Vodafone Idea's AGR burden. Trusted-source rules keep Chinese gear out and hand BSNL's 4G build to Tejas and C-DoT.

Jio's record IPO is priced and opens for subscription in October, set to give the whole sector a listed benchmark once it lists. The market waits for the next tariff hike after the listing, while satellite broadband prices its first plans.

hands.name: Average revenue per user
hands.meaning: Rising without subscriber loss means pricing power is intact

hands.name: Capex to depreciation
hands.meaning: Falling means the free-cash-flow phase; a jump means a new build cycle has started

hands.name: Vodafone Idea's cash position
hands.meaning: Its survival keeps a three-player market and a tenant for the towers; its failure makes a duopoly and empties tower slots

hands.name: Satellite broadband pricing
hands.meaning: Cheap satellite plans would cap rural and home-broadband pricing

clock.so_what: Mid up-cycle rewards the operator with the best balance sheet first and the towers second; equipment makers need a new build wave, which this phase does not give them.

dials.name: Tariff hikes
dials.channel: Revenue per user, straight to EBITDA
dials.rise_does: lifts operator profits within two quarters

dials.name: Interest rates
dials.channel: Cost of debt on spectrum and network
dials.rise_does: squeezes leveraged operators and tower trusts

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Imported equipment and dollar debt
dials.rise_does: raises capex and debt cost

dials.name: Spectrum pricing and auction timing
dials.channel: One-time outlay and yearly amortisation
dials.rise_does: adds debt and triggers the next tariff hike

dials.name: Rural incomes and inflation
dials.channel: Ability of prepaid users to absorb hikes
dials.rise_does: slows recharges and causes SIM drops

dials.name: Diesel and power prices
dials.channel: Energy cost at towers
dials.rise_does: raises tower costs, mostly passed through

dials.name: Smartphone sales
dials.channel: Upgrades from feature phones and to 5G plans
dials.rise_does: pulls users onto costlier data plans

dials.name: Global equity liquidity
dials.channel: Demand for large listings and dividend stocks
dials.rise_does: supports the Jio listing and tower yields

dials.name: US bond yields
dials.channel: The yardstick for tower-trust dividend yields
dials.rise_does: makes tower and InvIT yields look thinner

dials.name: China gear ban and satellite entry
dials.channel: Equipment supply and the substitute threat
dials.rise_does: helps Indian gear makers, threatens rural pricing

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track tariff hikes and interest rates; one sets the revenue line, the other decides whether anything is left after the spectrum bill.

bottlenecks.name: Government takes the first cut
bottlenecks.why: Licence fees, spectrum charges and auction prices mean a large slice of every rupee goes to the exchequer before the network is paid for. India's spectrum has been among the costliest in the world.

bottlenecks.name: Two and a half players
bottlenecks.why: Jio and Airtel set prices; Vodafone Idea follows and the state-owned BSNL lags. A hike needs the two leaders to move together, and the regulator does not stop them.

bottlenecks.name: Vodafone Idea's survival
bottlenecks.why: Its collapse would strand towers, dump subscribers on two networks and leave the government holding a loss, so the state keeps propping it up, which caps the leaders' upside.

bottlenecks.name: Low prices by habit
bottlenecks.why: Indians pay among the lowest data prices on earth and the political cost of hikes is real, so pricing power is used in steps every two or three years, not continuously.

bottlenecks.name: Imported radios
bottlenecks.why: Chinese vendors are banned, so operators depend on Nordic and Korean vendors in dollars; Indian gear makers are small and win mostly government orders.

bottlenecks.name: Right of way and permissions
bottlenecks.why: Fibre and towers need permission from every municipality and landlord; new rules have eased it, but a dispute with one state can stall a rollout.

bottlenecks.name: Lumpy capex generations
bottlenecks.why: Every network generation forces a multi-year spend before revenue follows, and 5G has not yet found a use that users pay extra for.

bottlenecks.name: Satellite substitution
bottlenecks.why: Starlink and its rivals can serve remote homes without towers; expensive today, but a cap on rural and broadband pricing tomorrow.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two bottlenecks explain why this sector earned nothing for a decade; the third and fourth decide how much of the current up-cycle the leaders are allowed to keep.

rulebook.what: Issues licences, auctions spectrum, collects licence fees and spectrum charges, enforces trusted-source rules on equipment
rulebook.why: The biggest cost line and the gatekeeper of every network decision

rulebook.what: Tariff forbearance, quality norms, interconnection, spam and messaging rules, recommendations on spectrum pricing
rulebook.why: It has let operators raise prices freely; a change of mood on tariffs or quality fines would matter

rulebook.what: Replaces colonial-era law; allows satellite spectrum to be assigned without auction and simplifies right of way
rulebook.why: Opened the door for Starlink and others at administered prices, which operators opposed

rulebook.body: Supreme Court AGR judgment and later relief
rulebook.what: Defined adjusted gross revenue widely in 2019, creating huge dues; the government later converted dues to equity and moved to ease the burden
rulebook.why: The reason Vodafone Idea is part state-owned and why relief headlines move the stock

rulebook.body: Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal
rulebook.what: Hears disputes between operators, the regulator and the government
rulebook.why: Interconnection and licence-fee disputes end up here; rulings move cash flows

rulebook.body: Trusted sources and the National Security Directive
rulebook.what: Only approved vendors may supply network gear; Chinese vendors are effectively excluded
rulebook.why: Protects Indian gear makers and BSNL contracts; raises operator costs

rulebook.what: Subsidies for domestic manufacture of telecom and networking gear
rulebook.why: Volume and margin support for Indian equipment names

rulebook.what: Uniform fees and timelines for laying fibre and erecting towers across states
rulebook.why: Cuts rollout friction and cost for towers and fibre

rulebook.body: Satellite spectrum pricing by TRAI and DoT
rulebook.what: Sets what Starlink and others pay for spectrum and how they are licensed
rulebook.why: Decides how cheap satellite broadband can be and how much it threatens rural pricing

why.rivalry: Two leaders price together and a weak third follows; towers compete little because each site is a local monopoly
why.supplier: The government sells spectrum and foreign vendors sell radios, both with pricing power; towers depend on steel, power and land
why.buyer: A billion prepaid users have no bargaining power; a tower company has three tenants and one of them is fragile
why.entrants: Spectrum cost and scale make a new operator nearly impossible; a tower landlord can be copied by an operator building its own
why.substitutes: Wi-Fi and satellite for operators; satellite and small cells for towers, slowly

forces.so_what: Operators keep the profit when there are only two strong ones, and towers keep a steady share as long as their tenants pay; equipment makers keep the least, squeezed between big buyers and foreign rivals.

cheat_sheet.tells: Pricing power and mix; the sector's heartbeat
cheat_sheet.good: Rising every quarter; ₹250+ for leaders, ₹300 is the stated target

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether hikes cost customers and whether users are upgrading
cheat_sheet.good: Positive net adds after a hike; 5G users rising as a share of the base

cheat_sheet.tells: Operating leverage from the fixed network
cheat_sheet.good: 55%+ for leading operators, 50%+ for towers

cheat_sheet.tells: Build phase or harvest phase
cheat_sheet.good: Below 1.0× in harvest; above 1.5× means a rollout wave

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the balance sheet can carry the next auction
cheat_sheet.good: Below 2.5× for operators; Vodafone Idea is far above

cheat_sheet.metric: Interest as a share of EBITDA
cheat_sheet.tells: How much of the operating profit the lenders and the government take
cheat_sheet.good: Under 20% and falling

cheat_sheet.tells: How many operators share each tower and whether they pay
cheat_sheet.good: Tenancy above 1.6×; receivable days under 60

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the up-cycle is reaching shareholders
cheat_sheet.good: Positive and growing; dividend yield 3%+ for towers

lead_indicators.name: Leader's tariff announcement
lead_indicators.channel: Prepaid users recharge over the next two quarters, so revenue per user lifts with a lag

lead_indicators.name: Spectrum auction calendar and reserve prices
lead_indicators.channel: An auction adds debt first and triggers a hike next

lead_indicators.name: Smartphone shipments, especially 5G handsets
lead_indicators.channel: New handsets mean plan upgrades two quarters later

lead_indicators.name: Repo rate and bond yields
lead_indicators.channel: Refinancing cost for operators and the yield yardstick for tower trusts

lead_indicators.name: Rupee against the dollar
lead_indicators.channel: Equipment contracts and dollar bonds reprice within a quarter

lead_indicators.name: Vodafone Idea funding and government relief headlines
lead_indicators.channel: Decides tower occupancy and whether the market stays three-player

lead_indicators.name: BSNL and government network tenders
lead_indicators.channel: Orders for Indian gear makers turn into revenue two quarters later

lead_indicators.name: Satellite plan pricing announcements
lead_indicators.channel: Sets the ceiling on rural and broadband pricing before any subscriber moves

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when revenue per user is rising without subscriber loss, capex is falling below depreciation, and the weakest operator is funded enough to stay in the market; two of three means the cycle is intact, one of three means it is ending.

signs.name: Revenue per user rising, subs stable

call.headline: Mid up-cycle with cash arriving: tariffs rise, capex falls, free cash flow jumps. Prefer the best-balance-sheet operator and the tower landlords over the stressed third player and the equipment makers.
points: Three rounds of tariff hikes since 2019 have gone through without meaningful subscriber loss, and the market expects another after the Jio listing.
The 5G build is largely done in the cities, so capex is falling below depreciation and the free-cash-flow phase has begun.
Vodafone Idea's state support keeps a three-player market and a third tenant for the towers, but its equity remains a bet on relief, not on operations.
would_change: A tariff hike that triggers visible SIM drops or plan downgrades
Cheap satellite broadband plans or a fourth operator funded by the state through BSNL
A new spectrum auction at high reserve prices or a reversal of AGR relief

explainer.tell_a_friend: Indian telecom is a toll road built with borrowed money. Operators buy airwaves from the government, hang radios on towers, and charge more than a billion people a monthly rent.
