For a decade after Jio launched with free service in 2016, nobody made money: tariffs collapsed, operators merged or went bust, and a court ruling added a mountain of back dues. Since 2019 the survivors have raised prices three times without losing customers, and the market is now two strong players plus a state-supported third. The 5G build is mostly done, so spending is falling and cash is finally arriving. Towers are the quiet winners: they collect rent whoever wins, as long as the weak tenant stays alive. Equipment makers wait for the next build wave and for government orders. Watch revenue per user, capex against depreciation, and interest rates, and keep an eye on satellite broadband, which could one day cap prices in the villages.

glossary.def: Average revenue per user per month. The one number the sector trades on.
The radio frequencies an operator is allowed to use, bought at government auction and paid for over up to 20 years.

glossary.term: Licence fee and spectrum usage charge
glossary.def: Yearly payments to the government as a share of revenue, historically around 8% combined.
Adjusted gross revenue: the revenue base on which licence fees are charged. The 2019 Supreme Court ruling defined it to include non-telecom income.
TRAI's policy of letting operators set prices without approval.
Prepaid users pay before use, usually monthly recharges; postpaid users are billed after. Most Indians are prepaid.
Tenants per tower. A tower with two operators on it has a ratio of 2; more tenants means more rent on the same steel.
Infrastructure investment trust: a listed vehicle that owns assets like towers or fibre and pays out most of its cash as distributions.
Capital spending divided by the depreciation charge. Above 1 means the network is growing; below 1 means harvest.
Cash from operations minus capex. What is left to pay down debt or pay dividends.
Borrowings minus cash, divided by operating profit. How many years of profit it takes to repay the debt.
Fibre to the home: a fibre-optic line into a house for broadband and TV.
The fifth generation of mobile networks, auctioned in India in 2022 and rolled out from late 2022.
A government list of approved equipment vendors; Chinese vendors are not on it.
Permission to lay fibre or erect a tower on public or private land, with fees set by new 2024 rules.
Satellite communications: broadband beamed from satellites, as Starlink does, without towers.
Leased lines, cloud links and managed networks sold to companies rather than consumers.
A pause on payments. In 2021 the government let operators defer spectrum and AGR dues for 4 years.
A market with two dominant sellers, here Jio and Airtel.

c1.story:
In September 2016 Mukesh Ambani walked on stage and announced that Reliance Jio would give India free voice calls and free data for months. Overnight, an industry that had argued over paise per minute found itself competing with zero. Within three years, most of the operators that had crowded the market were gone, merged or bankrupt, and the survivors were bleeding. Telecom in India is the story of what happened next, and to follow it you need to know that the word telecom covers four quite different businesses.

The first door is the operators, the companies whose name is on your SIM card: Bharti Airtel, its listed subsidiary Bharti Hexacom, which runs the network in Rajasthan and the Northeast, Vodafone Idea, and Tata Teleservices Maharashtra. Their revenue is simply subscribers times what each pays a month, and their fortunes turn on one thing: whether tariffs go up.

The second door is the landlords. Indus Towers owns a vast grid of steel towers and rents space on each to operators; Altius, a trust that holds the towers that once belonged to Jio, does the same. RailTel lays fibre along railway tracks. They charge rent per tenant per tower, pass the power bill through, and throw off cash. Their worry is not price but tenants: will all of them still be around to pay?

The third door is enterprise networks. Tata Communications, the old state-owned VSNL privatised in 2002, sells undersea cable capacity, cloud links and managed services to companies on long contracts. Its customer is corporate India and the world, not your phone bill.

The fourth door makes the hardware: HFCL and Vindhya with fibre and cable, Tejas Networks with routers and radios, Optiemus, Avantel, Valiant and Nelco with devices and satellite kit. They live on lumpy orders and starve between build cycles.

A tariff hike, a court ruling, a 5G auction: one headline, four very different reactions.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare the profit bars.

  • The name and the line under it say how the money comes in: monthly plans, rent per tenant per tower, multi-year enterprise contracts, or one-off equipment orders.
  • The tickers are listed names behind each door; click to open a stock page. Notice RailTel appears twice, as a fibre landlord and an enterprise network, because it does both.
  • The profit bar is how much of each rupee the business keeps. Towers sit at high: once a tower stands, each extra tenant is almost pure profit, and contracts run for years. Operators sit at medium, not high, because the government and the equipment vendors take a big bite first. Enterprise networks sit at medium. Equipment makers sit at low, squeezed between a handful of huge buyers and foreign rivals.
  • The last line is the bet. Read the operator tile's closely: a market with only two and a half players. The half is Vodafone Idea, and it shapes every other tile.

Under the tiles, the housing society analogy maps the doors: operators collect maintenance from every flat, towers own the land and collect ground rent, enterprise wires up office parks, and equipment makers sell the cables and starve between projects.

The so-what line is your filter for news. An operator moves on tariffs, a tower stock on its tenants' health, an equipment stock on order flow. Before reacting to any telecom headline, ask which tile it actually touches.

c2.story:
Think of Indian telecom as a kitchen where the two most expensive ingredients are bought from people you cannot bargain with.

The first station is the government. Airwaves, the spectrum that carries your calls and data, are a national resource, and the Department of Telecommunications auctions them. Operators pay enormous sums, often in instalments that behave exactly like debt, and on top of that hand over a slice of their revenue every year as licence fees. When Vodafone Idea could not pay the dues piled up after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, the government converted them into shares. The state is now not just the operator's landlord but its largest shareholder.

The second station is equipment. Every tower needs radios, every network a core, every street fibre. India excludes Chinese vendors on security grounds, so operators buy radios from Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung, priced in dollars. Indian makers like Tejas, HFCL and Vindhya supply fibre and some network gear, and Tejas, working with the state-run C-DoT and TCS, built the radio network for BSNL's homegrown 4G.

The third station is the physical grid: steel towers, rooftop sites, diesel generators and the fibre that links them. Indus Towers, Altius, RailTel and Jio's own tower arm own most of it. The fourth is running the network: billing, customer care, the recharge counter at every kirana shop. That is Airtel, Jio, Vodafone Idea and the smaller listed names. The fifth station is you, and more than a billion people like you.

Here is the trap in this layout. Costs rise at the first two stations, when an auction is held or the rupee weakens, and the only place to recover them is the last station, by raising your tariff. That is why tariff hikes tend to follow auctions. The biggest player, Jio, has sat outside the stock market for its whole life; its 2026 IPO brings the largest operator into the listed universe at last.

The two costliest ingredients are bought from the state and from abroad. The only place to pass them on is your monthly bill.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, from the airwaves to the subscriber.

  • Spectrum and licences: the government auctions airwaves and takes a yearly fee on revenue.
  • Equipment: radios, core network, fibre and routers, mostly from Nordic and Korean vendors, with Indian makers in fibre and some gear.
  • Towers and fibre: the steel, the power and the cables at each site.
  • Network operations: running the network and selling plans.
  • Customer: prepaid, postpaid, home fibre and enterprise.

Now the band row. The first cell is government, the second carries the rival colour for the Nordic vendors, the third and fourth are coloured India listed, and the fifth is subscribers. The Indian listed value sits in the middle two stations, towers and network, and is fenced in on the left by two suppliers with strong pricing power: the state and foreign vendors.

The rival line adds a twist: besides the vendors, it names Starlink and satellite broadband as the coming substitute. That substitute does not sit on any station in this kitchen. It goes around the kitchen, from satellite straight to the subscriber, skipping towers and fibre entirely.

The note under the diagram says the costly stations are the first two. Use the layout as a cause-and-effect chain: news at the left end, an auction, a rupee slide, a vendor price rise, is a cost that must eventually be recovered at the right end. When you see one, start watching for the tariff hike. The so-what line makes exactly that link.

c3.story:
The money in Indian telecom arrives a few hundred rupees at a time, mostly through a recharge at a corner shop or a tap on a payments app. Prepaid mobile users are the bulk of the market, and they are the people every tariff hike is really tested on.

Here is how the test plays out. When the leaders raise prices, most users grumble and pay, because data has become as essential as electricity. But some drop their second SIM: millions of Indians carry two, one for cheap calls and one for data, and a hike is the moment to consolidate. Others move down to a cheaper plan. Watching subscriber numbers and plan mix in the two quarters after a hike tells you whether pricing power is real or borrowed.

Above the prepaid mass sits the premium tier: postpaid family plans, bundles with streaming apps, international roaming. These users move with urban incomes and are where operators push hardest to raise revenue per user. Home broadband is the quiet growth story, as fibre reaches apartment blocks and cable television fades; it moves with housing construction and the habits that work from home left behind.

Prepaid is where the money is. It is also where the political cost of every tariff hike gets paid.

Enterprises buy leased lines, cloud links and secure networks, and move with corporate technology budgets and the data-centre boom; that is Tata Communications' and RailTel's world. Government networks buy BSNL's equipment, railway and defence fibre and rural broadband, in budget cycles. Other operators are customers too, buying tower space, fibre leases and roaming, which is why a tower company's fate is tied to its tenants' solvency.

And then the machines: SIM cards inside cars, smart electricity meters and card terminals. Small today, but every smart-meter rollout is a few million connections that never complain about a tariff hike.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, seven customer groups. Each has three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

Read the first tile first, as the so-what line under the grid tells you to. Prepaid mobile users buy monthly recharges, and what moves them is tariff hikes, rural incomes and smartphone prices. That third line is the most important watch list in the sector: after each hike, check whether users downgrade plans or drop a SIM.

Then group the remaining tiles:

  • Upgrade tiles: postpaid and premium users, and home broadband. These are where revenue per user grows beyond hikes, through better plans and bundles.
  • Business tiles: enterprises and government networks. These feed the enterprise door and the equipment makers, and they move with corporate IT budgets and budget allocations, not with consumer moods.
  • Industry tiles: other operators, and machines and devices. The first is how the tower landlords earn; its third line, rival capex and solvency, is the tower investor's whole worry. The second is a small, steady add-on.

Now link the tiles to card one's doors. Operators live on the first three tiles. Towers live almost entirely on the other-operators tile, which is why three tenants, one of them fragile, matter so much. Tata Communications and RailTel live on enterprises and government. Equipment makers depend on government networks and operator capex. If a company you own draws most of its revenue from a single tile, its third line is your single most important indicator.

c4.story:
The explainer calls a telecom operator a toll road built with borrowed money, and it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because it explains almost every line of the accounts.

Building the road is brutally expensive. Spectrum is bought at auction for sums that run into the tens of thousands of crores, often paid in instalments that are debt in all but name. Then every tower needs radios, every site needs power and every city needs fibre. All of that gets written off over many years as depreciation and amortisation, and the borrowed money behind it carries interest. Together, those two lines can swallow a huge share of revenue, which is why a telecom company can have a magnificent operating margin and a thin, or negative, net profit in the same year.

Running the road is cheap by comparison. Once the network exists, carrying one more subscriber, or one more gigabyte, costs almost nothing. So every tariff hike flows almost straight to profit. Before anything else, though, the government takes its cut: licence fees and spectrum charges are a fixed slice of revenue.

A telecom operator's EBITDA belongs to the shareholders only after the government, the lenders and the next network upgrade have been paid.

The tower company is a different animal on the same road. Its biggest cost line is power and fuel at the sites, but most of that is passed through to tenants, so it is closer to a reimbursement than a cost. Depreciation and interest are large too, because towers are steel and steel is capital. But each additional tenant on an existing tower costs very little, so tenancy is to a tower what tariffs are to an operator.

Working capital tells the last part of the story. Prepaid users pay in advance, a gift to operators. Tower companies are owed money by their tenants, and when one tenant is in financial trouble, those receivables are where it shows first.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: integrated operators on the left, tower and fibre landlords on the right. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • Network cost, the input bar, includes tower rent, power, licence and spectrum fees. It takes a bit under four of every ten rupees in both charts, but it means different things: for operators it is largely rent and government fees, for towers largely power passed through to tenants.
  • People, sales, marketing and customer care is modest in both, a little over a tenth for operators and a tenth for towers. Telecom is not a people business.
  • Depreciation and interest is the bar to stare at. For operators it takes roughly three of every ten rupees, for towers a quarter. Compare that with an IT services chart, where this bar is a sliver. This is what a capital-heavy, debt-funded business looks like.
  • What is left is about a fifth for operators and a little under three in ten for towers. The landlord keeps more than the tenant.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks what matters, and it is unusually long: revenue per user, depreciation and amortisation, interest and deferred spectrum dues, capex, and licence fees all get a yes. Working capital and energy get a sometimes. Tax gets a no, because years of losses left large tax credits. The so-what line gives the one pairing to watch: revenue per user rising while capex falls below depreciation. That is the free-cash-flow phase.

c5.story:
Most industries cycle with the economy. Indian telecom cycles with competition, and its cycles are long, painful and very readable.

The last full lap started with a crowded boom. In the early 2010s data was taking off and something like a dozen operators chased subscribers across the country. Then came the turn. In 2016 the government held a record spectrum auction, and that September Jio launched with months of free service. Tariffs collapsed. Telenor sold its Indian business to Airtel, Aircel went bankrupt, Tata's consumer mobile business was handed to Airtel, and Vodafone and Idea merged in 2018 to survive. In October 2019 the Supreme Court ruled that adjusted gross revenue, the base for licence fees, included non-telecom income, landing enormous back dues on the operators. The industry earned nothing for years.

The bottom was reached when there was nobody left to fight. With three private players, the operators raised tariffs together in December 2019, then again in late 2021, after a government relief package offered a moratorium on dues and the option to convert interest into equity. The first 5G auction in 2022 forced a final burst of record capex, which Jio and Airtel could afford and Vodafone Idea could not.

Then the harvest began. A third round of hikes in mid 2024, roughly a fifth higher, went through. By 2025 the 5G build had matured, capex fell, and free cash flow jumped. Starlink won its licence, the government moved to ease Vodafone Idea's dues, and trusted-source rules handed BSNL's 4G build to Tejas and C-DoT.

The price war ended the way price wars usually do: when there were not enough players left to fight it.

Now, in 2026, Jio's long-awaited listing is set to give the whole sector a public benchmark, and the market waits to see whether the next tariff hike follows it.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. One quirk to grasp first: the arc years and the arrow describe two different laps.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top. The years under them are the previous lap: the boom of 2012 to 2015, the peak of 2016, the bust from 2016 to 2019, and the bottom of 2019 and 2020. The arrow, though, points into the boom arc, labelled mid up-cycle. The industry has gone round once and is now climbing a new lap that began with the first hike in 2019. Hover an arc to read what defined it last time.

The timeline runs from 2019 and shows the new lap: 2019 coloured bust, the court ruling year; 2020 to 2022 neutral, the repair years; 2023 to 2025 coloured boom, as hikes and falling capex turned into cash; and 2026 marked now.

The four hands:

  • Average revenue per user: rising steadily, an up arrow. Rising without subscriber loss is pricing power intact.
  • Capex to depreciation: falling below one, also an up arrow, because falling capex is good news here. A jump would mean a new build cycle.
  • Vodafone Idea's cash position: fragile and state-supported, mixed. Its survival keeps three players and a third tower tenant.
  • Satellite broadband pricing: launching at premium prices, flat for now.

Two hands up, one mixed, one flat: a healthy middle of the up-cycle. The so-what line says who gains: the operator with the best balance sheet first, towers second, equipment makers not until the next build wave.

c6.story:
For a telecom company, two numbers decide almost everything: what customers pay and what lenders charge.

The first is tariffs. A hike flows into revenue per user within two quarters as prepaid users recharge at the new price, and because the network is already built, almost all of it drops to operating profit. No other dial comes close in force. The second is interest rates. Operators and tower trusts carry heavy debt, including spectrum dues owed to the government, so every move in rates changes how much of that operating profit survives to the bottom line. A highly leveraged operator can see a hike's benefit eaten by a rate rise.

Tariffs decide the revenue line. Interest rates decide whether anything is left after the spectrum bill.

Then come the middleweights. The rupee matters because radios are bought from abroad in dollars and some debt is in dollars too; a weaker rupee makes both dearer. Spectrum auctions are two-faced: they add debt and amortisation, but history shows they also trigger the next tariff hike. Rural incomes and inflation decide how much of a hike prepaid users can absorb before they drop a SIM. Smartphone sales pull users onto costlier data plans. And the twin dial of the China gear ban and satellite entry cuts both ways: the ban protects Indian gear makers but keeps operator costs high, while satellite broadband threatens rural pricing.

The light dials matter mostly to the landlords and to valuation. Diesel and power prices raise tower costs, though most is passed through. Global equity liquidity decides how hungrily big listings like Jio's are received and how richly dividend stocks are priced. And US bond yields are the yardstick global investors hold up against tower-trust yields: when Treasuries pay more, an Indian tower trust's dividend looks thinner.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial: the outside force, its channel into profits, what a rise does, its weight, and today's reading where it maps to a series we track.

  • The arrow: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways.
  • The dots: one to three for how much the dial matters.

Scan the three-dot rows first: tariff hikes and interest rates. Exactly as the so-what line says, these two run the sector. Tariffs carry no live series; you learn about them from operator announcements. Interest rates map to the Indian money rate, so the last column shows its latest value.

Now count the colours, because this table looks very different from an IT or software table. Five dials are red: interest rates, the rupee, rural inflation, diesel and power, and US bond yields. Only three are green: tariffs, smartphone sales and global liquidity. That colour balance is the signature of a capital-heavy, import-dependent, debt-funded industry. Most outside forces hurt it; the main thing that helps is its own pricing.

The two diamonds, spectrum auctions and the China gear ban with satellite entry, are the policy dials, and both cut differently for different doors: an auction hurts operators now but helps them later through hikes; the gear ban helps Indian equipment makers and hurts operators.

Seven rows map to series: the money rate, the rupee, consumer inflation, crude for diesel, consumer-durables output for smartphones, the Nifty for liquidity, and the US ten-year yield. The rest show a dash.

c7.story:
For most of the last decade, Indian telecom was a business that served more than a billion people and made almost no money. The bottlenecks on this card explain why, and how much of the current recovery the operators get to keep.

The first is that the government takes its cut before anyone else. Licence fees and spectrum charges come off the top of revenue, and auction prices in India have been among the steepest in the world relative to what users pay. The second is the shape of the market: two and a half players. Jio and Airtel set prices; Vodafone Idea follows; the state-owned BSNL lags. A hike needs the two leaders to move together, and the regulator has so far let them. That is a gift in an up-cycle and a reminder in a down one that pricing is a shared decision.

Then come the forces that cap the upside. Vodafone Idea's survival is a recurring drama: if it collapsed, its subscribers would pour onto two networks, the tower companies would lose a big tenant, and the government, as its largest shareholder, would book the loss. So the state keeps it alive, which preserves a third competitor. And Indians are used to some of the cheapest data on earth. Tariff hikes carry a political cost, so pricing power gets used in steps every few years, not continuously.

The leaders can raise prices. They just cannot raise them often, or alone.

The structural supply bottleneck is imported radios: with Chinese vendors banned, operators depend on Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung, priced in dollars. Right-of-way permissions for every tower and trench still flare up state by state. Each network generation forces a multi-year spend before revenue follows, and 5G has yet to find something users will happily pay extra for. And on the horizon sits satellite broadband, expensive today, but a potential ceiling on rural prices tomorrow.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, its reason and a severity label. In this card the label matters as much as the row.

  • Structural: the government's first cut, low prices by habit, and imported radios. Three permanent rows. They cap returns through every cycle and belong in your long-run valuation.
  • Two-sided: two and a half players. It allows coordinated hikes, the engine of the current up-cycle, but it also means a regulator's change of mood or one leader breaking ranks could end the party.
  • Recurring: Vodafone Idea's survival, and right-of-way disputes. These produce the headlines. Vodafone Idea's funding news moves three sets of stocks at once: its own, the leaders' and the towers'.
  • Cyclical: lumpy capex generations. Quiet now that 5G is built; loud again when the next generation arrives.
  • Slow: satellite substitution, which is far off but has a long reach.

The so-what line tells you how to read the ordering. The first two rows explain the lost decade: a big government cut and, until consolidation, too many players. The third and fourth rows, Vodafone Idea's survival and the habit of low prices, decide how much of the current up-cycle the leaders keep. When you weigh an operator stock today, it is those two rows, not the structural ones, that will decide the next few years.

c8.story:
No Indian industry has been shaped more by its rulebook than telecom. Courts, ministries and the regulator have, at different moments, created the industry's boom, nearly destroyed it, and then nursed it back to health.

Start with the courts. In 2012 the Supreme Court cancelled a large batch of mobile licences after the spectrum allocation scandal of the late 2000s, forcing spectrum to be sold by auction from then on, at prices that later weighed on every balance sheet. In October 2019 it went further, defining adjusted gross revenue, the base for licence fees, to include non-telecom income. That single definition created back dues so large that Vodafone Idea could only survive by turning the government into its largest shareholder. Relief headlines on those dues still move the stock more than its quarterly results.

The Department of Telecommunications is the industry's biggest single cost line: it issues licences, runs auctions, collects fees and, through the trusted-source rules, decides which vendors may supply the network. Chinese gear is effectively excluded, which protects Indian makers and BSNL's homegrown network but raises operator costs. The production-linked incentive for telecom equipment adds subsidies for local manufacturing.

In Indian telecom, a court definition once did more damage than a decade of price war.

TRAI, the regulator, matters as much for what it does not do. Under tariff forbearance, it lets operators set prices freely, which is what made the coordinated hikes since 2019 possible. Any change of mood there would matter enormously.

The newest rules point to the future. The Telecommunications Act of 2023 replaced a law from the telegraph era and allows satellite spectrum to be assigned administratively rather than auctioned, which opened the door to Starlink and was fiercely opposed by the operators. The Right of Way Rules of 2024 standardise fees and timelines for towers and fibre. And the pricing of satellite spectrum, still being set, will decide how cheap satellite broadband can be.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule: what it does, why you care, and a status tag. Read the status column to prioritise.

  • Always: the Department of Telecommunications, TRAI and the appeals tribunal, TDSAT. These are the permanent institutions. Two lines deserve a highlight: DoT is the biggest cost line, and TRAI's hands-off stance on tariffs is the quiet foundation of the up-cycle.
  • Live: the Telecommunications Act of 2023, the Supreme Court AGR judgment and its later relief, trusted-source rules, and the equipment incentive scheme. These are actively shaping cash flows now. The AGR row is the one that moves Vodafone Idea; the trusted-source and incentive rows are the ones that move equipment makers.
  • New: the Right of Way Rules of 2024, a slow positive for towers and fibre.
  • Coming: satellite spectrum pricing. A single row, but it decides how hard the substitute in card two can hit rural and broadband pricing.

A useful exercise is to map rows to doors. Operators care most about DoT, TRAI and AGR. Towers care about right of way and their tenants' AGR relief. Equipment makers care about trusted sources and the incentive scheme. Satellite pricing touches everyone, slowly.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. In telecom it is worth reading weekly, because rule changes here move stocks the day they land.

c9.story:
Run Indian telecom through Porter's five forces and you get a surprise: the operators and the tower companies, which share the same towers and the same customers, have almost opposite profiles.

Start with the operators. Rivalry is moderate, because two leaders price together and a weakened third follows. New entrants are almost impossible: buying spectrum, building a national network and surviving the years of losses it takes to fill one requires the balance sheet of Reliance, and even Reliance needed years and a free-service war to get there. Buyers have almost no power: a billion prepaid users cannot negotiate, they can only grumble or drop a second SIM. So far, so wonderful. The problem is suppliers. The government sells spectrum at auction prices it sets and takes a fee on revenue; the equipment vendors are a small club of foreign giants. That one spoke is where operator profits leak.

Now the towers. Each tower is a little local monopoly: an operator wanting coverage on that hill rents space there, so rivalry is low. Suppliers, steel, land and power, are manageable. But look at the buyers: a tower company has three tenants, and one of them is fragile. When Vodafone Idea delays payments, a tower company's receivables swell and dividends wobble. That single spoke dominates the tower investment case.

The operator's problem is the people it buys from. The tower's problem is the people it sells to.

Substitutes are a slow threat to both. Wi-Fi offloads data from mobile networks, satellites can reach where towers cannot, and an operator can always build its own towers instead of renting them. None of these bites hard today, but each puts a ceiling on how far either door can push.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, and they look like two kites pointing in different directions. The integrated operators' shape spikes out to the outer ring on supplier power and stays tight everywhere else, tightest of all on entrants. The towers and fibre landlords' shape spikes out to the outer ring on buyer power and is moderate elsewhere.

Read the spikes, because each one is the whole story for its door:

  • Operators, supplier spoke: the government's spectrum and the foreign vendors' radios. Watch auctions and the rupee.
  • Towers, buyer spoke: three tenants, one fragile. Watch Vodafone Idea's funding.

Then compare spoke by spoke. Operators feel more pressure on rivalry and suppliers. Towers feel more on buyers, entrants and substitutes, because an operator can always build its own towers instead of renting. The entrants spoke is low for both: nobody is starting a new national network, and even a tower grid is slow and costly to copy.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Check the buyer row's reason for towers; it is the single sentence a tower investor needs to remember.

The so-what line ranks the doors: operators keep the profit when only two are strong, towers keep a steady share as long as tenants pay, and equipment makers, not drawn on the radar, keep the least. If Vodafone Idea's finances were ever fully repaired, the tower shape's buyer spike would shrink, and that is the single biggest re-rating lever for the landlords.

c10.story:
Telecom results come with a fat investor deck: subscriber bases by circle, data usage per user, minutes of use, tower counts, 5G sites. Eight numbers cut through it.

The first is average revenue per user, the sector's heartbeat. It moves with tariff hikes, with users upgrading from feature phones to smartphones and from prepaid to postpaid, and with plan mix. Airtel's management has long argued the industry needs far higher revenue per user to earn a fair return on its spectrum and network; the good column puts a figure on that target. The second is subscriber and 4G and 5G adds, which tells you whether a hike cost customers and whether users are trading up.

Then operating leverage. EBITDA margin shows how much of each rupee of revenue survives network and staff costs. In telecom it can look spectacular, which is why the next numbers matter more. Capex to depreciation says whether the company is building or harvesting: below one is harvest, above one and a half is a new rollout wave.

A telecom EBITDA margin is a promise. Capex, interest and dividends tell you whether it is kept.

Then the balance sheet, because this is a debt-funded business. Net debt to EBITDA tells you whether the company can carry the next auction. Interest as a share of EBITDA tells you how much of the operating profit goes to lenders and the government before shareholders see anything. Vodafone Idea is the cautionary example on both.

For the landlords, the tenancy ratio, how many operators share each tower, is the growth engine, and tenant receivables are the stress gauge. Finally, the number that justifies the whole cycle: free cash flow and the dividend. An up-cycle only matters to shareholders if it reaches them, and in the harvest phase this is where it should show.
c10.read:
Eight rows: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company.
  • What good looks like carries the figures. Several rows give separate marks for operators and towers, so apply the right one. The revenue-per-user row also gives the industry's stated target, a useful yardstick for how far the hikes still have to run.
  • Today's median is the typical listed company. The first two rows, revenue per user and subscriber adds, show a dash: operators report them in their decks, not in the filing lines we hold.

Read two of the medians with care, because they are proxies. The tenancy row's median is receivable days, which speaks to the tenant-receivables half of that row but not to tenancy itself. The free-cash-flow row's median is return on capital, the nearest filing line, which tells you whether the capital earns its keep but is not the same as cash reaching shareholders.

Remember too that the median mixes all four doors: operators, towers, Tata Communications, and equipment makers big and small. It will rarely look like any one operator. The useful comparison for each company is three-way: its own number, the median and the good mark for its door. For an operator, start with capex to depreciation and interest share of EBITDA; for a tower company, start with receivable days. Those are the rows where this cycle is won or lost.

c11.story:
Telecom gives you some of the longest early warnings of any sector, because so much of it runs on announced decisions that take time to show up in the numbers.

The furthest-reaching signal is satellite broadband pricing. When Starlink and its rivals publish their plans, they set a ceiling on what rural and home-broadband users will pay, long before any subscriber actually switches. That speaks three quarters or more ahead.

Two quarters ahead sit three signals. A leader's tariff announcement is the strongest: prepaid users recharge over the following months, so revenue per user climbs with a lag, and you can model the next two quarters the day the press release lands. Smartphone shipments, especially 5G handsets, tell you who will upgrade plans. And BSNL and government network tenders become revenue for Indian gear makers about two quarters after they are awarded.

A quarter ahead, the money signals: the spectrum auction calendar and reserve prices, which add debt first and usually trigger a hike next; the repo rate and bond yields, which set refinancing costs and the yardstick for tower-trust yields; and the rupee, which reprices equipment contracts. In the same quarter, the headline that moves everything: Vodafone Idea's funding and government relief.

Put the core signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when revenue per user is rising without subscriber loss, capex is below depreciation, and the weakest operator is funded enough to stay in the market. Today all three are ticking. Revenue per user is climbing at the leaders, the 5G build is maturing, and state relief keeps Vodafone Idea alive, if fragile.

Three ticks out of three, with the third written in pencil.

Hence the call: a mid up-cycle with cash arriving. Prefer the best-balance-sheet operator and the tower landlords over the stressed third player and the equipment makers, who need a new build wave this phase does not give them.
c11.read:
The lead-time chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks; the further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Telecom is the rare industry with a dot in every column.

  • Same quarter: Vodafone Idea funding and relief headlines. These move tower occupancy and the market structure at once.
  • One quarter ahead: the spectrum auction calendar, the repo rate and bond yields, and the rupee. The money cluster.
  • Two quarters ahead: a leader's tariff announcement, smartphone shipments, and BSNL and government tenders. The revenue cluster.
  • Three or more: satellite plan pricing, alone on the far right, the slowest-burning threat.

Hover a dot to read its channel. A good reading order is right to left: check the satellite dot for long-run pricing, the two-quarter cluster for revenue direction, the one-quarter cluster for cost of money, and the same-quarter dot for the market-structure risk.

Below the chart, the rule shows its three signs, all ticked: revenue per user rising with stable subscribers, capex below depreciation, and the weakest operator funded. Read the notes, though. The third tick is annotated still fragile. By the rule's wording, losing one tick still leaves the cycle intact; losing two means it is ending.

The call box gives the view, three supporting points and what would change it. The would-change list maps neatly onto the signs: visible SIM drops after a hike would break the first, a high-priced auction would hit the second, and cheap satellite plans or a state-funded fourth operator through BSNL would challenge the market structure the whole call rests on.

explainer.tell_a_friend: Indian textile companies turn cotton and synthetic fibre into yarn, fabric, towels, bedsheets and clothes. Most of the listed ones either sell yarn to other mills or make goods to order for big Western retailers, and a few sell their own brands. The yarn makers live and die by the cotton price. The exporters live by Western shopping and by trade rules. After a boom in 2021 and a painful bust in 2022 and 2023, the industry was hit again in 2025 when the US put steep tariffs on Indian goods. In 2026 things turned. The US cut its tariff, the UK deal brought duty-free access and the EU deal was concluded. Spinners' margins also recovered. The catch is that US orders have not fully come back yet. Brands and integrated mills keep the most profit; small commodity mills keep the least.

c1.story:
Pick up the towel in your bathroom. If you bought it at a big-box store in America, there is a decent chance it was woven in Gujarat or Punjab. The bedsheet in a London department store, the knitted T-shirt on a Paris high street, the innerwear in your own cupboard: Indian textile companies are all over them, mostly without their names on the label.

India has a textile tradition older than almost any other industry on this page, and it is one of the country's biggest employers. But as an investment, textiles is not one business. It is four, sitting at different points between a cotton field and a shop shelf, and they keep very different slices of the money.

Door one is fibre and yarn. Vardhman in Punjab, Filatex and Sanathan making polyester, Alok: they sell yarn or synthetic fibre by the kilo to other mills, at a market price. Their profit is the gap between what cotton or polyester costs and what yarn fetches, and they control neither side.

Door two is the export maker. Welspun Living, Indo Count, Gokaldas Exports and Pearl Global make towels, bedsheets and garments to order for Western retailers' own labels. The retailer's name goes on the product; the Indian company's name goes on the invoice.

Door three is the integrated mill. KPR Mill, Arvind, Trident and Jindal Worldwide own several stages of the chain, from yarn to fabric to finished garment or towel, so the margin at one stage feeds the next.

Door four is where the pricing power lives. Page Industries sells Jockey innerwear in India under licence, and the shopper pays for the name. Garware Technical Fibres makes engineered nets and fabrics for fish farms and sports grounds, sold on performance.

In textiles, the closer you get to your own brand, the more of each rupee you keep.
c1.read:
Four tiles, one per door. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the profit bars from left to right. They tell a single story.

  • The line under the name says how the product is sold. Yarn by the kilo at a market price. Goods made to order for a Western retailer's label. A chain owned end to end. Or a brand and an engineered product sold on name and performance.
  • The tickers open each company's page. Some names straddle doors: TRIDENT, on the integrated tile, is also a big towel exporter, and WELSPUNLIV has its own brands alongside its retailer business. Value the pieces separately.
  • The profit bar climbs as you move right: low for fibre and yarn, medium for exporters and integrated mills, high for brands and technical textiles. This is exactly the line the so-what states: the further a company sits from raw fibre and the closer to its own brand, the more it keeps.
  • The bet line spells out what you are buying: a cotton-to-yarn spread, Western shoppers plus trade deals plus the rupee, full mills run cheaply, or pricing power.

Notice that two very different tiles both read medium. The exporters earn their middle slice from relationships with big retailers, which can be lost. The integrated mills earn theirs from efficiency across the chain, which is harder to lose but needs full factories. Same bar, different risks.

Before reading anything else, put each textile name you own on a tile. The cotton price means opposite things for the first two.

c2.story:
The textile kitchen starts in a field. At station one, cotton is grown across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Punjab, picked and ginned to separate fibre from seed. Alongside it, polyester is made from oil-derived chemicals and viscose from wood pulp. The Cotton Corporation of India buys from farmers whenever prices fall below the government's support price, which is why Indian cotton can sometimes cost more than cotton elsewhere in the world.

Station two is spinning, where fibre is twisted into yarn on spindles that run day and night. This is India's strongest station. Vardhman, KPR Mill, Trident and hundreds of smaller mills across Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Punjab make so much yarn that India exports it, much of it historically to China and Bangladesh.

Station three is fabric: weaving or knitting yarn into cloth, then dyeing and finishing it. Arvind is famous for denim; Jindal Worldwide and Alok are big here too. But this is where China looms largest. Chinese mills make a huge share of the world's fabric, with scale, integration and dyeing capacity that Indian mills struggle to match.

Station four is making up: cutting and stitching fabric into garments, towels and bedsheets. Here India splits in two. In home textiles, India is a world leader: Welspun, Indo Count and Trident supply towels and bedsheets to the biggest American retailers. In garments, Bangladesh and Vietnam have beaten India for years, thanks to lower wages, giant factories and duty-free access to Europe that India lacked.

Station five is the brand and the shelf, mostly Western retailers for exports, Page Industries and Indian brands at home.

So the Indian kitchen is strong at the start, contested in the middle and weak at the end: great at yarn and towels, outgunned in fabric and garments.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the station boxes left to right, then the two band rows.

The five boxes run from fibre to shelf. Each says what happens and who does it. Notice the cast change: farmers, the Cotton Corporation and synthetic fibre makers at station one; Indian spinners at two; Arvind and Jindal Worldwide at three, with a note that China dominates world fabric; Welspun, Indo Count and Gokaldas at four, with Bangladesh and Vietnam competing hard; Western retailers and Page at five.

The first band row labels who holds each station, and it is unusually candid. Stations one and two are Indian: fibre makers and Indian spinners. Station three is labelled China's fabric, marked as a rival. Station four is Bangladesh and Vietnam, also rivals. Station five is global retailers. In other words, the band row admits that Indian listed companies do not hold the middle and later stations, even though some of them operate there.

The second band row shows the rival across the producing stations, as labelled: China, with Bangladesh and Vietnam in garments, and World under the shelf.

The note underneath gives the geography: spinning near the cotton belt in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Punjab; garments and home textiles in Tiruppur, Panipat, Karur and Bengaluru. The so-what line draws the conclusion: because Indian listed names are strongest upstream and in home textiles, their fortunes swing with cotton prices and Western orders.

Use it to trace news. A bad monsoon hits station one first. A US tariff hits stations four and five. A trade deal that gives Indian garments the same access as Bangladesh's changes who wins at station four.

c3.story:
If you want to know how Welspun Living's next quarter will go, do not start with Welspun. Start with an American retailer's warehouse.

That is because the listed exporters depend heavily on a handful of large US retailers, the big-box chains and department stores that sell towels and bedsheets under their own labels. When those retailers' shelves are lean, they place big orders. When their warehouses are full of unsold stock, as they were in 2022 and 2023, orders dry up for months, regardless of how many towels American shoppers are actually buying. It is the same destocking pattern you see in chemicals: the middleman's inventory, not the end customer's appetite, drives the order book.

That concentration can be brutal. In 2016, a major American retailer dropped Welspun after discovering that sheets sold as Egyptian cotton were not, and the stock fell sharply. One customer's decision moved an entire listed company.

Beyond the US, there are European and UK apparel brands buying T-shirts, denim and knitwear to order, increasingly as part of a China plus one strategy: buyers adding a second supplier outside China. The US ban on cotton from China's Xinjiang region, which came into force in 2022, gave that strategy extra urgency. The UK is about to matter more, thanks to the new trade pact.

At home, Indian shoppers buy innerwear, ethnic wear and everyday clothes, moving with rural and urban spending and, crucially, the wedding season. Other mills, in India and abroad, buy yarn. Industrial buyers want fishing nets and agricultural textiles. The government buys uniforms.

For an Indian towel exporter, an American warehouse manager is the most important economist in the world.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them. Sort the tiles by where they sit and you will see the industry's exposure clearly.

  • The export tiles: US home-furnishing retailers, US and European apparel brands, and UK retailers. Their third lines are the global drivers: US housing activity, tariffs on Indian goods, store inventories, China plus one sourcing and the India-UK pact. Three of seven tiles, but most of the listed exporters' revenue.
  • The domestic tile: Indian shoppers, moving with spending and the wedding season. This is where Page Industries and the Indian brands live.
  • The intermediate tile: other mills, buying yarn, moving with Chinese and Bangladeshi demand. This is the spinners' customer, which is why China's yarn imports appear on the lead-time chart on card eleven.
  • The specialist tiles: industrial buyers of fishing nets, sports fabric and agricultural textiles, moving with aquaculture, infrastructure and farm spending; and government uniform tenders. These are Garware's world and a sliver of others'.

The most important tile is the first. Its third line names US tariffs on Indian goods, and the so-what line underneath warns that a US tariff or US inventory glut hits the exporters fast.

To use the grid, map each company. A towel and bedsheet exporter sits almost entirely on the first tile. A spinner sits on the yarn tile. A brand sits on the domestic tile. The more concentrated the map, the more one customer's cycle becomes your stock's cycle.

c4.story:
A spinning mill is a lot like a sugar mill. It buys its crop once a year, in season, stores it for months, processes it through the year and hopes the selling price holds. Get the cotton purchase right and the year is good. Buy at the top, as many mills did in 2022 when cotton spiked, and the inventory losses can wipe out a year's profit when prices fall.

That is why raw material is the line that matters most for a spinner: cotton or polyester is by far the biggest cost, and the spread between that cost and the yarn price is the whole business. Power comes next. Spindles run around the clock, and state power tariffs decide who can compete; a mill in a state with cheap industrial power has a real edge over one paying more. Working capital ties up cash because cotton bought in season sits in godowns for months, and interest on those working capital loans is what makes weak mills fragile when margins fall.

A brand's profit and loss looks completely different. Raw material is a much smaller share of sales, because the shopper is paying for the name, the fit and the trust, not the cotton. But the brand spends heavily on what the spinner barely needs: marketing, distribution, retail staff, a network of shops and dealers. Page Industries' innerwear sells for far more than the fabric in it costs, and that difference is the brand.

Then a line that only exporters fully appreciate: export incentives. Schemes that refund taxes embedded in exported textiles and garments can be worth a few percentage points of sales. For a thin-margin exporter, that can be the difference between profit and loss, which is why every change to those schemes makes headlines in Tiruppur.

A spinner bets on the cotton crop. A brand bets on the shopper. Their accounts look like two different industries.
c4.read:
Two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: fibre and yarn makers on one side, brands and technical textiles on the other. Read each left to right, and the contrast is the lesson.

  • The input bar is cotton and fibre. For the yarn maker it swallows roughly two-thirds of every rupee. For the brand it takes about four rupees in ten.
  • The opex bar is power, wages and freight. This flips: the brand's opex is double the spinner's, at over a third of sales, because selling a brand means people, shops, marketing and distribution.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small for both, a bit bigger for the yarn maker, whose spindles are capital-intensive and who borrows to carry cotton.
  • The last bar is what is left. The yarn maker keeps less than a tenth. The brand keeps more than twice as much. Spending more on people and marketing, the brand still ends up with a far bigger slice: that is pricing power, seen on a chart.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the line list marks what to watch. Raw material, power, working capital, capex and interest all get a yes: four of those five are about the spinner's cotton-and-spindle economics. Employee cost, depreciation and export incentives are sometimes. Employee cost is minor for a spinner but large for a garment maker who stitches by hand. Export incentives are minor for a domestic brand and potentially decisive for an exporter.

c5.story:
The textile cycle of the last six years has had more plot twists than most: a pandemic, a boom, a bust, a political upheaval in a rival country, a tariff shock and a trade-deal rescue.

In 2020 the lockdown shut mills and export orders vanished for months. Then 2021 and 2022 brought a boom. Western retailers restocked aggressively after the pandemic, and buyers shifted orders away from China, worried about supply disruptions and, from 2022, the US ban on Xinjiang cotton. Yarn prices hit records, and spinners made more money than they had in years.

The peak in 2022 came with a trap. Cotton spiked, and mills bought at the top, expecting the boom to continue. It did not. Western retailers discovered their warehouses were overflowing with unsold stock and slashed orders. Cotton crashed, and mills holding expensive inventory booked heavy losses. Through 2023 and 2024 the industry sat at the bottom: thin margins, slow orders and idle spindles at the smaller mills.

In 2024 came an unexpected boost: political upheaval in Bangladesh, which ended with Sheikh Hasina's ouster in August, pushed some garment orders to Indian makers. Then 2025 delivered a fresh blow. The US imposed steep tariffs on Indian goods, among the highest it charged any trading partner, and Indian exporters cut prices and lost orders to Bangladesh, Vietnam and others. The government waived its import duty on cotton for the second half of the year to give mills some relief.

By 2026 things had turned. The US cut its tariff under an interim deal, the UK pact brought duty-free access and the EU deal was concluded. Spinning margins recovered as synthetic fibre got dearer, making cotton yarn more competitive. The catch: US orders were still rebuilding.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock shows four arcs, clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each are from the last cycle: boom in 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust from 2022 into 2023, bottom across 2023 and 2024. The arrow points to today, just short of twelve o'clock, at the end of the bottom arc and about to enter boom: an early up-cycle. Hover an arc for what defined it.

The timeline is where this industry's story gets interesting. Read the colours: the pandemic bust of 2020, the boom, the bust of 2022 and 2023, a neutral 2024 when Bangladesh's turmoil sent orders to India, then a second bust colour in 2025 for the US tariffs, and finally the now entry for 2026. That 2025 entry is a double dip that the four-arc clock cannot show on its own: the industry left the bottom, got knocked back by policy, and is now climbing again.

The four hands let you read the clock yourself.

  • Cotton price: high and firm, arrow up. Good for spinners' selling prices, a squeeze on garment and home-textile makers.
  • US orders to India: recovering slowly, a diamond. This is the trigger for exporters' earnings, and it has not fired yet.
  • Yarn spread: wider than last year, arrow up. Spinning margins are back.
  • Rupee: firmer this month, arrow down for the industry, because a stronger rupee cuts exporters' earnings per dollar.

Two up, one mixed, one down: an early up-cycle that is real for spinners and still pending for exporters.

c6.story:
A textile exporter in Tiruppur or Karur is plugged into a wiring diagram that runs through Washington, the cotton fields of Gujarat, the oil market and the currency desk.

Three dials carry three dots each. The first is the rupee against the dollar. Exporters earn in dollars and pay most costs in rupees, so a weaker rupee directly fattens their margins, and on thin margins a few percent of currency move is a big swing in profit. The second is US tariffs on Indian goods. Textiles is a price-sensitive business, and US retailers will move orders to Bangladesh or Vietnam over a small price gap. When the US raised tariffs on Indian goods sharply in 2025, that gap became a chasm, and orders moved. When it cut them in 2026, the door reopened. The third is the cotton price, a classic two-faced dial: rising cotton lifts spinners' selling prices briefly but squeezes the garment and home-textile makers who buy their yarn and fabric.

The two-dot dials include crude oil, which drives polyester and nylon costs. When crude rises, synthetic fibre gets dearer and cotton yarn becomes relatively more attractive, which is part of why spinning margins recovered recently. India's overall export momentum signals fuller mills. And interest rates matter more here than in many industries, because mills borrow heavily to carry cotton stock for months.

The one-dot dials are domestic: clothing inflation, which tells you whether brands can raise prices at home, and factory output, a general read on domestic demand.

Notice what dominates: two of the three heaviest dials are about the export trade, the currency and the tariff. That tells you where the industry's fate is really decided: not in Indian shops, but at Western ports.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does and the weight.

  • The arrows: green for the rupee row, India's exports, clothing inflation and factory output. Red for US tariffs and interest rates. A diamond for cotton and crude, which help one part of the industry and hurt another.
  • A note on the rupee row: its green arrow refers to a rise in the dollar-rupee rate, which means a weaker rupee. A weaker rupee helps exporters. If you see the rupee strengthening in the news, read it as the dial falling, which hurts.
  • Weight: three dots on the rupee, US tariffs and cotton. Two on crude, exports and interest rates. One on clothing inflation and factory output.

The latest column shows live readings where a dial maps to a series we track: the dollar-rupee rate, Brent crude, India's exports, clothing and footwear inflation, the policy rate and manufacturing output. US tariffs and cotton show a dash: tariffs move by announcement, and cotton is best followed through the Cotton Corporation and global cotton quotes.

The quickest use of the table: scan the three-dot rows first. Then, as the so-what line suggests, pair the rupee with US tariffs. Together they decide whether an Indian exporter is price-competitive in America. A lower tariff with a weaker rupee is the best combination; a higher tariff with a stronger rupee is the worst. Today, the tariff has come down but the rupee hand on card five is firmer, so the two are partly offsetting.

c7.story:
India grows cotton, spins excellent yarn, has a deep pool of skilled workers and a centuries-old textile tradition. So why did Bangladesh, with no cotton of its own, overtake India in garment exports? The bottlenecks explain it.

The first is fragmentation. India's textile industry is made up of thousands of small mills and units, many family-run. In a downturn, they all cut prices to keep their machines running, so nobody holds margin. Bangladesh, by contrast, built giant garment factories that could take the enormous orders Western retailers like to place.

The second is input cost. Quality control orders on imported polyester and viscose, meant to protect Indian fibre makers, keep synthetic fibre prices in India above Chinese levels. That helps the fibre maker and hurts every garment maker downstream who has to buy that fibre.

Then the farm. Indian cotton yields per acre are well below those of other big growers, so the crop is vulnerable to bad monsoons and pests like the pink bollworm, and a short crop sends prices soaring. Most garment makers are too small to win the giant orders Bangladesh and Vietnam take; this is improving slowly as integrated parks and incentives push scale.

Customer concentration cuts both ways. A few large US retailers buy most of India's home textiles, which gives the exporters big, steady volumes, but it means one buyer's mood can move a whole stock.

In textiles, the downturn does not kill the weak mills. It is the cotton they bought before the downturn that does.

And finally, cash stuck in cotton. Mills must buy in season and hold it for months. When prices fall, the inventory losses and working capital loans can sink a weak balance sheet.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to think about each risk.

  • Structural: fragmented small mills and pricier fibre than China. These are permanent features that cap the whole industry's returns. Fragmentation means no pricing discipline in downturns. Pricier fibre means Indian garments start every race a step behind Chinese ones.
  • Recurring: low cotton yields. A bad monsoon or a pest attack spikes cotton prices every few years. Expect it; do not be surprised by it.
  • Slow: small garment units. This is slowly improving as integrated parks and incentive schemes push companies to scale up, but it takes years.
  • Two-sided: US customer concentration. Big, loyal customers are a strength in good times and a single point of failure in bad times.
  • Cyclical: cash stuck in cotton. Harmless when cotton is rising, dangerous when it falls, as the 2022 crash showed.

The so-what underneath draws the conclusion: scale and cheap inputs decide survival, and the integrated mills with strong balance sheets come out of each bust stronger.

A useful way to use the table: for each company you own, check which rows it has escaped. An integrated mill with a strong balance sheet has largely escaped the fragmentation and cash rows. A brand has escaped most of them. A small spinner is exposed to almost every one.

c8.story:
Textiles has one of the busiest rulebooks of any Indian industry, and right now it is the trade rules, not the domestic ones, that are driving the story.

Start at home with cotton. The Cotton Corporation of India buys from farmers whenever prices fall below the minimum support price. That protects farmers, but it can put a floor under domestic cotton that keeps it above world prices, which hurts the mills. The customs duty on imported cotton adds to that. When the government waives it, as it did from August to the end of 2025 to cushion the US tariff blow, mills can import cheaper cotton and margins improve.

Then the incentives. Export duty rebate schemes refund taxes embedded in exported textiles and garments. A production-linked incentive scheme pays for new man-made fibre and technical textile capacity. And PM MITRA parks offer large integrated textile parks with shared infrastructure, an attempt to give Indian companies the scale that Bangladesh and Vietnam enjoy.

But the rows that matter most today are trade deals. The US reciprocal tariff decides whether American retailers buy from India or from its rivals, and its swings in 2025 and 2026 were the biggest single influence on exporters' stocks. The India-UK trade pact gives Indian textiles duty-free entry into Britain, putting Indian makers on level terms with Bangladesh there for the first time. And the India-EU agreement, concluded and awaiting ratification, will do the same for Europe.

For a decade, Indian garment makers ran the race with weights on. The trade deals are taking some of the weights off.

Bangladesh's advantage in Europe was never just cheaper labour. It was duty-free access that India lacked. That gap is now closing.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care and its status. This rulebook has more live rows than most; the status column helps you sort them.

  • Always: the Cotton Corporation and the support price, and the export duty rebates. Permanent background. The rebate row matters disproportionately to thin-margin exporters.
  • Live: the cotton import duty, the fibre quality control orders, the PLI scheme, PM MITRA parks and the US reciprocal tariff. Five live rows. The tariff row is the most important on the page; the cotton duty and fibre quality rows decide input costs.
  • New: the India-UK trade pact. Duty-free access to Britain is a real, immediate advantage for companies with UK customers, which is why the call prefers exporters with UK and European reach.
  • Coming: the India-EU agreement. Once ratified, it removes EU duties on Indian textiles. The biggest future swing factor.

Notice how many rows pull in opposite directions. The support price and fibre quality orders raise input costs; the duty waiver and incentive schemes lower them. The trade deals open markets; the US tariff can close one.

A practical habit: for each company, tick the rows that touch it. A US home-textile exporter is most exposed to the tariff row. A UK-focused garment maker benefits most from the new pact. A domestic brand barely touches the trade rows at all.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks who keeps the profit: rivals, suppliers, buyers, new entrants or substitutes. Few industries show the answer as starkly as textiles.

A yarn maker faces near-maximum pressure from almost every direction. Rivalry is relentless, because yarn is a commodity sold by thousands of mills, and in a downturn they all cut prices together. Buyers have all the power: a weaving mill shops on price and switches suppliers for a small saving. Suppliers are a mixed bag, since cotton follows the crop and the support price, which the spinner cannot influence. New entrants are a constant threat, because a small mill is cheap to start. Only substitutes offer relief: clothes themselves have no substitute, and cotton and polyester simply substitute for each other.

A brand faces almost the opposite. Page Industries does not compete with thousands of mills; it competes with a few other innerwear brands, on name and fit. It buys finished fabric and can switch mills, so suppliers have little power. Its buyer, the shopper, pays for the name and rarely haggles. New entrants face a long climb, because building a trusted brand, or a technical product that a fish farm or a stadium will rely on, takes years.

That gap in bargaining power is the single most important structural fact about this industry. It explains why a spinner and a brand, which both turn cotton into something, earn such different margins and trade at such different valuations. The spinner earns what the cotton cycle allows. The brand earns what its name allows.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure on the business, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: fibre and yarn makers, and brands and technical textiles. This is one of the most lopsided radars on any industry page. The yarn shape reaches the full three on rivalry and buyers, two on suppliers and new entrants. The brand shape is a small, even pentagon, scoring one on every spoke.

Look for where the shapes meet. They touch on just one spoke: substitutes, where both score one, because clothes have no substitute and cotton and polyester swap for each other for both groups. Everywhere else, the yarn shape is far bigger.

The biggest gaps are on rivalry and buyers, both three against one. Those two spokes together are the commodity problem: many sellers, price-shopping buyers.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Use it to place companies that fall between the two shapes. An export maker sits somewhere in the middle: its buyer spoke is long, because a few large US retailers hold the power, but its rivalry spoke is shorter than a spinner's because qualifying as a big retailer's supplier takes time. An integrated mill shortens the supplier spoke by making its own yarn.

The so-what line puts it in a sentence: profit sits with the brands and specialists, while commodity spinners keep only what the cotton cycle allows.

c10.story:
A textile company's results call can wander through cotton crop estimates, US retailer commentary, freight rates and new spindle counts. Eight numbers cut through it.

Gross margin comes first, because it is the spread between fibre cost and selling price, the core of the business. The benchmarks are very different for spinners and brands, which tells you how different the two businesses are. Operating margin tells you what is left after power, wages and freight.

Then the two working capital numbers that are especially telling in textiles. Inventory days tell you how much cotton and finished stock the company is carrying. A spinner with rising inventory days going into a falling cotton market is sitting on future losses. Receivable days tell you how fast customers pay, and a slowing payer is often an early sign of trouble at a retailer.

The cost lines come next. Power and fuel as a share of sales measures a mill's energy efficiency and the power tariff in its state. Employee cost measures labour intensity: low for an automated spinner, much higher for a garment maker who stitches by hand.

Debt to operating profit is the survival number. Mills that borrowed heavily to carry cotton or build capacity are the ones that struggle in a bust; mills with low debt can buy cheap cotton when others are forced to sell.

Finally, sales growth, but with a twist. In textiles, revenue can rise simply because cotton got more expensive, with no extra volume at all. So the real question is whether sales growth is running ahead of the cotton price change, with volumes up.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: these rows group into spread (gross and operating margin), working capital (inventory and receivable days), cost structure (power and employees), survival (debt) and growth (sales).
  • What good looks like: the benchmark, and the only column with figures. Several rows give different marks for different doors: gross margin separates spinners from brands, operating margin lists spinners, exporters and brands, inventory days separates mills from brands, and employee cost separates spinners from garment makers. Always judge a company against its own door's mark.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest filings of listed textile companies in our database. Every row here has a median, because all eight numbers come straight from standard accounts.

A caution: the median blends spinners, exporters, integrated mills and brands, so it sits somewhere between their benchmarks. It is most useful as a cycle indicator. If the median operating margin is recovering, the industry is recovering.

The best way to use the table is a three-way comparison: the company's own number, the median and its door's good mark. The sales growth row deserves special attention. Compare a company's sales growth with the change in cotton prices over the same period. Growth that merely matches cotton inflation is price, not progress.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings for Indian textiles come from far away: American retailers' inventory reports, US customs data, the global cotton market, the monsoon map, oil prices and Chinese import statistics.

The furthest-reaching signals speak two quarters ahead. US retailers' inventory levels are the most important: lean shelves today mean fresh orders for Indian exporters in six months; bloated shelves mean another lean stretch. Monsoon and cotton sowing data tell you the size of the next crop, and so where cotton prices are heading.

One quarter ahead sits a cluster: US imports of textiles from India show order flow before company results; the global cotton price sets raw material costs and inventory gains or losses; crude oil moves polyester cost and the cotton-polyester balance; and China's yarn imports matter because China is a big buyer of Indian cotton yarn. The rupee works immediately.

Now the rule. This rule is stricter than most: it does not grade on a curve. An up-cycle needs three things together: open market access, Western retailers restocking, and Indian cotton no dearer than the world's. Today only one is in place. Market access has improved dramatically: the US tariff cut, the UK pact live, the EU deal concluded. But US orders are still soft, and Indian cotton is priced high.

So how does that square with a clock reading early up-cycle? The worst is behind the industry, and spinners' margins have recovered, but the full up-cycle the rule describes is not here yet. The access door has opened; customers have not yet walked through it.

Lower tariffs open the door. Only an American restock fills the order book.

That is why the call is cautiously positive, preferring integrated mills and exporters with UK and European reach over pure US home-textile names until US orders clearly recover.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter, far left: the rupee against the dollar, which changes exporters' rupee earnings immediately.
  • One quarter ahead: US imports of textiles from India, the global cotton price, crude oil and China's yarn imports. A busy middle that tells you about next quarter's margins and volumes.
  • Two quarters ahead, furthest right: US retailers' inventory levels and monsoon and cotton sowing. These are the earliest warnings, and the first is the one that will tell you when the exporters' recovery is coming.

Use the chart as a reading order. Start with US retailer inventories: if they are lean and falling, orders are coming. Then check the middle cluster for confirmation: rising US imports from India would be the first hard evidence.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means off, and the note gives today's state. Market access: a tick, with the US tariff cut and the UK pact live. Western restocking: a cross, US orders still soft. Competitive cotton: a cross, Indian cotton priced high. One tick out of three, which is why the call is cautious rather than outright positive.

The call box gives the direction, the points behind it and what would change it: a new US tariff increase or the interim deal collapsing, a cotton spike from a weak monsoon that mills cannot pass on, or a sharp rise in the rupee. Set an alert for each; any one of them would knock the early recovery back.
